author: Hector_Lenovo
text:
Hi ata03!
Welcome to Lenovo Community, and thank you for describing the issue so clearly. I understand how concerning an audible high-pitched noise can be, especially when it changes at 240Hz and with different on-screen content.
Based on what you described, that behavior does not sound typical for normal use, especially if the noise is clearly noticeable from the rear of the monitor and becomes more pronounced at the native 240Hz setting. Since you have already isolated several common variables by testing a separate wall outlet and observing how brightness, HDR, and image content affect it, this may require further investigation for possible hardware inspection or warranty review.
A few practical checks you can still try:
- Test the monitor at 240Hz with a different video cable if available.
- If possible, try another power cable that is known to be compatible with your setup.
- Check whether the sound changes when the monitor is disconnected from the source device but still powered on.
- If available, test with another source device to see whether the noise behavior remains the same.
If the sound stays very faint, brief, and only happens occasionally during load changes, it is often considered normal electrical behavior /
coil whine
.
At 240Hz, does the same high‑pitched whine occur if you switch from DisplayPort 1.4 to one of the monitor’s HDMI 2.1 ports using an HDMI cable? This can help determine whether the behavior is tied more closely to the connection path or to the monitor itself.
We will be waiting for your response.
Best regards,
Hector_Lenovo

source_title: 11-24-2026 08:06:18 Lenovo Legion 24-15 – High-Pitched Coil Whine at 240Hz (Color/Load Dependent) byata03inY Gaming Accessories & Curved Gaming Monitors Hello Lenovo Support Team, I recently purchased a Lenovo Legion 24-15 monitor, and I am experiencing>Here are my specific findings after troublesho
author: ata03
text:
Hello Lenovo Support Team,
I recently purchased a Lenovo Legion 24-15 monitor, and I am experiencing an audible high-pitched coil whine coming from the rear of the unit (near the power and DisplayPort input area) when running at its native 240Hz refresh rate.
Here are my specific findings after troubleshooting:
Refresh Rate Dependency: At 144Hz, the monitor is relatively silent. However, switching to 240Hz produces a noticeable high-pitched whine that is audible from a normal seating distance in a quiet room.
Color/Panel Load Pattern: At 240Hz, fullscreen pure black screens produce relatively little noise, whereas fullscreen solid RGB colors (Red, Green, or Blue) and bright/colorful desktop content immediately trigger and amplify the whine.
Setup & Verification: Tested via DisplayPort 1.4 and directly connected to a separate wall outlet. Adjusting brightness and disabling HDR slightly reduces the intensity, but the issue persists at 240Hz.
Could you please confirm whether this level of coil whine at 240Hz is considered within normal operating specifications for the Legion 24-15, or if it qualifies for a hardware inspection/replacement under warranty?
Thank you for your assistance.

author: Hassen_Lenovo
text:
Hello Nate23__,
Sorry you're experiencing this issue with your monitor.
Does the dimming occur with every game and content type on the PS5, or have you only noticed it with specific games after longer play sessions?
Since you've already performed factory resets, disabled HDR, Dolby Vision, OLED care options, and recalibrated HDR, try the following:
Test the monitor with another device such as a PC, laptop, or different console for an extended period to see whether the same dimming behavior occurs.
If available, switch to a different video input on the monitor and retest.
Try a different HDMI cable to rule out a signal-related issue.
For testing purposes, temporarily disable VRR and 120 Hz output on the PS5 and check whether the behavior changes at 60 Hz.
Leave the monitor at its default picture settings during testing and avoid enabling additional image enhancement features.
Observe whether the dimming appears across multiple games or only under specific conditions.
If the monitor behaves normally with other devices, that would help narrow the focus to the video signal configuration being used with the PS5. If the dimming also occurs with different devices, inputs, and cables, please let us know the results of those tests so we can continue troubleshooting with you.
Best regards,
Hassen_Lenovo

source_title: 索尼三星在OLED裡互相卡脖子，為什麼被海信從側面捅穿了？
author: @江南春观世界
text:
你说的没错，QD-OLED 和 Tandem（双层）WOLED 确实极大地解决了亮度和寿命问题，在手机和显示器上，OLED 绝对是目前的王者。但在电视这种动辄 75 寸、85 寸甚至 98 寸的巨幕市场，OLED 有一个绕不开的死穴——蒸镀工艺的有机材料极其昂贵，尺寸越大，良率越低，成本呈指数级飙升。
反观中国厂商主导的 Mini LED，本质上是沿用极其成熟的 LCD 产线，通过增加 LED 灯珠数量来提升画质。这等于用极低的边际成本，打出了接近 OLED 的效果。
所以，OLED 在“中小尺寸高端市场”是最优解；而 Mini LED 则是“超大尺寸大众市场”的版本答案。这不仅是利润的博弈，更是两条供应链的生死战。欢迎订阅频道，之后我会做更多不同面向的影片！

source_title: 索尼三星在OLED裡互相卡脖子，為什麼被海信從側面捅穿了？
author: @江南春观世界
text:
你说到最核心的痛点了！淘宝上 85 寸 TCL Mini LED 卖五千多，这个价格杀伤力太恐怖了。
索尼为什么“玩不下去”？因为电视市场的消费逻辑变了。大众消费者最直观的感受是“大就是爽”，而 OLED 有一个致命的物理限制：尺寸越大，成本呈指数级上升。大尺寸 OLED 面板产能几乎被 LG 和三星捏在手里，85 寸的 OLED 电视动辄两三万甚至更高，根本没法打。
反观中国品牌，靠着极其成熟的 LCD 面板产业链，加上 Mini LED 背光技术，硬生生把 85 寸、98 寸这种巨幕做成了平民价。当 85 寸 Mini LED 只要五千多的时候，绝大多数普通家庭根本不会去管什么是“纯黑位”、什么是“像素自发光”，大屏幕带来的视觉冲击力直接碾压了一切。
索尼的高溢价在这种“规模+供应链”的降维打击下，确实很难受。欢迎你订阅频道，之后我会做更多不同面向的影片！

source_title: 11-14-2026 20:34:34 ThinkVision P40WD-40 – split brightness/color display with macOS scaling and color errors bySelteinDisplays, Options and Accessories Good day, I am using a new Lenovo ThinkVision P40WD-40 with a new 14-inch MacBook Pro withDifferent display of the two halves of the screen At cert
author: Selte
text:
Good day,
I am using a new Lenovo ThinkVision P40WD-40 with a new 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 processor. Two display issues occur:
1. Different display of the two halves of the screen
At certain scaled resolutions, the monitor shows an exactly centered split: the two halves of the screen differ significantly in brightness or color saturation.
With the macOS setting “Default,” the split disappears.
It reappears as soon as I switch to the next higher scaling setting at 3200 × 1350.
The behavior occurs both via a direct HDMI connection and via the included Lenovo Thunderbolt 4 cable.
With HDR enabled, the left half sometimes appears heavily oversaturated, while the right half displays significantly paler colors.
2. Severe color distortions via Thunderbolt with HDR disabled
With the included Thunderbolt 4 cable, severe color distortions occur when HDR is turned off. App icons and images in PowerPoint show colorful color fringing, jagged edges, and distorted areas of color.
With HDR enabled, these artifacts largely disappear, but the colors appear excessively vivid. Correct color display was possible via HDMI; however, the scaling-dependent split described in point 1 also occurs there.
The errors are clearly visible in photos taken with the iPhone. Screenshots generated by the Mac, on the other hand, do not show the anomalies in the same way.
Measures already taken
Reset the monitor to factory settings
Completely disconnected the monitor from power and turned it back on
Tested different Thunderbolt ports on the MacBook
Tested a direct HDMI connection for comparison
Reduced the refresh rate to 60 Hz
Tested different scaling settings as well as HDR on/off
Checked the monitor color modes and macOS color profile
Updated macOS
The measures have not permanently resolved the issues. However, switching back to “Default” reliably eliminates the centered split—both via HDMI and via Thunderbolt.
Thank you very much for your support.
Kind regards, Andreas

text: @ZakariyaElBaghdadi Yes. And miniled is better than OLEDs actually, so never buy an OLED panel. What people don't mention is that OLEDs are unable to maintain display brightness. They are stuck to 220 nits paper white and midtones. IPS HDR can have 1000 nits paper white and maintain peak brightness of 2000 nits on the whole screen, while OLED is restricted to 2% of the screen's surface due to display overheating. Also, OLEDs make 30 fps gaming impossible. The instant pixel response time eliminates natural ghosting, which is the reason 30 fps looks buttery smooth when combined with heavy blur. OLED eliminates it and makes 30 fps look like 25 fps. Mini LED backlighting is in fact better than OLED.

text:
My 9 year old desktop bit the dust yesterday and I went over to bestbuy to take a look at what current gen PCs looked like across the range. I ended up finding this in an openbox container without a price tag. I never heard of this PC before then and just saw the SPEC sheet on the side. I was blown away as no other laptop in store had this spec sheet but also this item didnt have a price tag. I ended up having a cashier ring it up and CRAZY it was on discount for 1600 USD. I didnt even get to look at the laptop before taking the gamble of buying it on the spec sheet alone. Boy, was i surprised when i got home to unveil what I had just saved a fortune on. I still am in shock. I dont think it could have turned out any better. I havent been a laptop user in over a decade and just wanted to give it a go since its been a while and its been a dream. The GPU compares pretty closely to the 4070ti i had in my desktop but the CPU blows the 10 year old i7 I had out of the water. List price was 4099$ and out the door with a 2 year accidental damage package i spent 1800. 

TLDR: Check your local shops returns and open box sections, you could find a hell of a good deal in there.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @DylanNelUSA
text:
PRODUCT DETAILS
- Laptop Model: 
Lenovo - Legion 7i 16" 2.5k OLED Gaming Laptop - Intel Core Ultra 7 255HX 2025 - 32GB RAM - NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 - 1TB SSD - Glacier White
- Processor: Intel Core Ultra 7 255HX 2025


THE TECHNICAL DEFECT
I have had about 5 different laptops (HP Victus, being the best so far, but many other monster laptops too, and a few not so well spec’d laptops too) in the last 7 years 

Many issues with the Legion:
1.	This PC was stuck in dark mode. 6 hours of research, I finally found something called Burn Prevention which is found in Lenovo Vantage, and then hidden away. What this stupid setting does is override Windows setting and enforces dark mode.
2.	PC kept changing Outlook, Word, Excel settings back to default
3.	My Victus, I could connect a 4-in-1 4K USB C to Dual HDMI Adapter Hub 60Hz, Includes USB 3.0 & PD Port to the C Type Port, 2 screens + headphones connected to the Adaptor, then a fourth screen connected to HDMI (that would be PC screen (1), 2 through the adaptor and then a fourth through the HDMI. 
4.	This poor Legion will not allow a set up for 2 extra screens through the adaptor. Originally when purchased, it worked this way. But now, if I do somehow get this set up working, it will work for an hour or 2, but as soon as I open a PDF (for example), the system reverts back to 1 pc screen, and the 2 extra screens are now showing the same display. I then push W+K, go to settings, and screen 3 is not available there. Again, about 6 or 7 hours of reading done on this. I have not found a resolution.
5.	Today, all of a sudden, this laptop will not connect to my printer. All of my other laptops connect, not this one. I was previously connected, but now there are some how 2 drivers for the printer on this laptop, no clue how the second got there, and the printer will not connect, to this laptop only. It just loads the queue.

These are just a few of the issues, but If I can advise anyone wanting to purchase this laptop, I would say stay clear.

6.	Fans are always blasting away.
7.	Temp is always extremely high just below the screen (top of keyboard)
8.	Super slow at start up
9.	Take a second to realise what I am requesting, for example, open excel, it could take about 3 seconds to get the process started. The little men inside are too busy…. Doing nothing, I need to wake them up first.

These technical defects render a brand-new $1,700 premium laptop completely unusable for its intended purpose.

author: @fttmvp
text: I noticed the lenses in your glasses are decently thin. Is your prescription not very strong or are you using a high index plastic lens (1.61 +) or god forbid polycarbonate? If so I would definitely switch to aspheric Trivex lenses, or regular Trivex are just as good just not as flat. The aforementioned lenses have terrible abbe values and cause tons of fringing especially when looking at white text. Trivex has 43+ abbe value and is incredibly tough and versatile. I recently bought 4 pairs of glasses to run the experiment myself and the difference in clarity and comfort is huge when using a lens with a good abbe value.

text:
I can't agree with you on the QD issue. Sure, it's an inherent panel problem, but it's not really problematic?
I've been using my QD OLED (Samsung G8QNB) since it came out. It's only a 110 PPI monitor and even so, I don't have any issues with it. Yes, if you look very, very closely at just a wall of text you might notice some fringing. But NOT when working. It's really such a nanometer issue, that I truly don't see it while using the display. So I don't mean "comparing" it, or "testing" it, or "searching for issues" (as one understandably does when getting new hardware; I am the same in that regard!).
No issues in Windows, Word, Excel what have you. And yeah, like every normal person, I'm also using dark mode :P
So... try this technology for 1 week or something and you'll not have any issues with it (there are some text anti-aliasing settings in Windows. Having set that wrongly for a LCD screen will give you headaches though!).

I can't talk about W-OLED though. I've had it only for comparison for a few days...

source_title: Buying an OLED monitor in 2026 is insane - DON'T make my mistakes
author: @Tankie-comrade
text:
Maybe think with your brain and not your wallet next time?...
I went from a 24 inch 1080p IPS to a 27 inch 1440p 3rd gen QD-OLED and I did notice a slight increase in image clarity
In the first few days I used it, the text color fringing was noticeable, now I got used to it and it's a non-issue
Jokes on you, I used it on light mode for the first 2 months, after doing a power consumption test while displaying various shades of gray and different images, I realized I can halve the draw (and relax my eyes) by using dark colors, the color fringing doesn't bother me at all, and I code
Expecting a weirdly shaped subpixel layout on the OLED to perform like the RGB stripe one on the LCD is nuts
The only way to attack this problem is increasing PPI massively (either by shrinking the diagonal at the same resolution or by increasing the resolution above 4K at the same diagonal)
Also, do your research properly, on your own, about the tech, tech reviewers are salesmen with extra steps, WOLED has the issues it's plagued with due to the white subpixel and how it's powered relative to its siblings from other pixel column groups
Gray is a very difficult color to reproduce by any OLED due to how fine grained the pixel current control has to be for each subpixel
If you get a QD-OLED, you have to learn to accept purple-ish blacks in the day and minimize room brightness in the evening to truly enjoy the infinite contrast
With the currently available tech, QD-OLEDs can't get bright enough to overpower a polarizer layer and WOLED introduce such a big issue (banding, amongst others) to solve it
Maybe experiencing a 27 inch 1440p or 4K IPS would've changed my opinion on clarity, but the other issues an LCD has (uneven brightness (which leads to uneven colors), vignette effect, ghosting (which can be solved with BFI most manufacturers implement), gray blacks) are by far worse than the OLED downsides (of current gen panels, early adopters are scammed beta testers, it's the same for every new technology these days)

author: @tylerweigand8875
text:
I also did a lot of research before buying an OLED and had many of the same concerns as you did. I think it's the true the tech is not fully mature yet and they need to work out the issues, but my perspective after trying a 280hz tandem OLED is that at least for me, the benefits from OLED are so good that I can live with the issues. Picture quality, contrast ratio, and motion clarity is just so much better than any IPS I've tried. I was also eyeing mini-LEDs but quite frankly I was not that impressed by the one I tried, it only felt like a modest improvement over traditional LCDs whereas OLED actually feels like a true upgrade.

I also think I got somewhat lucky with my unit, as the grey banding is not noticeable except at pretty low greyscales so it's almost impossible for me to notice it during day to day use. The dirty screen effect is definitely there but given I used it mostly for games/videos and rarely for non-black static backgrounds it doesn't really bother me. If I got a bad unit I might be saying something totally different, though this is also why I made sure to purchase my monitor through a retailer that allows free 30-day returns.

Also glad you covered the text fringing issue because it's super true that there's really no good solution on windows. Even though tandem woled is better than qd-oled, there's still very visible text fringing issues on it. I spent quite some time wrangling with mactype tuner and better cleartype tuner and found that while mactype can fix the text rendering in certain apps, fixing it in some apps will also completely break text rendering in other apps so it's really not a viable solution. The tuning you can get from better cleartype tuner is too limited to truly fix the text rendering. Personally, I ended up just using greyscale rendering and living with the somewhat blocky text in some places because at least it gets rid of all the fringing everywhere and doesn't break text anywhere. I think this is all really a windows issue since windows text rendering is heavily optimized for RGB sub-pixels, but unfortunately if they never add support for other sub-pixel layouts this will remain an issue.

text:
Hello
Sarker_Shuvo

If reinstalling the Integrated Monitor does not help, the next things to check would be the display and graphics drivers.
In Device Manager, try uninstalling the Intel UHD Graphics driver (check
Delete the driver software for this device
if available), then restart and install the Intel graphics driver provided for your model from the Lenovo support page. Brightness control on the internal display is typically handled through the integrated graphics driver, so a driver issue can cause the slider to move without any actual brightness change.
Since you are currently on BIOS R3CN39WW and a newer R3CN44WW version is available, it may also be worth updating the BIOS. BIOS updates can include fixes related to hardware control and device compatibility.
If the issue persists, boot into the BIOS setup and check whether the display appears to remain at a fixed brightness there as well. If brightness cannot be adjusted even outside of Windows, that could help determine whether the issue is software-related or related to the display hardware/firmware.
You can also test whether the problem occurs in Safe Mode. If brightness control works there, it would further point toward a driver or software conflict in Windows.
Just to confirm, did the brightness controls work normally when the system was new, or did the issue start after a Windows update, driver update, or BIOS update? Also, are you using the original Lenovo graphics drivers or drivers installed directly from Intel/NVIDIA?
Best regards,
Hassen_Lenovo

source_title: 10-08-2026 01:13:42 Monitor screen blanks for a few seconds bylevidinGaming Laptops Lenovo Legion Pro 7 connected to an external screen. USB-C connection to external monitor and hub HDMI connection to HDR externalmonitor Updated all software and drivers; tried changing power settings. Replies(2/2)
author: Hassen_Lenovo
text:
Hello levid,
Welcome to the Lenovo Community, and sorry you're experiencing this issue.
Since the black screen occurs on both the built-in display and an external monitor, and you've already tested two different connection methods (USB-C and HDMI), it sounds less likely to be an issue with a specific monitor or cable.
When both screens go black, does audio continue playing and the system remain responsive, or does it appear the entire system briefly freezes?
Please try the following:
Update both the integrated graphics driver and NVIDIA graphics driver from the Lenovo Support website for your Legion Pro 7, or check for available updates through Lenovo Vantage.
Check in Lenovo Vantage for any BIOS or chipset updates that may be available.
If HDR is enabled on the external display, temporarily disable it and test for a period of time.
If your model supports GPU working modes in
Lenovo Vantage
, test whether the behavior changes in Hybrid Mode versus dGPU Mode, restarting after each change.
Open Event Viewer and check for any Display, nvlddmkm, or graphics-related warnings/errors around the time the screens go black.
If you're using a dock or hub with the USB-C setup, temporarily connect the monitor directly to the laptop and test again.
The answer to the question above may help determine whether this is a display signal interruption or whether Windows itself is briefly becoming unresponsive.
Best regards,
Hassen_Lenovo

source_title: 10-08-2026 01:13:42 Monitor screen blanks for a few seconds bylevidinGaming Laptops Lenovo Legion Pro 7 connected to an external screen. USB-C connection to external monitor and hub HDMI connection to HDR externalmonitor Updated all software and drivers; tried changing power settings. Replies(2/2)
author: Sharan2050
text:
Both screens going black at once, across two different connection types, usually means the GPU driver is resetting or the system is switching graphics modes. It's unlikely to be a cable, hub, or monitor problem.
Check what Windows logged
Open Event Viewer → Windows Logs → System and look for events at the moments of the blackouts. "Display driver nvlddmkm stopped responding and has successfully recovered" (Event 4101) confirms a GPU driver reset. Messages about a display or power transition point to mode switching instead. This tells you which of the fixes below to focus on.
Most likely fixes, roughly in order
Change the GPU mode.
The Legion Pro 7 has a MUX switch. In Legion Space, Vantage, or the BIOS, try Discrete GPU mode instead of Hybrid/Advanced Optimus (or the reverse if you're already on Discrete). Hybrid mode switching is a very common cause of both screens blanking, especially with external monitors. A reboot is required after changing it.
Turn off variable refresh and HDR as a test.
Disable G-Sync in the NVIDIA Control Panel and turn off HDR and Auto HDR in Windows Settings → System → Display. Set both screens to a fixed refresh rate. HDR and VRR renegotiation between the monitor and GPU often causes brief blackouts.
Do a clean driver install.
Run Display Driver Uninstaller (DDU) in Safe Mode, then install the latest NVIDIA driver from NVIDIA directly. Updating over the old driver can leave bad settings behind. If the problem started after a recent driver update, try the previous version.
Disable Multiplane Overlay (MPO).
This is a known cause of brief black flickers on NVIDIA systems with multiple displays. NVIDIA has published a registry fix, and a quick search for "disable MPO NVIDIA registry" will show it.
Turn off hardware-accelerated GPU
scheduling in Settings → System → Display → Graphics → Default graphics settings.
Reset any GPU tuning
. If you've overclocked or undervolted the GPU or used a Legion performance preset, return everything to stock. Unstable clocks can cause driver resets.
Update the BIOS
and EC from Lenovo's support page, since Legion BIOS releases often include display and MUX fixes.

source_title: HDR Dimming Issue on Lenovo Legion Pro, Can't Update Firmware 27Q-10
author: Phobsen
text:
Hello everyone!
I bought this monitor in January of this year.
The faulty firmware of this monitor makes it unusable, especially in HDR mode.
I run the monitor in the certified True Black 400 mode, and even here it is aggressively dimmed after 30–60 minutes.
It stays in this state until the input signal is changed, the monitor is turned off/on, or the driver is reset via a key combination. This dimming is normally desired with still images or an unmoving picture to protect the monitor; however, it should be lifted again as soon as motion on the screen is detected, and that does not happen here.
This is clearly due to faulty safety mechanisms within the firmware!
To this day, Lenovo has not managed to provide a firmware update, so the monitor is being returned today.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @Silece88
text:
The last hardware upgrade with a comparable impact was the switch from HDDs to SSDs. Moving to an OLED Display is an even bigger leap forward than most people realize, especially because of the motion clarity and near-instant response times.

People are always ready to drop thousands on a new GPU or CPU just to satisfy the itch for top-tier performance, but then they run it on a subpar VA panel. They spend a fortune for the "ultimate" visuals, completely ignoring that their monitor is the real bottleneck.

It’s not even just about image quality or contrast - it’s about how it actually feels in action. OLED delivers lightning-fast response times with zero motion blur, no ghosting, and no smearing. When you're using a mouse, that instant responsiveness makes the cursor and camera movement feel uniquely direct in a way you just can't even get on a OLED TV with a controller. For PC players it's easily the most impactful hardware upgrade of recent years.

author: @youplaycomputer
text:
將色彩完全恢復為系統預設值的操作步驟：

按 Win + R 輸入 colorcpl 打開「色彩管理」。

在「裝置」頁面選取你的螢幕，找到剛產生的 ICC 校正檔並點擊「移除」（或取消勾選「在此裝置使用我的設定」）。

或切換至「進階」頁面，點擊左下角的「重設為系統預設值」即可。

author: @Case_
text: Mactype doesn't just allow greyscale font smoothing, it more importantly also allows you to define your own subpixel layout (essentially any subpixel layout, see Freetype 2 documentation), at least in recent versions. The problem with Mactype however is that it's best at hooking into the old GDI font rendering and struggles (not for any fault of its own, it's just much harder or almost impossible to do) with the newer DirectWrite rendering that is used more and more in Windows, most notably in browsers. So its usability is limited.

text: Unfortunately nothing helped, but I switch the HDR mode to Photo and then back to Auto and it resets, so I don’t have to turn the monitor off and back on. I think it’s a monitor software issue.

source_title: 09-30-2026 14:26:11 Re:Lenovo Legion Pro 32ud10 Brightness dimming byHector_LenovoinGaming Desktops Since changing the monitor HDR mode from Photo back to Auto restores the brightness, the issueis most likely happening in the monitor’s HDR/image processing rather than normal Windows brightnessAs for
author: Hector_Lenovo
text:
Hi HuniKha!
Thank you for reaching out to the Lenovo Community. Sorry to hear about your experience and I understand the concern with your external monitor brightness dimming after some time, especially since it returns when you power the monitor off/on or toggle HDR.
Since the brightness returns when you power the monitor off and on, or when you toggle HDR, the best path is to check the display and graphics settings in order.
1. First, turn off any automatic brightness controls on your laptop:
- Open Settings > System > Display.
- Look for Brightness settings and turn off Adaptive brightness, Change brightness automatically, or similar power-saving dimming options if present.
- If your system has HDR enabled, turn HDR off temporarily and test the monitor for more than 40 minutes.
2. Check the external monitor’s own on-screen menu:
- Disable any setting such as Dynamic Contrast / DCR, Auto HDR, Eco Mode.
- If the monitor has a local dimming or automatic power-saving feature, turn that off as well.
3. Reseat the video connection:
- Disconnect and reconnect the cable on both ends.
- If possible, test with a different cable.
- If available, try another port type such as HDMI instead of USB-C/DisplayPort, or vice versa.
4. Check refresh rate and HDR format:
- Go to Settings > System > Display > Advanced display.
- Select the external monitor and test a standard refresh rate such as 60 Hz.
- If HDR is enabled, test with HDR off first. If the issue stops, it is likely related to the HDR handshake or display processing.
5. Isolate whether the issue is with the monitor or the laptop:
- Test the same monitor with another computer for at least 40 minutes.
- If the dimming still happens, the monitor is likely causing it.
- If it only happens with your laptop, the issue is more likely related to the laptop’s graphics settings, driver, or signal output.
If you’ve already tried different cables and HDR settings, let us know your monitor connection type (HDMI, USB-C, or DisplayPort) and whether the dimming happens only on the external monitor or also on your laptop screen if you're using one.
We will be waiting for your response.
Best regards,
Hector_Lenovo

author: Hector_Lenovo
text:
Thanks for the update!
1. On the monitor OSD, switch from HDR Auto/Movie/Photo (Peak 1000) to another HDR mode if available, especially True Black 400, then test for at least 40 to 60 minutes. If the dimming only happens in Peak 1000 modes, that helps isolate the issue to that HDR mode behavior.
2. In Windows, turn HDR off, restart the PC, then turn HDR back on and set the monitor as the only active display during testing. If you use multiple monitors, disconnect the others temporarily to rule out HDR mode negotiation issues.
3. Set the refresh rate to a standard test value such as 144 Hz or 120 Hz at the monitor’s native resolution, then retest HDR. This helps check whether the issue is tied to the current high-bandwidth display setting.
4. If you are using any graphics software features such as Auto HDR, RTX HDR, AMD video enhancements, dynamic contrast, content-adaptive brightness, or color enhancement, disable them and test again. Also leave Windows HDR/SDR balance at the default position during testing.
5. Reset the monitor OSD settings to factory defaults, then enable HDR again and test only one HDR picture mode at a time. Do not enable additional image enhancements while testing.
6. Install Lenovo Artery if you have not already, and check whether the monitor is detected there. If available, confirm the current monitor software or driver package shown by the app and apply any offered monitor-related update from within the app rather than through manual Have Disk installation. You can download the tool
here
.
7. About the file you downloaded: the .inf package is a monitor driver/extension package, not the same as a direct firmware flash utility. If Windows reports that the folder does not contain a compatible driver, perhaps you can try extracting both x64 and x86 folder file to Desktop then try again.
Best regards,

text:
Thanks for getting back to us
mjeshurun
,
What you are describing sounds more like an installation/alignment issue than a broken screw, especially since it happened on two new units.
Please try this in order:
1. Remove the webcam completely and inspect the mounting area on the monitor and the webcam attachment point. Make sure there is no protective film, packing material, or insert blocking the mount.
2. Position the webcam exactly as shown in the setup guide and seat it fully before turning the locking screw. The screw usually will not extend or catch correctly unless the webcam is properly aligned in the mounting slot first.
3. When tightening, turn the screw gently clockwise only after the webcam is sitting flush. Do not force it with a screwdriver at first.
4. If it still does not catch, back it off completely, reseat the webcam, and try again while applying light inward pressure so the threads can engage.
5. If the screw spins freely even when the webcam is correctly seated, avoid forcing it further with a screwdriver, as that can damage the mount.
Since you already saw the same behavior on two units, the most practical next step is to have the seller or
technical support
physically verify the webcam mounting method as they can confirm whether the webcam module or mount is faulty. If possible, ask them to test with another webcam from the same model in front of you. You can contact the technical support at 1-809-456-979 and their operating hours are 8:00 -18:00 Sunday - Thursday.
Best regards,
Adriel_Lenovo

author: Hector_Lenovo
text:
Hi Angelo1234!
Thank you for reaching out to the Lenovo Community. I understand you’d like to restore your factory color profile after a fresh Windows installation.
To try to restore your factory color profile after the fresh Windows install, follow this order:
1. Turn off HDR in Windows first.
Go to Settings > System > Display > HDR and make sure HDR is off.
2. Install all Lenovo updates before reinstalling X-Rite.
Open Lenovo Vantage and install all available updates, especially display, chipset, and related system updates. Restart the laptop after updates finish.
3. Remove X-Rite completely.
Go to Settings > Apps > Installed apps, uninstall X-Rite Color Assistant, then restart your device.
4. Reinstall X-Rite Color Assistant.
Install it again using the Lenovo-provided version for your device, then restart once more and test the app.
5. In X-Rite, try restoring the profile.
Open X-Rite Color Assistant and go to Settings > Restore profiles.
6. If the profile is still missing, run the profile recovery tool.
Browse to C:\Program Files (x86)\X-Rite Color Assistant\ and run ProfileUpdaterForDisplayReplacement.exe. Keep your laptop connected to the internet and follow the prompts.
7. If setup still fails, check for software conflict.
Make sure no other color calibration or display tuning software is installed, then try again after a clean boot.
Please share the model type that would look like 81C70000RK or 20UD000BUS from the sticker underneath, Vantage, or by typing sysinfo using Windows search so we can check the exact model and specifications.
We will be waiting for your response.
Best regards,
Hector_Lenovo

source_title: Lenovo - Legion Pro 27Q-10 Longterm review ("don't do it!"); incredible MOTION RESOLUTION.
author: @whitedragem
text:
Yes, different manufacturers can really go the distance for 'better products', and some- its like they never had 'real world testing'.

OLEDs at max brightness (a value that changes based on screen content/'average picture level'), can really etch a pixel into a users' brain.. 

eg this lenovo HDR monitor has a white text branding /logo that takes up part of the screen, but is introduced to screen over a 'few frames'; and its brightness value varies in stages as it renders this.

Shows 'nobody cares'; just a logo and we have to have it..
But for end users;?
Partner hates this OLED so much due to 'bedroom' time..
It lights the space like a lamp and the values vary "too much".
A system reboot (randomly required by techs like myself when doing stuff), will have this monitor "light house'" my sleeping space before settling to users preferences..

And it's sleep timeouts seem built to coincide with large signal handshaking times, this thing will happily do a few power cycles to rapify its product lifecycle to the trash can (it is, after all, 'Lenovo').

The irony that I replaced a 27"OLED with a 65" Samsung LCD.. (VA panel, 'quantum dot').
Samsungs quantum dot panel has such great backlight bleed control that blacks are black, and even though only 'single array' dimming; has exceptional screen brightness control and goes brighter and has better OLED range and pop.

Sure the Samung TV, on clearance, cost more.. (and is still junk from a manufacturer who builds for the scrap heap!)
But, menus and TV/monitor panel logic should be set in concrete by now; we have had decades to master this stuff.
My 35year+ ancient JVC TV cpuld rename inputs inside of twenty second.. (first time might take a minute to learn), that Samsung TV? Took minutes ad required help even though it has a graphical menu system, hi res, and lots of text.. just didnt care about 'end user' expereince..

Complex products?
Hardly..
Just not well thought out.

source_title: HDR Dimming Issue on Lenovo Legion Pro, Can't Update Firmware 27Q-10
author: mudamuda
text:
My Legion Pro 27Q-10 QD-OLED monitor has an issue in the HDR Auto/Movie/Photo (Peak 1000) modes, where after 30-40 minutes of use the monitor dims permanently until I turn it off and on again. This is not because of ABL, if I pause a scene and turn it off/on in the same scene, the brightness immediately restores and the difference is obvious.
I tried installing the firmware using the steps provided on the site, but it fails the same as it does for everyone else using this monitor, per complaints on this forum and Reddit, since the provided files are not actual firmware updates but a Dolby Vision extension.
Please, Lenovo, upload the proper updated firmware files for this monitor.
This is on the Legion Pro 27Q-10 True Black 400 QD-OLED.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @NickFje
text:
OLED is so great for gaming, burn in is not much of an issue anymore. Only the most extreme usage with high brightness on static content will cause it nowadays.
When I got my first QD OLED which had a 3rd gen samsung panel I played Arc Raiders for hundreds of hours at max brightness without doing much else inbetween and even then there was not any visible image retention on hud elements.

Now I have a LG C6 Tandem OLED tv as a monitor and it features even better protections against burn in, much higher brightness and better color volume. The estimated half life of the pixels on single layer oled models is 50 000 - 100 000 hours according to the pace the pixels degrade on Rtings tests.
This means if you treat your display well and we assume the panel lasts for 50 000 hours it will last 17 years if you use it 8 hours every single day. Tandem OLED degrades at roughly half the rate so that is over 30 years before the pixels is at 50% brightness compared to new. It does not mean 30 years without image retention or burn in but it will take a very long time and that tv/monitor would likely be replaced way before you get issues.

With this display I get the same brightness and even more than some mini led monitors I have owned while retaining the perfect black levels and the superior motion clarity. Other display technologies are too slow when it comes to pixel response time. They don't change colors nearly as fast as the panels refresh rate.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @CalamityStarForce
text:
I finally got my first QD-OLED (a Samsung G50SF) a few days ago and I have to say, you are spot on.  I have only ever had LED monitors before this.  

Today my friend was over playing Pal World with me on another PC in my office and he audibly gasped when he looked back over his shoulder at my screen after playing a while on the other monitor.  Looking back and forth between the screens, it was apparent on my new OLED that the accuracy of the colors, the smoothness of the motion, and sharpness of the contrast made the game look like it was exploding out of my screen.  

In comparison, his older LED screen made the game look washed out, blurry, and desaturated, akin to the difference between a clean monitor and a super duper dusty screen.  I honestly didn't know how much of the color gamut and finer details of the image being rendered was lost just to the nature of the screens I had been playing on.  It feels like I am truly seeing games and other media as they were meant to be seen for the first time.  Simply dragging windows between my new monitor and my other two LED screens has become a geek out moment.  

I have also been playing all the Resident Evil games recently and this OLED takes the horror to the next level.  Hearing a zombie growl and seeing something form itself out of the inky black beyond my flashlight is insanely immersive.  I can never go back...

author: @jimmy92goodwin
text:
If you're wanting 95% of the OLED experience without the burn-in possibility at all (I do 8 hours of productivity use for every 2 hours of gaming) I can't recommend enough the 32" 4K 144hz Mini-LED monitor - Philips Evnia 32M2N6800M.

It has 1152 individual zones for backlighting so like OLED can switch off entirely for inky blacks, vibrant colours and punchy contrast etc. It has 1500 nit max HDR brightness but even SDR is about 1200 nits max (even with direct sunshine in the room it's still able to go too bright for comfort haha) and the response time is tested by YouTube channels at 2.3ms which is insanely fast compared to the real world 8ms average of a lot of gaming monitors. I don't see any smearing at all like I used to, colours are unreal, the clarity is actually ridiculous too.

I'm not saying it's better than OLED before people feel tribally attacked, I'm just saying it's an unbelievably brilliant monitor at £500/$700 and I work all day not remotely concerned about static elements, I don't need pixel refresh cycles in the middle of games and can use this for 10 years without the concerns of long term burn-in.

I couldn't be happier with this purchase and have now had 3 friends buy this exact one after seeing mine. It feels like I own an OLED so I relate to basically every statement of joy in this video!

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @hugevibez
text: It's not an extra layer of quantum dots, it's that the color filter is made out of quantum dots for red and green and because the light source is blue for that subpixel color you have just a hole. This is an improvement over LG's WOLED that uses white light with a white subpixel that boosts brightness, but what you get is when you measure the display using a spectrograph (to get a waveform of the colors of the light) is that this white light washes the light output together whereas with QD-OLED you get very pure peaks of R, G and B. Though phone/tablet/handheld/laptop screens are even better because they don't use a color filter at all and having individual emitters per subpixel which gets you even tighter peaks per color. LCD TVs often apply a quantum dot enhancement film to improve color performance, but that is not the case here. A quick 2 minute Google search could have told you that information

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @Solus793
text:
Effectively infinite contrast is great sure, but this isn't anything new. We already had plasma displays that could do the same decades ago.
I've been using OLED displays for over 14x years already and can't wait to move on to something better.

OLEDs are far from display nirvana. They suffer from panel uniformity issues and artifacts, noise/dithering and poor gradation near black.

They're also a sample & hold based technology, so the motion clarity is always going to be bad without BFI at a very high panel framerate, since OLEDs are self-emissive you can't just strobe the backlight like with an LCD whose light source can be addressed independently.

Yes I know someone is going to say "oh but OLED has instant pixel response, how can you say that!1!", this is not relevant - learn how the human visual system works, even at 240 Hz just pan around in an FPS game and it's a blurry mess.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @Square_Penix
text: Hi, Principal Research Scientist here, I have a PhD in Materials Science and Engineering and create these technologies. I’m happy you’re loving OLED and I’d really encourage you to look into RGB Mini LED. Burn in is not so much an issue as peak HDR brightness is. Most games are graded to 1000 nits or above brightness and QD-OLED can’t sustain this level on a full screen window. OLED also loses peak brightness very quickly and permanently. Your monitor won’t be nearly as bright year 2 as it is year 1. This is an issue because the starting brightness is already low. It looks nice to you due to the contrast but RGB Mini LED achieves this as well but at higher peak brightness levels. Enjoy your screen for the time being but I’d recommend RGB Mini LED instead! Once other tech like Q-DEL and MicroLED take off, OLED will be dead as there will be no advantages to owning a low lifespan piece of tech

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @thenonexistinghero
text:
The thing with most of these OLED fanboys is... that they do not have any experience whatsoever with MiniLED other than watching it in a store with basically the worst viewing conditions.
That said, if you're using a TV as a monitor, a good MiniLED is great. No risk of burn-in and it gets brighter as well. Black levels are very close to OLED, but there may be some blooming (and how much depends on the MiniLED. Something like the Bravia 9 has pretty much none for most part, but something like one of those cheaper bright HiSense or TCL TV's go for extra brightness at the cost of having some blooming).

If you intend to buy a monitor... well, MiniLED monitors are still quite a bit behind their TV counterparts in terms of display quality. But you do get a higher refresh rate. Well, OLED monitors are behind as well compared to their TV's, but not as much. And if you're sitting up close to a monitor, the flaws of MiniLED and strength of OLED will be quite noticeable.

But OLED still hasn't solved burn-in. If you like to pump up your brightness and use your monitor or TV a lot, it's probably best to avoid OLED because it'll get burn-in in about 2-3 years. If you're more of a casual user and are willing to turn down the settings, OLED is a good choice. As for me, I expect my expensive displays to be a work horse, not a prancing horse. Spending big bucks on an expensive display only to use it with half of its potential 90% of the time? To me that's a waste of money.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @whitedragem
text:
I've bought a few 'reference OLEDs' (flagship/top tier panels, used by Hollywood for colour grading etc), and kept them calibrated -as every six months the green, red and blue channels all wear out at different rates, and hence need 'slight' adjustment to maintain perfect colour...

As an advocate for OLED since inception, "now"?

No way!
Never suffered burn in; lived on reference plasma panels 'for years'; not an issue (but I do limit my sources, ie no Wonderboy with bright red hearts in corner of screen entire game..

For me, someone who owns a third generation quantum dot panel (akin to the one used for the above video), a Quantum Dot 'upper tier' LCD TV is amazing.
Quality of the quantum dot layer matters; eg hisense/tcl is budget quantum dot (not very good), whereas Samsung top tier quantum dot is awesome.

Using "a shitty sidelit" (one zone) Samsung Quantum Dot TV; the ability for Quantum Dots to control backlight bleed, ad hence the bugbear of 'cheaper LCDs'; is incredible.

dialing down the absolute brightness a bit, the colour responce in HDR, at high brightness is insanely good.


vs my tiny 280hz Lenovo OLED monitor, the 165hz Samsung 'the frame' TV, at 65" diagonal and sub 10ms (8.1ms) time for render to screen (better than most LG OLED TVs at 9ms).. playing in an ultrawide resolution on a screen so big O can use a steering wheel and it feel like it is 'in a car'.

size matters.
a lower nit brightness 'capable' screen is bright when we factor the actual screen real estate.

(is why cinema at 100nits is BRIGHT!)

Samsung the frame, bought for near equal money to a budget 32"OLED monitor; depends on game genre..

I'd take a 240hz OLED over a 340hz LCD (true) -for online competitive gaming,..
but-
for offline play or solo play or story games (etc etc),.. big wins out.

colour and contrast is what matters most (our eyes have rods and cones, we see 'colour and contrast'), then motion resolution..

pixel structure maybe (desktop publishing and productivity)..("legibility of fonts")..

and the big TV feel is hard to beat.
sadly OLED is premium market space and so has traditionally been paired with great motion picture processing (price war dictates that is starting to slide and sort the wheat from the chaff)..
some LCDs, like Samsung the frame, get top tier pocessing AND quantum dot fidelity regarding controlling backlight bleed'

latest models now process picture (near) equal to Sony and Panasonic picture processing. (reference/'the best').

I was surprised when a budget Samsung TV, less than the cost of a gaming console (sale time), and bang to buck is hard to beat.

I literally moved OFF an OLED (my fourth!) to 'go LCD'.

pricepoint dictates feature capability.
the Frame TV I refer to wpuld NEVER have made my shopping shortlist (based on spec sheet and internet reviewers).. but three days of using it, when setup correctly;

colour fidelity and motion processing matter.
"may paths to the summit".
(I lost viewing angle and 'absolute black' value)(,gained massive screen size, flexibility (eg 21:9 mode) and brightness and colour!!, daytime viewing etc)

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @exlibrisas
text:
I'm one of the weird people, who can easily switch between OLED and IPS without whining. My PC is connected to two setups: ultra wide IPS (with additional monitors) and right behind the wall - C3 setup for gaming in bed with either a controller or laptop bed tray and wireless M&K. I play different games on these setups. My IPS has "game color" mode increased (vibrancy and contrast). Within reason, of course, oversaturation is not good. DLDSR+DLSS looks amazing. Vibrant, lively colors, ultrawide form factor and completely jaggyless geometry because of DLDSR pixel density. And then it's OLED times: HDR and inky blacks, large screen. I switch between two setups with no issue. Console like titles are great for a TV. Shooters, RPGs and everything, that requires to look at small details, goes to my monitor. For example, for some reason, HDR is broken on an OLED for KCDII and it looks not so good. But on my IPS monitor, pixel density and vibrant colors make forests and plants pop, even without HDR. Or E33 is the opposite: RTX HDR makes this game take my breath away on my TV, but looks not so impressive on a monitor. 
So I switch between and it works well.

@haewymetal OLED are supposed to have perfect black but instead you get VRR flickering in dark scenes that completely ruins the experience. IPS VRR flicker is imperceptible, I haven't ever seen any sort of VRR flickering on IPS unlike OLED. Its getting better but this tech isn't mature yet enough with too many downsides including worse motion blur reduction with BFI that cuts refresh rate by half, regular motion with VRR a good IPS with variable OD isn't that far behind OLED with fast motion.

Burn in is still an issue because of how the chemical reactions that turn voltage into light are limited, you can add more reactions or lower the reaction rate but there is still a limit. If you can't use a monitor normally with static UI without worrying about burn in then its shit. If you have more money than sense which these OLED manufacturers are banking on then its a great purchase but if you have a brain and research you quickly find out its not that big of a leap, most of these techtubers are paid for their opinions and they just end up parroting Reddit comments or AI prompts because they have no clue how the tech actually works.

author: @DeagleIsL1fe
text:
I got my Acer Predator 1440p 240hz QD-OLED monitor 5 days ago. And wow, it's insane. Going from my old 1080p TN panel feels crazy, I thought it looked good but now I think my old monitor sucks lmao. The MOST insane thing about it is that it only costs $315, yes $315. 3 years ago I used to dream of being able to afford one, and here we are.

And to be honest, I don't even notice really any of the flaws people keep mentioning. Everyone always talks about text fringing, brightness, and burn in but those just aren't a problem, at least not on this monitor. I don't notice the text fringing like 90% of the time, this thing gets BRIGHT, also 1000 nit peak, and it literally hurts my eyes to play at HDR max brightness, so I don't understand the complaint there. It also has a bunch of tools to prevent burn in, as well as being a 3rd gen panel meaning it's more resistant anyway, and a 3 year burn in warranty because why not. 

If you're thinking of buying an OLED but you're scared of the potential cons, I wouldn't be. Hearing all of these "issues" online almost made me not buy one, but man I'm glad I did lol.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @joelrodriguez9611
text: @Parthurnax52  It's not a matter of visual quality but of resfresh rate that the Dual mode exists, those panels can do +240 hz but due to signal bandwith can only do it in FHD. Monitor scaling algorithms (not to be confused with upscaling like DLSS/FSR) will hamper quality when in non-native resolution unless it's mathematically pixel perfect as you already explained. The quality loss does not apply to FHD in an UHD monitor, regardless of dual mode feature or not. My old UHD monitor panel can only do 144 Hz so there was no point on featuring a dual mode back then because PC's of the time were able to run e-sports @ UHD +144 fps, and the DP v1.4 port allows to UHD 120Hz which is pretty close. Nowadays, PC's can run e-sports @ +240 fps or more, the panels are able to run twice as fast than mine, but the conectivity is still DP v1.4 (just check the link left in the description and see yourself). Dual mode is the response to such limitation, you trade resolution bandwith for refresh rate bandwith so those extra 120 Hz of the panel you worked so hard to buy doesn't go to waste.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @Parthurnax52
text: ​ @joelrodriguez9611 If your view 1080p content on a native 4k display, it will look worse than on a native 1080p display. That's why these monitors have the option to display native 1080p. It is possible because 4k has exactly 4 times the pixel count. It is achieved by combining 4 pixels into 1 so that 1080p content can look like on a native 1080p display.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @joelrodriguez9611
text: @Parthurnax52  Mine doesn't have it due to age, and it is a matter of setting the render resolution in games to 50 or manually lowering to 1080p. After all, if I have to go a lower resolution, it is because I can't fullfill the monitor (144hz in my case, 165hz on new ones) at 2160p. The dual mode is nice because of that extra boost in framerate but it isn't a must unless you play games like CS2 or Valorant (low settings) and you can render the game at +300 fps to take advantage of it.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @Joakim.Bengtsson
text:
QD-OLED has triangular subpixel layout. This causes fuzzy text rendering.
Most WOLED are RGBW, which also causes fuzzy text rendering.

WOLED with RGB-stripe subpixel layout works well for text rendering and gives you a high color brightness (but not  as many colors as QD-OLED).

I think QD-OLED still has higher burn-in risk than WOLED with RGB-stripe subpixel layout, correct me if I am wrong.

I have a QD-OLED TV and a LCD computer monitor with 3000:1 contrast ratio. A high contrast ratio on a non-oled monitor looks rather decent, but OLED is indeed better.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @SparkerR1987
text:
I bought the F048U oled and used it for a year. Ended up going back to my CRT. Oleds are the closest thing to a CRT by far, but they still have blur due to sample and hold. The fast pixel response time only makes the frame stay on the screen even longer, causing even more blur in motion. They need to ditch sample and hold and do scanning like a CRT. Nvidia recently created pulsar to mimick a CRT but sample and hold is still at the root of how the image is drawn.

CrT at 160hz is much much clearer in notion than a 540hz oled.

text: I just don't get it. I bought OLED monitor expecting to be blown away, but its honestly nothing special. People always fall for all sorts of hype and everything is amazing and life changing for them. Few things are in reality. OLED has massive drawbacks in daily use such as burn in and flicker. No OLED monitor is flicker free. Source of the flicker is adaptive refresh rate, the fix is to turn it off. source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @IlsuemOkosch196
text:
Burn in's are arguments of people who don't wanna accept OLED is taking over the screen world.
I have one of the first gaming monitor OLEDs, from LG.
I have exactly 9717 hours at this moment writing it (it shows in the OSD of the screen). ZEEEEEEROO burn in. I am basically hardcore using it every day for hours for years, because I turned into a unemployed no-lifer, do to certain circumstances.
And as I said, I have zero burn in.
The only thing I would look out on OLEDs is vertical striping. Mine has a little of it. And no, it didn't disappear as everyone claims online, over time. I also actually sent the first one back, after testing it because of heavy vertical striping. The second one I received wasn't as bad, but still slightly noticeable in dark grays. Sadly they claimed they tested it, so they didn't accept another refund. So I was sticking with it. I do barely notice it, and I am overall still pretty happy with it. The response time, the clean colors and blacks, is just way too good, compared to a VA panel or many others.
So, yeah I can definitely recommend it, but, please don't believe people online saying vertical striping will go away after few hundred hours. If you are not daily playing, you might sit out your guarantee and can't refund anymore, as soon as you realize, it doesn't actually disappear. If your monitor has heavy vertical striping, give it back to them, let them replace it. It's nothing you need to accept or should. But just know, depending on where you buy you might not be able to resend it 3 times, if all your products end up having it.

I think it was a little bit of a issue of early OLEDs, because my buddy recently got a new one from MSI and doesn't have any striping at all. At least, nothing he notices (he might be blind for it you know, since he has glasses lol).
But I do think it was a little weakness of one of the first OLEDs ever on the market.

But yeah, once you own some OLED monitor for gaming, you never go back, trust me.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @scudo5242
text: You forgot to mention one important thing. You don't see burn-in on them because they have an image cleaning feature. It works by having the software degrade all the healthy pixels down to the level of the ones that have already burned in. As a result, the entire display degrades evenly, rather than just a specific part like the taskbar. Even though these monitors don't have static artifacts burned into them, their colors and contrast are already much worse than when they were brand new

This is so true. I have a 5700x3d and 7800 xt setup and i plan to move to AM5 and at least a 5070 or 9070xt, but I would have to pull out lots of money given the ram crisis. I saw the Gigabyte GO27Q24G, a budget 3rd gen WOLED at 240 hz. I specifcally chose this than QD OLED due to better black handling on bright room and more resistant glossy screen. QD Oleds at 400-500 dollars are just scratch magnets. I know newer but more expensive models have better coating, but at this price range, WOLED is better.

author: @roebucksruin
text:
I have a 39" 1440p OLED using an older WOLED panel. I write code 10+ hours a day in dark mode. I do not understand the complaint about text fringing.

Whether you are picky or not, there is no technology that will meet 100% of your needs 100% of the time. IPS will smear at high refresh rates due to GtG times and poor viewing angles. VA will have poor color depth. OLED will have some text fringing and some burn in. Screen uniformity lottery across all panel types is a mixed bag. Mini RGB LED will have bas pixel refresh times and smearing...

Expectation is the root of heartbreak. If you expect that there is a perfect product, you will be disappointed in the reality that there isn't.

author: @ResolveReviews
text: It's unfortunately not that simple. People talk about how this is an issue with windows and ClearType, and while that's definitely a part of it, the real culprit is actually tyhe subpixel layout of the display. With the current;y available QD-OLED options (not RGB stripe), fringing occurs on high contrast material in general, it's just most noticeable on text because it's static, and of course because of how this is handled by ClearType. But if you use dark mode and look at any high contrast static material for non-text related elements, say even UI elements, you can also see it. It's not typically as noticeable, usually because those static elements are larger. But this is also one of the reasons why greyscale solutions don't actually fix the problem entirely. They minimize the ClearType issues at the cost of blocky and unrefined looking text, but the fringing is still visible and distracting due to the subpixel layout of the display.

author: @aidanm.1683
text:
Hey man, I have an aw3225q; 3rd gen qd-oled. I am the kind of person who notices the smallest issues and hyperfixates. I use my monitor for productivity, gaming, and engineering, and I actually bought it used (technically... i think the seller got a new model from the dell warranty).

I was extremely proud of owning what I thought was an incredible, endgame monitor. And the colors were unlike anything on my budget VA. But I do remember that the moment I booted up windows on this new monitor, I was like... what am I looking at. For some reason, the text just looked so odd. I searched up the pixel density compared to my phone and laptop, and I just decided that that was the issue, and moved on.

Recently, with the huge price cuts in OLED monitors recently, I've realized I didn't get the very best monitor or deal. I considered selling my aw3225qf and then using that monitor to sponsor a better panel. 

But then, I took a second to relax, and compared my new and old monitor, and I realized that my 3rd gen QD-OLED panel was absolutely beautiful, despite not being the brightest or best hdr implementation. 

Even now, I learned for your video that the reason the text looks weird (mind you I use dark mode for everything) is because of the color fringing. I looked close at the text, and I saw exactly what you showed. But even now, I have gotten used to it after months of ownership, and it doesn't bother me compared to how gorgeous video games and movies look now. 

I don't think this video is ragebait, so I really wonder, how is this not enough for you? Yes, there's a chance your eyes are simply more sensitive to the color fringing than mine. You probably sit closer considering your monitor is smaller. But I feel like you have become noseblind to the benefits of improvement in your technology. I enjoyed your video nonetheless, but I really wish you'd put your 1440p and 4k panel side-by-side and tell me you can't be happy with the improvements in video, gaming, and certain productivity tasks. 

(I am not talking about Tandem OLEDs in this spiel. I think the panel lottery and the greyscale banding is a stupid thing for paying that much money, for what, a slightly brighter, more contrasting screen?)

author: @TheOnceAndFutureDoug
text:
Here's my hottest of takes: OLED's were never about providing a better experience for users, they were about selling more monitors. LCD panels can die but it's usually from some kind of abuse. You can buy a cheap $100 IPS LCD and expect it to last you 10 years. Find me a single OLED at any price that is expected to last 10 years of service without terrible burn-in.

My current setup, two 27" 4K@144hz Dough monitors, is over 5 years old and the panels are perfectly fine. I'd love to upgrade to something with better color accuracy (I do photography) as well as pixel response times but I can't reasonably drop $1,000 x 2 on monitors that I'd be expecting to replace in 3-5 years due to burn-in. And I know I'd deal with that because I work from home and 50 hours of screen-on time a week is pretty typical for me. So I want a monitor that can happily do 15,000 hours of screen-on time and not degrade in that time and I'm TIRED of people telling me that's unreasonable. It's not. It's only unreasonable for OLED.

And that's why the industry is pushing them: They are expensive and they have a shelf-life. Who cares that we're creating all this e-waste? The picture was a bit better!

text: No one mentions this when talking about qd-oled, but one of the reasons they have better near black performance than woled is because they flash alternating columns of pixels between a darker and brighter color, creating the illusion of it being the correct color. This is all good when watching a static image, but as soon as something moves across the screen at just the right speed, your brain will see the columns. In a game like cyberpunk the walking speed is just perfectly aligned so that while walking through a dark corridor you will see the columns on the walls going past you on each side. I don't know why so little people mention this as an issue.

author: @Sinsanatis
text:
i had a similar journey starting in, i think late march. i bought the asus 27in 1440p 280hz tandem. out of the box it had horrendous gray banding, but thats kinda normal. after just one pixel refresh, about 80% of it was gone. over time it became less and less. but dse seemed to become worse and worse. i only learned about the batches later on so i dont know if i got the good or bad batch. id assume it was the bad batch. i think i had it for little over 2 weeks and returned it. oh yeah and the neo prox sensor was crap. didnt work properly. it would shut off no matter what distance i set it to. would happen to me mid match/game so i just turned it off. but aside from that, the deep blacks and the trueblack glossy clarity was amazing.

next i tried qd oled it was the msi MAG 272QP QD-OLED X50. also 27in 1440p, but with 500hz. checked uniformity, it was pretty much perfect. maybe u could say u could see a super tiny bit of dse if u used a specific grayscale and put ur eyeballs on the monitor, but it was realistically perfect. the text fringing was noticeable tho and felt like it was fucking with my eyes. i forgot how i came across it, but i found posts and discussions on reddit about eye strain from qd oled. doesnt seem to affect everyone, but some stated much higher eye strain from qd oled. saying things like it would feel like it was searing their eyes, red eyes, headaches, and poor sleep. i actually did notice i was experiencing all of the above aside from the sleep prob since im always sleep deprived anyway. many of those ppl reported the issues going away when switching over to woled. but as for visuals, it was nice and vibrant with the colors. the raised black levels was definitely an issue for me tho. i have lamp behind me, which isnt super bright, but i also have white walls that would bounce some sunlight, and also i use a monitor light bar. i noticed the warmer the lighting, the more purple the blacks would become. my light bar has a slider for warmer or colder light. also i felt that the bfi was unusable because of the lack of brightness, but it was smooth. compared to the tandem which in order to use bfi, u would have to half the framerate unfortunately. 

i started deciding if maybe i should just go 3rd gen woled. then decided that i really liked tandem oled as the brightness really hit for when i was viewing hdr oled videos plus the trueblack glossy coating. the better lifespan was an added bonus. so i just went for trying the lottery again. this time i went for the gigabyte model since idgaf about the neo prox sensor and the gigabyte model was a bit cheaper. again out of the box there was banding, but very little dse. good start as dse is more what i was worried about. pixel refresh pretty much gets rid of the banding. dse is still there ofc, but is quite minimal. overall it was good enough so i decided to keep it after continuing to trial it. im 734hrs and 114 pixel cleans in now. dse and banding is pretty much a non issue. i can see it very slightly occasionally, but its almost never noticeable in any actual content. only thing is that i think part of  the cost difference from the asus is the display bandwith. the asus can do the full 280hz without dsc, but the gigabyte only does 200hz without dsc.not a huge deal, but i do notice that it has significantly longer wake times than anything ive ever used. even with dsc off. but ive largely just been dealing with it. its not the end of the world. just a few more seconds. overall pretty happy with it tho. the new hypernits feature is pretty nice too. just wish that the state of hdr in games wasnt so shit.

author: @kaylee42900
text:
You're definitely wrong about the fringing issue being "inherent" to OLED.  It's inherent to Windows.  Mac and several Linux distros have fixed this. 

Whenever i use my OLED on my work Mac it's night and day.

 Microsoft made a decision during the switch from crt to LCD to display text in a specific way that specifically looks good on LCDs.  It doesn't look good on OLED.  Other operating systems have responded and allowed their text to use a variety of sub pixel layouts.

text: My biggest gripes with LCD monitors (IPS, VA, TN) are backlight bleed (panel lottery) and poor contrast/black levels. OLED fixed both of those issues for me. author: @ZeDestructor00
text:
Yeah.. I concluded many years ago that 280+ppi is the target to properly solve all the text-, scaling- and fps-related (integerscale or DLSS/FSR/XeSS a lower res) issues. Laptops hit that over a decade ago whey they hit 4K, but man is it ever so slow on the desktop front.

I recently picked up a lightly-used Dell UP3218K from (as you might have guessed) 2018 (though my specific one was manufactured in 2025), a 32" 8K60 IPS LCD monitor delivering 280ppi. It really, truly, permanently solves all text issues for me, but it's a pain to drive, needs 2 DP cables, doesn't work properly under KDE (yet), isn't OLED and was recently discontinued. Asus has the PA32KCX that solves many of the QoL/usability issues but it is oh so expensive and still not OLED. If they would just give me a 32" cut of the 4K 16" Samsung OLED in my laptop I would gladly pay 5 grand a monitor and get 3.

Linux user here. I've switched to greyscale font rendering immediately after getting my OLED monitor, and later on fully disabled font hinting, while keeping anti-aliasing on, and I find this to work best. Subpixel rendering is a useful hack, but a hack nonetheless, so if a tradeoff for OLED is that I can't use it, I am OK with it.
On Windows you guys don't have the same options, but check BetterClearType to make ClearType rendering greyscale. This should fix fringing in the browser, but Windows UI font will look different and a little awkward.

author: @Faraldir221
text:
Hi, I’d like to share my own experience. My first OLED monitor was the ASUS PG27CDM, and just like you mentioned, there was noticeable fringing around text. However, the biggest issue for me was how incredibly sensitive glossy screens are to scratches, fingerprints, and dirt.

After doing a few hours of research, I found that Samsung was basically the only manufacturer using a matte coating on these panels, so I went ahead and bought one. I can comfortably say that text looks noticeably cleaner and sharper compared to glossy OLEDs. Of course, you can still see some green and pink fringing around text, but compared to glossy panels, I find it much more satisfying and most of the time I don’t even notice it.

The main downside of the matte coating is that it doesn’t look quite as visually impressive as glossy, and when looking at a completely white page, you can notice a slightly grainy texture from the coating.

I’m currently using the 27-inch Samsung G81SF, but if you want a QD-OLED with a less aggressive matte coating, you could also take a look at the Samsung G80SD, which uses a 3rd-gen QD-OLED panel.

author: @EaZynite
text:
I was an early adopter of WOLED monitors. For more than 3 years, I’ve the ASUS ROG Swift OLED PG27AQDM at home. And I agree 100% with you that reviews did a really poor job of informing people about potential issues. Everybody talks about burn-in, but they don't talk as much about banding and the dirty screen effect.

As an early adopter, I had worse banding than I would have liked. But the truth is, I mostly saw these issues in Teams or Discord (around 85% greyscale). Nevertheless, I kept the monitor and always used those types of apps on my secondary screen. And I'm glad I did. The blacks, contrast, and colors are really great, but most of my work (I'm a software dev) is done on my secondary monitor.

The banding started becoming less noticeable after a few Pixel Cleaning cycles. Now, I only notice a few bands in Discord and Teams, and it doesn't bother me anymore (or maybe I just got used to it).

So in the end, I completely agree with you: I would never buy an OLED for text-heavy work. But for a normal user, I would still recommend it, even after all the issues. And for anyone wondering—still no burn-in in sight! :)

author: @CollinKree
text:
VRR flicker is my biggest gripe with OLED panels, and is ultimately the entire reason I'm still on a regular IPS monitor and haven't upgraded to OLED. It's infuriating to see so many people online brush it off by saying that they only notice it in menus, or they just turn off VRR completely because the flicker is horrible. Turning VRR off is not a solution. Then you'll see other people say, "just cap your frames lol". That is also NOT a solution. Capping your fps will do nothing to fix VRR flicker if the game your playing has an unstable frametime even if the frames are capped. And then you'll see people go into this whole monologue about all the software they use to stabilize frametimes and eliminate flicker, and it just sounds exhausting. You shouldn't have to do all that for every game you play. And what's even worse is popular reviewers recommending these panels despite having horrible VRR flicker. 

I fell into that trap once with the AOC Q27G3XMN, a VA Mini-LED monitor. RTINGS gave it a great review despite it having the worst VRR flicker of ANY panel they had EVER tested. I bought one, thinking maybe it wouldn't bother me that much, but I was wrong lol. I don't think I'll ever be purchasing an OLED until there's some sort of tech that eliminates VRR flicker without introducing another equally annoying drawback.

author: @pabloezcurlbar7253
text:
My first OLED was the LG C7 and I got one with no banding in actual content and very low banding in the test patterns and I was super hyped about the tech when it finally hit the desktop monitor sizes.

I ended up getting an early AW3423DW and I was super interested in checking out how it handled the stuff where I saw flaws in my C7. Turned out the stuff I was interested in improving turned out to be perpetual issues, banding was similar to the C7, colors are hard to argue due to Windows HDR implementation, my gut feeling says the QD OLED reds are overpronounced, text requires ClearType tinkering but is fundamentally flawed and just banks on you being able to accept it.

I tortured the AW with static content and ended up with a free replacement 2.5 years in. The C7 never suffered even though it has basically been a JRPG machine for 1000s of hours with static UI. I hate bloom and glow far too much and haven’t bought any non-OLED since then but for my use the progress kind of stalled since 2017. higher refresh rate is pretty much the only thing I'd argue makes my C7 look weak, brightness is already higher than my treated room needs, and even the full screen white on the C7 hurts.

If I get anything soon, it would probably be something like 2 AW2726DM as side monitors. Cheap enough to not care about longterm burn-in issues and using the 3423DW for 4 years now, I acquired fringing immunity

source_title: Buying an OLED monitor in 2026 is insane - DON'T make my mistakes
author: @HawtDawgBro09
text:
​ @juniperpansy  you might have VRR co figured incorrectly, are less sensitive to flickering, you avoid games that have FPS dips and also you have a4090 you get less FPS fluctuations, or you got lucky with a monitor that doesn't have VRR flicker. Any of these and more could be the answer.

I would also check if DSC isn't forcing composed flip as that can cause other issues with frametimes and also causing DSC to toggle on and off.

Also in general TVs are better manufactured than monitors as TVs have data harvesting features that allow them to recoup profits and have a much bigger market than monitors so you get better products as more competition. Generally TVs have better processing so it could be that they mapped gamma values at certain refresh rates, especially lower ones. 

Most of the time sensitivity to flickering is the biggest issue. I can't use MBR or other strobing tech because it gives me headaches shortly after.

source_title: Buying an OLED monitor in 2026 is insane - DON'T make my mistakes
author: @HawtDawgBro09
text:
​ @maynardburger  All OLED have VRR flicker because they don't have the processing power to map gamma values for each frame rate so instead they map the value for native refresh rate. 

It's just that the severity of that VRR flicker is the lottery, some flicker more than others even with the same model because of slight variances in voltage.

source_title: Buying an OLED monitor in 2026 is insane - DON'T make my mistakes
author: @maynardburger
text: That's not even a lottery.  Most OLEDs have VRR flicker.  Some people are just not running into it often so dont notice it, like if they play content that's at more static framerates(say, a capped 60fps).

source_title: Buying an OLED monitor in 2026 is insane - DON'T make my mistakes
author: @HawtDawgBro09
text: Another thing not mentioned is that VRR flicker and burn in are both also a lottery and another set of variables. Slight differences in voltage across the panel when FPS changes along with VRR and you get a ton of flicker and faster burn in.
