author: @terraincognitagaming
text:
This video is extremely misinformed in regards to Banding, Vertical Banding may disappear almost entirely over time, the biggest issue with it was the early 6 months of batches, theyve since refineda nd improved it massively, its ofcourse no guarantee you'll get a flawless panel, hardly anyone ever will, but once you recieve your unit you are asked by Asus/Gigabyte whatever to run a pixel clean, once before actual use, if you dont you'll notice very obvious vertical bands against a very specific few shades of darkest grays (aswell as pixel width thin lines that go alongside these bars) after teh clean, on my unit, all bands vanished (XG27AQWMG) and the monitor looked almost identical to my PG279Q IPS in regards to gray uniformity. Keep in mind even if it doesnt all vanish on the first one, it may do so within the first 100 hours of use (thats like 10 days for work from home/gamers) or 2-3 weeks for a "4 h a day" user. And in most first world countries we have good return policies, not happy? Return within 30 days, 60 days, 90 days (Sweden) open box. So its not like a money thrown into fire situation. If it doesnt improve at all (i.e. to the point of being usable in all scenarios) then you just return it, you either try a new model or ask for your money back, no fuss here atleast. 

Getting upset that discord doesnt look completely uniform is funny though. Who runs discord in fullscreen theres so much meaningless dead space. Discord does not need to be wider than the Grid of embedded images for text messages and you certainly dont need to keep the members tab open ever. Regardless, dont buy anything except CRT if youre bothered by various issues: Banding, Clouding, DSE, Grid, Dithering, VRR Flickering. All of which may appear on: TN, IPS, VA, MINILED (IPS/VA), OLED and QDOLED monitors.

Also, what these videos NEVER tell you is that they OVER EXPOSE the photos (either unknowingly or knowingly to exaggerate the problem massively, and viewers, dont figure this out on their own, even when they can see the overexposure clear as day, the text literally glowing should be a hint) and the guy doesnt even tell us whether he ran the first initial pixel clean or not. We also dont know how old his monitor is and when he bought it (such as the batch) this video lacks so much information and just seem sensationalist, like hes trying to hit the algorithm.
QDOLED monitors also have a form of this except its a GRID that goes horizontal and vertical, these bands are much smaller, usually around 3-10 pixels in height/width and are completely random, and may shift around depending on the pixelclean (that you do atleast once per day, either manually or in standby/off). QDOLED monitors also come with VERTICAL DITHERING lines (its very LOCALIZED) and occurs in dark parts of an image, in particular when brightness is below 100% (but also happens in HDR) in again dark parts of a scene. Was very noticable in Cyberpunk at night against dark reds, magentas etc, aswell as Dead Island 2, this was on 4 separate QDOLED Monitor MODELS btw. Its never been improved since its an issue inherent to the panels. The Vertical lines are effectively the same as the DIAGONAL lines you can find on LG B/C/G series from the B3 and onwards. Though TV owners usually dont notice it as much since they sit over in africa to view their displays. Both technologies (WOLED and QDOLED) come with VRR Flicker. WOLEDs usually tend to have slightly less and the TVs have the least amount of VRR flicker, C5 42 had none when I used it paired with Gsync in the 144hz mode.

Also why is this guy using an OLED to browse discord?  
You buy OLED displays to use it as a MEDIA display primarily (games movies youtube twitch, light cad/productivity work). You place it in your center of the desk. You then use any other monitor, you know, 99% of us come from a PREVIOUS monitor or sets of monitors, that we then use as SECONDARY monitors, where you know, we have discord on and browsers and spotify and what not without any risk of burn in. "bbut my ddesk can only ffit one mmonitor.." almost like arms were never invented or something.

I also love the Miniled marketers in the comments spewing as if Miniled is somehow free from issues, and its obvious theyre really poor. Because you know OLEDs come with 3+ year burn in warranties meaning if your monitor were to somehow get burn in in 3 years (unlikely) you'll just get a new one in 3 years and that will last you another 3 years meaning 6+ years of use, for $500 (XG27AQWMG is really cheap btw) with no downsides really besides muh 1000ni t fullscreen that only minileds can achieve. That no one ever needed and no content actually makes use of. 99% of hdr movies and series are mastered for around 100-400 nits average brightness in a scene with only specific highlights going beyond that. (mad max fury road reserves most of these bright highlights for the lightning in the sandstorm for example)

Minileds out of the box: DSE, Clouding, VRR Flicker just like OLED, Grainy coatings because theyre always Matte making bright colors appear grainy or hazy. Local Dimming ZONE Flickering. Local Dimming ALGORITHM tuned only for when the display gets an HDR signal. in SDR content it doesnt work anywhere near as good as it does in HDR. Not to mention most miniled IPS panels are slower than normal IPS equivalents without miniled backlight and sometimes as bad as VA panels when it comes to pixel response. Minileds with VA panels have pixelnoise in motion and black smear (theyve yet to eliminate this fully). Not to mention all VA monitors have bad viewing angles even when sat head on, you get a cone view of proper correct gamma in the center and then in a cone outside of this center you get a wash out that gets worse the closer to the edge youre looking (your head remains static in position, otherwise this will all shift) If you lean back in your chair watching a dark or dim movie/game the experience will shift overall because VAs dont allow you to move around without shifting gamma. IPS monitors have IPS Glow still as miniled monitors, its massively reduced when you have the local dimming enabled, but when you turn it off, its a normal IPS; typically with more bleeding and glow than a normal IPS.

If youre stingy and paranoid just stick with a regular fast ips.

If your desk somehow cant fit two or three displays, dont bother with anything past a regular fast ips or an ultrawide ips.

author: @Baeloro1481
text:
​ @VividlyHeejin kind of a misunderstanding of the tech. QD oled is simply Samsungs Quantum Dot Oled. WOLED is simply LGs version of Oled. Both companies sell their panels to other companies to make monitors and TVs.

QD uses a sub pixel arrangement of red, blue, green. There is no black pixel or black filter applied. What you are seeing is the natural black level of... Oled. The reason you don't see that on WOLED is because WOLED used RGB sub pixels with a 4th white pixel added. 

QD oled is blue filtered, WOLED is yellow filtered. Meaning any QD oled panel is going to be using a blue light filter with red and green sub pixels resulting in a true color image... where oled/tandem oled are going to be using a yellow filter to add brightness with a white sub pixel in addition to RGB. 

Side by side under a microscope, the pixel arrangement of QD oled looks color accurate to RGB. The WOLED looks very washed out and RGB looks more like 'red green brown' with a white pixel in there. 

If you prefer a brighter overall image, that's cool. WOLED all day i guess. If you prefer something more color accurate, QD oled. If you want to see QD oled with an additional filter applied, go look at a Sony bravia Oled. Literally added a filter for image darkening and it shows. 

Right now HDR sucks. It's just not a good tech. SDR on a mini led with local dimming enabled is a much better experience depending on the game. 

I play SDR on an IPS without local dimming for some games. Other games, where the lighting and realism are important... SDR with local dimming.

author: @MoireFly
text:
I completely disagree with your take on the color fringing. Not only is it much less noticeable as resolutions rise (naturally, since subpixels are relatively smaller), it's also almost entirely a learned thing.  You'll get used to it.  Prior text-rendering tech had issues too; notably cleartype always introduces color fringing, by design, since that's clearer on a vertical stripe LCD display (and people complained about that, too!).  Prior to cleartype, fonts were often aliased, which is another flaw, and yet still readable. And that's the point of text - to be readable. On a QD-OLED with cleartype set to grayscale (i.e. no EXTRA color-fringing), text is clearly legible, although not as clear as on an LCD with cleartype.  But you've tried a 1.5x scale by the sounds of it - a 2160p display rather than a 1440p, and the res difference probably fully compensates.  You can definitely read such text clearly, and will get used to it.  If it bothers you as much as you're describing, it sounds to me likely you're triggered more by the change than in any reasonable way proportional to the problem.

Sure, it's a downside; but the description in the video and especially the unreasonable closeups just misrepresent how you'll use a display.  If you're staring at text so closely each subpixel is a very clearly identifiable blob, you're sitting too close.

I tried ips without a certain filter, said to improve light bleed. Oh yes it does decrease light bleed! Problem is, left side is green, right side is purple!!! Straight from the middle, you can clearly see it. The filter was making the screen uniform. Less bleed, crazy colors! No thanks I said and returned it. 

My current monitor is ips and it too has some movement artifacts (pixel switching is too slow). These days I have difficulty telling between dlss artifacts and slow transitions. I think getting copies of my car on the side when I'm turning in forza is dlss issue, while my antennae smeared trail is more likely a pixel color transition issue, but I'm not sure.

Basically: if its not okay for you, its not okay.

Apart from texts looking ass and grey-banding (what was never that big an issue to me), my main issue were color-shifts and the fact that in real everyday situations it simply never looked that much better than my <$150 IPS screen.
Especially the color shifts were irritating. Wood and darker skincolors became literally chocolate, a lot of things that are meant to be blue would turn teal/turquoise colored and some colors were just aggresively so more saturated than others. Its like you are getting a monitor out of the box with a "showroom calibration". And unless ones brain connect "a lot of strong colors = better", all of them just looked like trash out of the box. Non-Tandem WOLEDs were honestly the least bad, simply because they had less strong colors, due to the screen-tech.
What i loved were the blacks in the few situations, where one would actually see 0% dark blacks or high contrast content and the clear image. But none of it in comparison with the issues all of them have would be worth $300-$500 to me. And looking at how many of the shops (Germany) have boatloads of returner-devices severely discounted, the disappointement seems to be quite widespread.
My next attempt will be an RGB-stripe OLED, when they come down in price. Everything else, i wouldnt even consider, until they drop below 200-250 bucks.

"Am I being a pedantic asshole about this?"

I would say the answer to that kind of question when dealing with a consumer good is almost always no.  Whether a run-of-the-mill jabronie will accept a lower quality product because they're not concerned with its flaws is irrelevant to the discussion—we should be demanding better quality from our goods and services.  Modern consumer goods have been continuously degrading in quality because we allow companies to be profitable by producing garbage quality products.

If you buy something and it's bad, return it.  Doesn't matter how pedantic you think you're being—unless it's an absolute necessity that you cannot source elsewhere for whatever reason (availability, price, time, you name it), then return it and demand better.

text:
I also have roughly the space for two 27" monitors on my desk. Around 4~5 years ago I decided to get a LG C1 48", the same horizontal space as two 24", as a monitor for mixed media and programming. This year I switched to a G6 55". (Banding is basically imperceptible on my unit unless I squint.) Even though the PPI is pretty low on paper (80PPI), sitting a bit more than one arms length away, the text clarity actually doesn't bother me much, despite being on a Mac that does not do subpixel rendering at all.

So I'm really surprised to hear that text clarity after disabling subpixel rendering would be an issue for QD-OLEDs at 4k 27" (163PPI). That's double the PPI as the display I'm looking at right now, and almost approaching the Studio Display XDR (218PPI), which should be designed to work without subpixel rendering.

OLED monitors aside, I'd still vouch for the cult (?) of using a single OLED TV to replace a multi-display setup. Even if clarity is a concern, a 42" C6 still has higher PPI than a 2k 27" monitor, and it's awesome to have just the content in front of you without bezels in the center.

source_title: QD OLED Is Better Than WOLED
author: @andrewmorris3479
text:
@Her_Patriarch  1. Banding that changes in response to refresh rate 
2. Dirty screen effect to include carpet like greys which changes in response to refresh rate 
3. VRR flicker tied to gamma
4. Gamma varies at different refresh rates 
5. Factory calibration is tied to a 60Hz refresh rate 
6. The activation of the white subpixel at certain thresholds can cause abrupt changes in luminance, leading to visible steps or “posterization” in gradients extremely noticeable when HDR was enabled. 
7. Contrast and overall image reduces as brightness is increased 
8. In low APL HDR scenes highlights looks lackluster and washed out
9. Overall poor uniformity in all grey or white scenes with noticeable uneven color tint

text:
​ @oroborus2063  I love it! Only the dimming, especially with the Peak1000 HDR mode, is something I'm still considering if it's worth it or if I should go for the more consistent HDR Standard or HD Game modes. However, I don't notice this while gaming, but moreso when browsing the internet and switching between bright and dark pages (The other HDR modes can also have that noticable dimming depending on the "APL" setting used). So I'm still going back and forth between HDR Peak1000 (Hypernits High), and HDR Game (APL Medium) occasionally.

Also, I had to activate the Anti-Flicker in the VRR settings (I set it to medium), because in a few instances I noticed some flickering. So my VRR (Gsync) probably doesn't have the full 49hz-240hz range.

Other than that, full-on happy. Everything looks so good! Yum yum!

As a bonus that surprised me: I didn't pay much notice to the connections when ordering. But now I can also use my Steam Deck on a screen with mouse and keyboard, without changing the setup, nice! Never had a dock, so I was bound to handheld use. And for the Steam Deck with its low performance, I can make great use of the mode switch. One button press, and the screen changes from 32" 2160p to 24" 1080p. There are some old games that fail to run on Win11, but SteamOS can handle them. Now I can play those on a proper screen.

Me happy.

Both of my OLEDs are using uniform brightness, with equivalent settings on other options.

author: @StoneyWoney
text:
I got myself the Gigabyte MO32U24 as my first ever OLED monitor (QD OLED). It's quite the experience, I'm happy with it!

However, the Peak1000 mode with Hypernits is a bit of a double edged sword. For gaming, it seems to work fine faking the 1000 nits so far. But when browsing the internet, I encounter the limitations behind this "magic". Whenever I visit a bright site, suddenly all the bright elements, including browser UI and windows taskbar, get darker. That's because hypernits can't keep up with completely bright pictures - the monitor still only has the roughly ~530 nits to spare on the screen. Seems a bit "muddy" in direct comparison when switching from a darker site or one with more contrasts to a bright site.

author: @blue4k-XLR
text: I happen to love this YouTuber.  And I agree QDOLED is better than WB-OLED.  The problem was saying that one is better than the other is that you think one of them is bad or not good because there is something better.  The truth is they are incredibly similar and they so much more in common than they do that is different.   Both have perfect black levels. Both have an infant contrast both can do 1,000 nits and a small window, both have excellent viewing angles, and both will give you the best movie watching experience that is possible today and probably will be because there’s not much you can really improve.  I know everyone wants brighter and brighter TVs.  But even if your TV is 100,000 nits, it won’t make whatever movie you’re watching any brighter.  Most movies are mastered at very low brightness levels.  Most movies are mastered in HDR 600 or 600 nits or HDR 1,000 nits.   Before HDR even was a thing, movies were in the 100 to 200 dnits range.  The question is why don’t movies need to be super bright and the answer is because you’re supposed to watch them in a dark room.  Like a commercial cinema that has no windows at the ceilings are painted black. The walls are very dark and so is the floor.  When movies are made they’re mastered for the end goal of a cinema, not a 10,000 nit tv.   The main advantage of  QD-OLED is the color brightness, and as someone that owns both, I can tell you they’re incredibly similar. I can tell them apart if I look hard.   Not one member of my family can tell the difference.  In fact, they think I’m a little nuts trying to point out the difference differences.   Take that for what you will.   One other thing about tandem OLED is that it has a much lower chance of burnin.  That’s what Apple uses so that should be a good guiding light if you’re unsure.

text:
Hi Sannya08!
Welcome to Lenovo Community. I understand you're trying to use 240 Hz on your Legion 27Q-10 OLED and Windows is only showing up to 165 Hz, even with the included DisplayPort cable.
If 240 Hz is available for your setup, a few things can affect whether Windows shows it: the connection type in use, the current display resolution, the graphics settings, and whether the refresh rate is being checked in both Windows display settings and your graphics control panel. It can also help to reseat the cable firmly on both ends and test another known-good high-bandwidth cable or port if available.
Also, in monitor's OSD Menu, set DSC to disable and check again if you can adjust the refresh rate afterwards.
We will wait for your reply.
Best regards,
Hector_Lenovo

Yeah I ceased using for three months; and now, having hooked up to a nice PC- (using a 300 brand new hdmi cable bought a month ago, with top tier bandwidth and 'build'), and Dolby Vision (???) wouldn't let Dirt Rally run at a 'lowly' 240hz (280hz tried first; BAD)..

BLACKSCREEN.
fade out
Blackscreen.
Three seconds of game, 'black'..

Its a combo of 'spoofing 4k', and ''compressed bandwidth' etc..
Sadly the soft logic controls deny doing anything but switch hdmi inputs. (~to turn off Dolby Vision would require finding another source, as, no input locks out menus from doing anything bit input switch).

Its budget built internals, but spec sheet/pricepoint attractive.
Modern junk.
The parts that work, great, but vs traditional well built electronics (that don't spoof inputs they don't actually do etc)(4K!?); this is lovely as a gift from a relative upgrading past this..

But to buy it?
Lots of remorse moments of ' shitty budget soft logic controls with bad logic design'.

A firmware might fix some menus, but the timeouts --going to standby, quick, uninteruptable, "power off cycle", then bounces back, but timings are not built to handshake well..some of this is time to handshake /maintain the fake capabilities.. (needing compression for colour depth and only 2/3rds the real resolution)..

CHEAP.
Get what you pay for

Buy smaller ('better built unit') or recommend to save for something built 'pro end users'.

source_title: Lenovo Legion Pro 7i (2026) Review - Still one of the Best?
author: @kursah
text:
I have a 2025 Legion Pro 7i 275HX/5080/64GB DDR5, and it is an amazing laptop. Picked it up for $2500 new from BB around Christmastime. Kinda disappointing to see just the 290HX change, but impressive they get an additional hour of battery life out of it. This laptop is not great for doing remote work on when you're in a pinch unless its only for a couple of hours. 

Beyond that though, love this laptop. When I travel I take my 135W Lenovo GAN charger, and it works great. 

The key is also enabling Silent Performance mode, which very few reviewers seem to touch on (maybe I missed it here?). But that increases GPU power, and decreases CPU power & fan speed in silent mode. Using that with the 400W charger or 135W GAN charger seems to work well. Even with that, you must use the 400W charger to get "full" silent performance mode power. 

But it is pretty rare I even need to switch to Balance, let alone Max Performance to play the games I play. With Silent Performance disabled, you have more CPU power which makes more sense if you're doing more CPU-intensive tasks. But if you want extra GPU grunt, the 275HX, and I assume 290HX, do well with 60-65W power limitation and are quite efficient in that area. I didn't notice any performance degradation by "seat of the pants" measurements. YMMV, but well worth checking out if you own one of these amazing laptops.

Hopefully we can get back to more appropriate prices that make these more acquireable than they currently are, prices are disgusting.

author: @trainee5560
text:
Some things I dont agree with. Many things and misconceptions caused because the HDR on Windows is just too buggy and require so many steps to activate it as intended. I recently swapped my laptop panel with a mini-led 1200 nit peak-brightness HDR panel. So SDR content on a HDR monitor is not supposed to look washed out (I believe this caused by color profile's wrong gamma management). I had the same issue in the beginning "washed out SDR" and almost accepted that I should only turn it on when I will watch or play HDR content. Wasnt necessary after doing some tweaks. Now my desktop and SDR content still looks vivid when HDR turned on.

-Uninstalled both GPU drivers with DDU, Uninstalled Armory Crate (Has Game Visual managing screen color profile on ASUS products)
-Removed all color profiles from Color Management in Control Panel (I believe this has fixed the issue for me as I believe Windows Color Management is buggy too)
-Installed new GPU drivers with clean installation, installed Armory Crate
-I needed my Panel's ICM profile since my laptop doesnt come with this panel originally (but it is present in newer Asus models) so Armory crate cant download and apply it. Someone on GitHub shared his laptop's GameVisual folder so I grabbed the files from there. There are only 4 files you need and to understand which one is which you look at the file name. It will have laptop model, followed by a number or number letter combination which is actually GPU brand's hardware ID, and followed by panel's EDID. I found the 4 files (2 for my intel gpu that has my panel's EDID, 2 for my Nvidia gpu with my panel's EDID) and renamed the file with my laptop's model number so Armory Crate can see and use the file. So gamevisual started working correctly.
-Make sure you turn off "Change brightness based on content" in Windows settings as it bugs with HDR sometimes and make your screen lot more dimm when you activate HDR
-I activated HDR, made sure the brightness and HDR content brightness slider is to the max. This is important otherwise you wont be able to do HDR calibration correctly. 
-Started windows HDR calibration and Saved the profile. (Ive done it for both my GPU's so I have 2 different calibration file)


And hopefully these should make it work for you too.

text:
Hello and welcome to the Lenovo Community
purple240
,
I understand you're having trouble accessing the monitor settings of your Lenovo Legion Pro 27Q-10 monitor. May I ask first, what joystick are you using to access the monitor settings? Is it the built-in controls to access the OSD menu?
Based on your description, it seems that your monitor’s OSD (joystick) menu is being restricted by the current signal mode or by another enabled monitor feature, which can make items like Brightness unavailable.
Please follow this single path in order:
1) Power-reset the monitor (clears many OSD lock states)
- Turn the monitor off.
- Unplug the monitor power cable from the wall.
- Wait 60 seconds.
- Plug it back in and turn it on.
2) Make sure you’re adjusting settings while a supported video signal is active
- Connect a device that is actively outputting video (PC/laptop/console) and make sure you can see the desktop/game.
- If you’re on a console, open the console Home screen (not a “no signal” screen).
- Then open the OSD again and check if Brightness becomes selectable.
3) Switch to a different picture mode/preset (common reason Brightness is locked)
- Using the joystick, go to the monitor’s Picture/Preset settings.
- Change the preset (for example from a gaming/HDR/special mode to a Standard/Custom mode).
- After switching the preset, check Brightness again.
4) Temporarily disable HDR / special dynamic features (these often lock Brightness)
- In the OSD, look for items such as HDR, Dynamic Contrast, Eye Care/Low Blue Light, or similar “enhancement” features.
- Turn them Off (temporarily) and re-check if Brightness becomes adjustable.
- If you are using Windows: go to Settings > System > Display and toggle “Use HDR” Off to test.
5) Try another input and cable (rules out signal-format limitations)
- Switch from HDMI to DisplayPort (or another HDMI port) if available.
- Use a different cable if possible.
- Re-test the OSD Brightness control.
6) Factory reset the monitor settings
- In the OSD, find Reset / Factory Reset / Recall and perform the reset.
- After reset, re-check Brightness.
7) Update monitor firmware
- Click
here
to download the necessary firmware/driver for the monitor.
Let us know how it goes.
Thanks,
Adriel_Lenovo

author: Adriel_lenovo
text:
Thanks for getting back to us
yilmazryucel
,
Your CPU briefly reaching the high‑90°C range can happen on gaming laptops under burst load, but the severe FPS drops in Performance mode with the CPU clock collapsing to ~0.4 GHz (while the GPU is fine) plus very high RAM/SSD temps suggests the system may be hitting a thermal/firmware control limit and needs targeted checks. Since this has happened since day one and Lenovo diagnostics shows no error, please follow this single path:
1) Confirm cooling/airflow basics (quick but important)
- Use the laptop on a hard, flat surface (no bed/blanket).
- Make sure the rear/side exhaust vents are not blocked.
- In Windows, set screen/keyboard brightness and background apps normally (don’t run extra overlays at first).
2) Reset performance profiles and remove conflicts (Legion Space can influence power/fan curves)
- Reinstall Legion Space (from Microsoft Store/Lenovo official source), then open it and choose “Restore/Reset to default” for Thermal Mode/Fan settings (delete any custom profile).
- After resetting, reboot the PC.
- Test again in Balanced mode first for 10–15 minutes.
3) Standardize your test to identify whether it’s CPU power spikes causing the throttling
- In Windows Power Options, temporarily set:
- Power mode: “Balanced”
- Processor power management > Maximum processor state: 99% (this disables aggressive turbo boost)
- Retest the same game for 10 minutes.
- If the FPS drops disappear and CPU no longer hits ~97–99°C, the issue is likely turbo/power behavior rather than a failing part. You can then re-enable turbo and instead cap FPS (in-game or NVIDIA control panel) to keep temps stable.
- If the FPS drops still happen and CPU still collapses to ~0.4 GHz, continue to step 5.
4) Check for thermal throttling vs. power/current throttling (1 quick HWiNFO check)
- In HWiNFO sensors while the FPS drop happens, look at CPU “Thermal Throttling” and any “Power Limit/Current Limit/EDP” indicators.
- If Thermal Throttling is triggered at the same moment and clocks drop hard, cooling transfer/assembly (heatsink pressure/thermal paste/pads) can be the cause—even on a new unit.
- If it’s mainly power/current limit flags (without thermal), it points more to firmware/power control behavior.
5) High RAM/SSD temps (80–83°C) — immediate mitigation
- Ensure the area under the laptop is not trapping heat.
- Consider a simple stand/cooling pad to increase airflow.
- If the SSD temperature repeatedly reaches ~80°C during normal gaming, that’s higher than we’d like long-term; it can reduce performance and lifespan.
6) When to request service (recommended given day-one behavior)
Because you’re seeing repeatable, extreme clock drops in Performance mode and very high component temperatures since purchase, please open a warranty service request so an authorized technician can inspect the cooling assembly (heatsink seating/thermal paste/pads/fan operation) and confirm normal behavior for your unit.
You can contact our
technical support
at 0212-9120-134 (Standard charges apply) and their operating hours are 9:00 - 18:00 Monday - Friday. Provide them its serial number so they can also review its warranty info.
Otherwise, you can also visit any
authorized service centers
in your area if you prefer in-person inspection of the unit. Don't forget to ask how their store, including their repair policy work first before you bring it in.
Thanks again,
Adriel_Lenovo

text: Hello. I bought the Loq essential 15ırx11 83SC product 3 weeks ago. I am experiencing overheating problems with the device. text:
Fixed it. gemini told me to type this on bash:
lspci -k | grep -A 2 -E "(VGA|3D)"
then, looking at the photo of the answer from bash that I sent, told me that kernel driver in use or something was missing there. my driver was there, hardware was there, but drivers could not do the connection in between the hardware and software. so he made me use these commands in bash in a row;
sudo ubuntu-drivers autoinstall
sudo prime-select nvidia
sudo update-grub
and then I restarted the pc and my refresh rate was 144 instead of 60 and I could set my brightness from the battery button. though, it might not be same with yours, copy paste these to gemini and ask him help you check these maybe it helps you. love you gemini 😗

author: @FrostysGamingBenchmarks
text: ​ @drants-d6y  Take a look at the desktop side of things, the 9950x3d is quite a bit faster then the 270k plus while having better 1% lows, and the same thing is true on laptops since both the 9955hx3d, and the 290hx are both desktop cpu's stuffed into laptops, and as such their performance numbers won't change too much compared to the desktop side, only a bit lower on both due to laptops having much worse ram specifications, which x3d chips are less impacted by due to the 3d vcache compensating for slower ram unlike non x3d cpu's, tho the intel side does have the benefit of faster 6400mhz ram vs 5600 on the 9955hx3d.

source_title: Lenovo Legion Pro 7i (2026) Review - Still one of the Best?

source_title: Lenovo Legion Pro 7i (2026) Review - Still one of the Best?
author: @FrostysGamingBenchmarks
text: ​ @drants-d6y  In true cpu limited scenario's the 9955hx3d smokes intels best. If you don't play esports titles, get the 275jx, it is still plenty for even a 5090 laptop gpu, but in cpu bound scenario's it's not even close + the x3d chip has better 1% lows overall.

source_title: Lenovo Legion Pro 7i (2026) Review - Still one of the Best?
author: @drants-d6y
text:
​ @RealNaris I honestly don't know much x3d beats new Intel in the esport you are talking about. As I also understand, eSports optimization has gone towards getting mad when you get 500 fps instead of 520, so it's not like we are talking anything noticable.
In short, my argument is about the laptop as a whole. Ideally, this will be your main device and you will keep it for at least 2 generations of hardware, if not 3 or 4. At that point, it matters less if a device is slightly better at one thing and more attention should be given to versatility. That is where Intel shines.
The only exception to this is if you play the esport professionally, but at that point you would just get a top of the line desktop and get a handheld/ strix halo laptop/ zephyrus to do other gaming on the plane or whatever.

source_title: Lenovo Legion Pro 7i (2026) Review - Still one of the Best?
author: @drants-d6y
text:
Jarrod tested the x3d against last gen Intel. Even with Intel given the same bad ram, it was only around 10% behind in most games, especially at 1440p. There were a few games which were flukes.
Assuming the new Intel gen has close to the same improvements as it did on desktop, paired with even faster ram, it should be around as good in games.
Intel also has double the battery life, a much better igpu and typically ships with faster USB C and better wifi. AMD is also more expensive.

author: @Winnetou17
text:
The biggest factor (if there's no weird issues) of battery drain during sleep is RAM + VRAM. Normally that would consume 90% of the sleep battery as the RAM is the only one not powered off at all and constantly refreshing, even if not used actively (otherwise all the data is lost).

So if you compare a laptop with 32 GB RAM + 24 GB VRAM it will absolutely consume significantly more than a 16 GB RAM + 8 GB VRAM laptop.
In this case, the Legion Pro 7i tested last year had RTX 5080 with only 16 GB VRAM, I'm sure a good chunk of the difference is because of that.

author: @Winnetou17
text:
Thank you for including what you can customize in BIOS. Most miss that.

I have several questions:
- will you be reviewing Framework 13 Pro with Panther Lake ? It's not a typical gaming laptop, but if you get a CPU with B390 it's got basic gaming covered.

- this might be a bit too niche, but there's a chance there's increased interest into it, it certainly is for me: any chance you can test memory speeds with 290HX ? Including with 128 GB if you can. Technically the memory controller is a bit better. Intel haven't increased the official support for 290HX in order to not stress the manufacturers with extra testing and validations. 290HX might stretch its legs a bit more if it can run at, say, 8000 MT/s, while 275HX might only be able to do 7200 MT/s. Or maybe there's a difference at 128 GB, where the speeds, sadly, are lower. Might be the difference between 6000-6400 and 5200-5600 MT/s. Tightening the timings, if available, might also improve the 1% lows significantly. But that should be the same for 275HX and 290HX, if I'm not mistaken. And it's tedious to do and validate, so I'm not asking for that.

- have you tried Intel's PPP and BOT ? (terrible names, I know. And terrible in general to need this, though in case of BOT I understand that's just trying to redo the compilation for the current CPU when the devs didn't) In theory it might help 290HX, though from what I saw on the desktop with 270K and 250K it's kind of meh, nothing significant. But that was also several months ago, maybe now it's in a better state.

source_title: Every PS5 User Gets This WRONG! - HDR Settings Guide
author: @brunobatistacabral
text:
O recomendado para a grande maioria dos jogadores é usar a opção *Ativado quando compatível* (On When Supported).
Aqui está o porquê de essa ser a melhor escolha e como cada uma das opções afeta a sua imagem:
### 1. Ativado quando compatível (Recomendado)
Essa opção faz com que o PS5 mude de comportamento dinamicamente com base no conteúdo que você está assistindo ou jogando.
 * *Como funciona:* Se o jogo ou aplicativo (como Netflix ou YouTube) foi feito em HDR, o PS5 ativa o HDR. Se o jogo é antigo ou não tem suporte (SDR), o PS5 desativa o HDR e entrega a imagem original.
 * *Vantagem:* Você sempre verá a imagem **exatamente como os desenvolvedores a criaram**. Jogos em SDR manterão as cores corretas, sem distorções, e jogos em HDR aproveitarão todo o potencial de brilho e contraste da sua TV.
### 2. Sempre ativado
Essa opção força o PS5 a converter absolutamente tudo o que sai dele para um sinal HDR, mesmo que o conteúdo original seja SDR.
 * *Como funciona:* O console tenta "adivinhar" e mapear as cores de um jogo comum para o espectro HDR.
 * *Desvantagem:* Isso costuma causar uma distorção chamada black crush (onde os tons escuros perdem detalhes e viram um borrão preto) ou deixar as cores excessivamente estouradas, artificiais e saturadas (como tons de pele muito vermelhos ou laranjas). Além disso, a imagem pode parecer estranhamente lavada ou escura em telas que não possuem um gerenciamento perfeito dessa conversão forçada.
### Resumo da ópera
| Opção | O que acontece na prática | Veredito |
|---|---|---|
| *Ativado quando compatível* | Imagem precisa e natural. HDR só liga quando o jogo realmente tem suporte. | *Escolha ideal* para a melhor fidelidade visual. |
| *Sempre ativado* | Força HDR em tudo. Pode estragar o visual de jogos SDR antigos ou retrocompatíveis. | **Evite**, a menos que você goste de cores artificialmente vibrantes. |
> *Dica extra:* Sempre que selecionar "Ativado quando compatível", certifique-se de ir logo abaixo no menu em *Ajustar HDR* para calibrar os níveis de brilho máximo e preto do console de acordo com o painel da sua TV. Isso garante que os destaques brilhantes não fiquem "estourados" e os detalhes nas sombras apareçam perfeitamente.

​ @n7x  I have to say, currently using QD-OLED, the negatives are severely overstated in a lot of the monitor videos. I went QD because I wanted to avoid gray banding and more vibrant colours, even in my room where 1 wall is just a window and one of my lights is a Govee wallmounted piece right across from the monitor. The 'purple' blacks are really not that bad, especially when you're actually doing something on the monitor.

These videos with the people going all black screen and blasting studio lights directly onto it really don't do justice to how minor the purple blacks are in a real world scenario. Granted this will differ per panel and panel finish, but having used QD-OLED for 2 months now the downsides are really not all that.

(27inch, 4k, Asus ROG PG27UCDM)

TN, IPS and VA all have horrible downsides, some have issues which are apparent and quite intrusive from the minute you first get them. I just find it extremely odd that people bash OLEDs for their burn-in issue when it’s actually less distracting and annoying than the common issues of the other display types.

author: Adriel_lenovo
text:
Hi and welcome to the Lenovo Community
asisqt
,
Thanks for the detailed breakdown—very helpful. I’ll address your points and share the quickest next steps.
Key design notes for IdeaPad Gaming 3 15IHU6 (82K1) - On most configs the HDMI port is routed through the Intel iGPU. There’s no MUX or BIOS option to force the HDMI output through the RTX 3050 on this platform. - The maximum external refresh rate over HDMI depends on the HDMI version implemented on your exact sub-model and firmware. You can check its specifications by clicking
here
.
About the sudden HDMI failure mid-use - Given Windows/Intel GCC can detect the monitor (EDID present) but the screen shows no image, it can be a signal/handshake path issue (e.g., level shifter/retimer/port hardware) or firmware/driver state. - A quick way to separate OS vs. hardware: connect the monitor and try entering BIOS (F2/F1 on boot). If there’s still no image on the external display even before Windows loads, that strongly suggests a hardware issue.
Try these steps (in order)
1) Full power/EC reset - Shut down the laptop completely. - Unplug AC and any peripherals. - Hold the power button for 60 seconds. - Reconnect AC only, then boot and test HDMI.
2) BIOS defaults and updates - Enter BIOS (F2/F1) > Load Setup Defaults > Save & Exit. - Update BIOS/firmware via Lenovo Vantage System Update or your product page on
Lenovo Support
.
3) Clean reinstall Intel graphics - Uninstall Intel Graphics in Device Manager (check “Delete the driver software for this device”). Reboot. - Install the Lenovo-recommended Intel graphics package from your support page (preferred), or use Intel’s driver after testing Lenovo’s. Then reinstall NVIDIA and run Windows Update/Vantage again.
4) HDMI handshake checks - Test different power-on order: boot to Windows first, then plug HDMI; also try plugging before power on. - In Intel Graphics Command Center, set 1920×1080 at 60Hz first, disable HDR, set 8-bit color to test. - Disable Windows Fast Startup (Control Panel > Power Options > Choose what the power buttons do). - If possible, test the laptop with a different display or TV to confirm behavior.
Regarding 60Hz limit and higher refresh options - On this model, HDMI is routed via the Intel iGPU and may be limited by the port version/firmware. If your specific 15IHU6 configuration supports USB-C with DisplayPort Alt Mode, you can often achieve higher refresh rates by using a USB-C to DisplayPort cable directly to the monitor’s DP input. If your USB-C does not support DP Alt Mode, a USB graphics (DisplayLink) adapter can be a functional workaround for desktop use, but it’s not ideal for gaming due to added latency and potential frame drops.
Service/repair expectations - The HDMI connector and its associated circuitry are part of the system board. Lenovo-authorized repairs do not perform micro-solder/component-level fixes; the standard remedy is system board replacement. - If BIOS/driver resets don’t restore output (and no pre-OS image is shown), service is likely required. You can: - Check warranty and options:
Warranty Status
- Submit a ticket:
Service Request
- Or locate another Authorized Service Center for a second opinion/quote:
Authorized Service Centers
- For out-of-warranty, you may ask about depot flat-rate repair if available in your region. You can contact
technical support
at 1800-419-7555 / 1800-121-5366(Tata Subscribers) and their operating hours are Monday to Saturday 9:00 AM to 18:00 PM IST.
Answers to your specific questions:
Is HDMI soldered/no component-level repair? Yes—the port is on the system board; Lenovo’s repair procedure is board replacement rather than port-only repair. -
Sudden HDMI failure mid-use seen before? It can occur, though it’s not common. Your symptoms (EDID detected, no image) align with a hardware signaling fault or a persistent firmware state—hence the reset/update steps above.
Any BIOS/firmware setting to restore HDMI? No specific switch for HDMI routing; try BIOS update and Load Defaults as above. If no output even in BIOS, it points to hardware.
Route output through RTX 3050 instead of Intel? Not on this model; there’s no MUX/“dGPU only” mode for the HDMI port.
Goodwill repair/support? Please contact our support team still with your case history and the monitor replacement details—regional teams can review options based on warranty status and service policies.
Hope this helps. Please let us know if you have any other concerns or questions.
Best regards,
Adriel_Lenovo

author: asisqt
text:
I own a Lenovo IdeaPad Gaming 3 15IHU6 (82K1) with Intel Core i5 11th Gen, NVIDIA RTX 3050, 16GB RAM, running Windows 11 Home.
I recently purchased a Lenovo Legion 24-10 240Hz monitor and connected it via HDMI. I discovered that the HDMI port on this laptop is hardwired to the Intel Iris Xe integrated GPU, not the dedicated RTX 3050. This means I am completely unable to use my Legion 24-10 at its rated 240Hz — I am locked to 60Hz maximum.
Here is the full timeline of what happened:
I was actively using my monitor — watching a show — when the HDMI port suddenly stopped outputting any signal completely without any warning. No physical damage occurred, no cable was moved or disturbed. It just stopped working mid-session.
I initially suspected the monitor was faulty, so I raised a warranty claim with Lenovo. My Legion 24-10 was replaced under warranty. However, even with the brand new replacement monitor, the HDMI port still does not output any signal. This confirms the issue is with the laptop's HDMI port, not the monitor.
Issues I was facing even before the port stopped working:
Locked to 60Hz — unable to use the Legion 24-10 at its rated 240Hz due to HDMI being hardwired to Intel Iris Xe
Random blackouts — monitor would occasionally lose signal and go blank before recovering
Laggy video playback — 60fps video content played with noticeable frame drops on the external monitor
All software fixes I have already tried:
Updated Intel Iris Xe drivers via Device Manager
Updated NVIDIA RTX 3050 drivers manually from NVIDIA website
Ran Lenovo Vantage System Update
Checked Display Settings — Windows detects the monitor under Monitors in Device Manager
Intel Graphics Command Center fully detects the Legion 24-10 as connected via HDMI — but no signal is output to the monitor
Tested with multiple HDMI cables
Tested both HDMI ports on the monitor
Performed full laptop restart and shutdown cycles with monitor connected
Tried Windows + P display switching options
Despite all of the above, the monitor shows "Not Connected" and receives no signal.
A local Lenovo authorized service centre has quoted ₹25,000 for a full motherboard replacement, which seems disproportionate for what appears to be an isolated HDMI port failure.
My questions:
Is the HDMI port on the 15IHU6 truly soldered onto the motherboard with no component-level repair possible?
Has anyone experienced sudden HDMI port failure on this model mid-use?
Is there any BIOS setting or firmware fix that could restore HDMI output?
Is there any way to route display output through the RTX 3050 instead of Intel Iris Xe on this model?
Can Lenovo offer any support or goodwill repair given this is a known hardware limitation of this model?
System Details:
Model: Lenovo IdeaPad Gaming 3 15IHU6 (82K1)
CPU: Intel Core i5 11th Gen
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 3050 + Intel Iris Xe (Optimus)
RAM: 16GB
OS: Windows 11 Home
Monitor: Lenovo Legion 24-10 (240Hz) — replaced under warranty, issue persists
Connection: HDMI
Any help from the community or Lenovo support is greatly appreciated.
Thank you.

source_title: OLED Burn-in : 1 Year Update
author: @darkblooster9937
text:
Technically speaking, nothing “burns in” on an OLED screen; rather, the pixels burn out.
The problem is maximum brightness. With HDR, this is pushed to the limit in certain spots. The closer pixels are operated near the maximum brightness threshold, the faster they burn out. OLED pixels have, so to speak, an expiration date, which cooling mechanisms attempt to delay. And the mechanisms used for “cleaning/refreshing/whatever” ensure that the pixels under less stress burn out just as severely as the pixels under the most stress. This problem will never be completely eliminated.
In displays with LED backlighting, the backlight breaks down if it is set too bright and gets too hot over a long period of time. With OLED, it is the individual pixels themselves.

author: Hassen_Lenovo
text:
Hi @guest27235_,
Thanks for sharing your workaround. A quick note from our side:
Windows 11 Home doesn’t include the Local Users and Groups snap-in (lusrmgr.msc) by design, so that message is expected.
Manually altering membership of “ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES” or “ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES” isn’t required for enabling HDR/Dolby Vision on Legion systems and isn’t something we recommend as a general fix. Changes to these built‑in groups can have broader permission implications for apps.
For HDR/Dolby Vision issues on Legion laptops, we suggest focusing on the official pipeline instead:
1) Update through Lenovo Vantage - Install/update via
Lenovo Vantage
and run System Update to pull Lenovo‑validated BIOS/EC, firmware, display (monitor INF), NVIDIA GPU, and display feature services.
2) Dolby components - Ensure Dolby Access is installed/updated from Microsoft Store. - If a Dolby Vision Provisioning/Dolby Color package is listed for your model on the
Lenovo Support Website
, install it from there rather than modifying system groups.
3) If a Dolby installer fails (e.g., MSI error 1603) - Fully update Windows, reboot, then re‑run the package as Administrator. - Temporarily disable/uninstall third‑party color/profile tools before installation. - If the error persists, please open a
Service Request
and include installer logs and a DxDiag so our team can review.
If you’ve already applied the localgroup commands and everything works, great—but for others reading, we recommend the Lenovo Vantage + official driver/firmware route first.
Best regards, Hassen_Lenovo

author: Lorenzo_Lenovo
text:
Hello davidhaller,
Welcome to Lenovo Community
I understand that the OSD (On Screen Display) of your Legion 27Q-10 monitor is not working.
When did the issue started? Any changes on your set up or monitor?
Based on what you’ve tried and the symptoms you’re seeing: brief logo flash, immediate power-off, unresponsive power/menu buttons, and the same behavior across different inputs/PCs, most likely this points to a hardware fault in the button/OSD control board or main logic board.
Before we proceed to service, please try these steps:
1) Power isolation reset: Unplug power and all signal/USB cables from the monitor. Press and hold the power/joystick for around 30 seconds. Plug the monitor directly into a different wall outlet (bypass any surge protectors/UPS) using a different power cable if available, then test with no video cable connected to see if a “No Signal” screen or OSD responds.
2) Physical check: Ensure the joystick/button isn’t physically stuck or obstructed by the stand or a VESA mount. Gently move the joystick in all directions to confirm it clicks and recenters.
3) Minimal setup: Connect only power and a single video cable from a known good source (try both DP and HDMI). Avoid docking stations/adapters.
4) If accessible, go to the
support page
and search for “Legion 27Q-10 OLED” to check for any monitor firmware/utilities or the user guide instructions for a factory reset.
Let me know how things go.
Best regards,
Lorenzo_Lenovo

author: kofolak
text:
Error 1603 is caused by:
The ExecSecureObjects error: Error 0x80070534: failed to get sid for account: ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES occurs because the Lenovo installer is hard-coded to look for English names of system groups instead of their universal identifiers (SID).
Since you are using a Slovak (or other non-English) version of Windows, this group is named differently in the system (e.g., VŠETKY OBMEDZENÉ BALÍKY APLIKÁCIÍ). The installer cannot find it (error 0x80070534 means "no mapping between account names and SID"), and the whole installation fails with error 1603.
Solution:
Run cmd as administrator and proceed like this
C:\Windows\System32>net localgroup "ALL RESTRICTED APPLICATION PACKAGES" /add
The command completed successfully.
C:\Windows\System32>
Now repeat the installation; it will go through without problems.

author: @whitedragem
text:
I would seek out the best brand, then their better lineups, and then buy the one with the LEAST features at the highest price.
This is based on decades of buying reference screens.
Littlest model in the flagship lineup from brands like Sony/Panasonic (TVs), or, and its hard to qualify modern PC monitors, but brand preferences like Asus look after customers/'consumers' well.

regarding OLED/'modern screens'; great ones make 30frames per second sources perfectly fine, even without picture processing engaged (latencies added, "soap opera effect" etc).

monitors do outpunch TVs, generally speaking,.. but everything by PRICEPOINT.
(you get what you pay for);
my advice is look for the best rated product with the biggest discount you can find in your local market.

If it isnt for 'desktop productivity' (first/foremost), then a slightly older OLED (rgb layout less than ideal for text), might prove a great bargain.
I saw a few Philips ultrawides at 60% off, and they included Philips ambilight which was based on commissioned research for cinema industry; Philips ambilight is good enough to buy one of THEIR products (true), but can be added (at big $ addition) to some other screens (eg some Samsung TVs allow running a Philips light control system/'ambilight').

I love power over USB input to monitors, and a 65watt margin would be my target.
as for screen update rate? anything above 120hz (to 165hz) (assuming OLEDs) is pretty top tier value to performance..

just know in the brightness war and cost war, a lot has gone downhill for OLED over the last decade.
Marketing insists things keep improving, but there is a LOT of half truths regarding this..

I moved on from the Lenovo (still beside my bed, not turned on for three months!) due to a budget Samsung 'the frame' being a vastly better fit for my needs. (it replaced my Panasonic reference OLED!)

Marketing/'reviews' sell stuff.
Always NEW stuff..
which means last years products need be talked down or new bullet point features heavily talked up..
Nothing gets around 'you get what you pay for'..
(second hand Sony flagships are ALWAYS great buys!!)

Motion resolution matters massively for media consumption (/gaming), yet is costly to implement and has generally slipped/downgraded when prices come down.
to this end, spec sheets are manipulative rather than truly informative..
eg the colour capability of my 'budget' sammy LCD TV when doing high brightness HDR is unseen by most OLED screens.
Samsung the frame is great in lit room, but low quality screen when considered in 'total darkness'.
OLED refresh rate greater than LCDs (120hz OLED a better choice than 240hz LCDs etc), but OLEDs generally are built for black environments..
eg Why my Lenovo is unused for three months (windows on all four walls AND daytime usage)

Consider YOUR needs and find reviewers matching those end goals!
cheers

source_title: 05-03-2026 22:42:06 HDR, Dolby Vision not working byJosefCZinGaming Laptops issue concerning the deployment of Dolby Vision and HDR management on the flagship Lenovo Legion 9 16IRX9Electro-Optical Transfer Function) curve is clearly receiving incorrect metadata and the MiniLED panel’s local dimmingD
author: Hassen_Lenovo
text:
Hi JosefCZ,
Thank you for the detailed analysis and for documenting the steps you’ve already tried. Based on your description (HDR washout after a clean Windows 11 install, Dolby Access shows “Ready,” but Windows HDR lacks Dolby Vision options), the most reliable way to restore the Dolby Vision/HDR pipeline on Legion 9 after a clean OS is to ensure all Lenovo-specific services, firmware, and display components are reinstalled via Lenovo channels.
Recommended actions:
Install and run Lenovo Vantage
Allow it to apply all Lenovo updates/services for your system, including display firmware, color profiles, and device-specific packages.
Update drivers and firmware from the Lenovo Support Website
in this order:
System BIOS/UEFI and EC
Chipset/ME (if applicable)
NVIDIA GPU driver (use the Lenovo-provided version for your model)
Any available “Monitor/Display” driver/INF and color/profile packages for Legion 9 16IRX9
Reboot
and then re-check Windows HDR settings and Dolby Access.
If the Dolby Vision Provisioning Kit MSI continues to fail with error 1603, the next step is to verify logs (DxDiag, Windows event logs, screenshots) to confirm whether the installer is completing correctly and whether the display EDID/license state is intact. Since Dolby Vision is a licensed technology, issues at this stage are typically tied to the provisioning kit itself rather than Lenovo drivers.
If you prefer not to use recovery media, the combination of Lenovo Vantage plus Lenovo Support drivers/firmware typically restores the display pipeline without additional software. If the issue persists after these steps, reviewing the Dolby installer logs will help identify what’s blocking the provisioning.
Best regards, Hassen_Lenovo

source_title: 05-03-2026 22:42:06 HDR, Dolby Vision not working byJosefCZinGaming Laptops issue concerning the deployment of Dolby Vision and HDR management on the flagship Lenovo Legion 9 16IRX9Electro-Optical Transfer Function) curve is clearly receiving incorrect metadata and the MiniLED panel’s local dimmingD
author: JosefCZ
text:
Good day,
I am turning to the technical community and Lenovo engineers regarding a deeper architectural issue concerning the deployment of Dolby Vision and HDR management on the flagship Lenovo Legion 9 16IRX9.
After performing a clean install of the Windows 11 operating system, an irreversible breakdown of the HDR and Dolby Vision color pipeline occurred. Although the hardware is fine and the display worked precisely on the factory image, on a clean OS there is a complete loss of proper tone mapping and the image in HDR mode is extremely washed out, with a strong gray haze. The EOTF (Electro-Optical Transfer Function) curve is clearly receiving incorrect metadata and the MiniLED panel’s local dimming is not working with the appropriate contrast.
1. Detailed environment specifications:
Device: Lenovo Legion 9 16IRX9 (Intel Core i9, NVIDIA RTX 4090)
Display: Internal 3.2K MiniLED panel (Hardware-calibrated, Dolby Vision certified)
OS: Windows 11 (Clean install, fully updated)
GPU Mode: Tested primarily on dGPU via the MUX switch
2. Detailed description of the error symptoms:
After switching Windows to HDR mode (Win+Alt+B), the image loses contrast and saturation. A strange paradox is the system’s behavior regarding the Dolby Vision license:
The Dolby Access application (downloaded from the MS Store) detects the panel and reports that Dolby Vision is "Ready to use". This means the license written in the BIOS/display EDID is readable.
However, at the level of the Windows operating system itself, in the native settings System -> Display -> HDR, there is absolutely no toggle or mention of Dolby Vision integration. The system offers only the basic VESA DisplayHDR protocol.
3. Comprehensive overview of troubleshooting so far (What has already been done):
To rule out user error, I performed the following steps in the image pipeline:
Codec installation: I purchased and installed the official HEVC Video Extensions.
Lenovo Provisioning Kit installation (Error 1603): I tried to install the official package ds543424.exe (Dolby Vision Provisioning Kit) from the support website. However, the MSI installer consistently and irreversibly fails with Fatal Error 1603.
Manual bypass (PQCONFIG.DV): From the installation package or community sources, I isolated the calibration file PQCONFIG.DV created for this MiniLED panel. I manually copied this file with administrator privileges into the Windows system folder: C:\Windows\System32\spool\drivers\color\. Then I restarted the PC. No change.
Removing conflict with X-Rite (SDR mapping): The X-Rite Color Assistant application is known to force its 8-bit SDR ICC/ICM profiles even for an HDR signal, which causes color washout. I completely uninstalled X-Rite, including deleting remnants in Color Management. The list of profiles for the internal monitor is now clean so there is no conflict with the Dolby protocol.
NVIDIA Control Panel: In the desktop color settings section, I checked the option "Override to reference mode". With this step I prevented the NVIDIA drivers from making any of their own software adjustments to brightness or contrast that would conflict with the native HDR signal. Output is set to 10 bpc, Full RGB.
Windows HDR Settings: Auto HDR is strictly disabled (so it does not apply fake HDR to the SDR desktop) and SDR content brightness is reduced to a reasonable value.
4. Technical analysis of the problem and hypothesis:
From the above, it is clear that merely placing the calibration file PQCONFIG.DV into the spool/drivers/color/ folder is not sufficient for Windows 11, after a clean installation, to fully initialize the Dolby Vision pipeline for this specific MiniLED panel.
If the Lenovo Provisioning Kit (ds543424.exe) does not work and returns Error 1603, the system is probably missing the "software glue" between the .DV file, the operating system, and the display EDID.
5. Key questions for Lenovo engineers and developers:
I ask the technical team to answer the following questions from the installation architecture perspective:
What exactly does the Provisioning Kit installation package do beyond simply copying the PQCONFIG.DV file? Does it create specific registry keys (e.g., under Computer\HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\OEM\DolbyVision)? Does it run hidden background processes, or modify the WMI database?
Does the Legion 9 16IRX9 require a specific monitor driver (.inf) after a clean installation? Most clean Windows installations detect the MiniLED panel only as a "Generic PnP Monitor". Is Windows missing a native Lenovo ICC profile that would tell the system to even start reading the .DV file?
Why does the ds543424.exe installer end with error 1603 on clean Windows 11 installations? Is this a known installer bug unable to detect a specific E-Core/P-Core setup, or is some proprietary Lenovo service missing (e.g., Lenovo Vantage Service or Advanced Display Topology) without which the kit refuses to unpack?
What is the exact architectural manual procedure? If I don’t want to restore the computer to the factory “bloatware” image via Lenovo Recovery Media (which is a workaround, not a fix for the root cause), which exact files, drivers, and registry entries do I need to add to a clean Windows installation so that the panel correctly reads the tone-mapping from PQCONFIG.DV and gets rid of the washed-out colors?
A device with a price tag exceeding high-end market standards should have clearly documented support for clean operating system deployment (OS Deployment).
Thank you very much in advance for your expert insight and for helping the user community. Of course, all diagnostic logs (DxDiag, DISM) and screenshots (Windows HDR menu without the DV toggle, NVIDIA Reference Mode, etc.) can be provided.

author: Lorenzo_Lenovo
text:
Hello guest57610,
Welcome to Lenovo Community
I understand that you are concerned with the ABL behavior on your Legion Pro 27UD-10.
May I know what device are you using with it?
What you’re describing (brightness stepping down after 30 to 40 minutes and not recovering on darker scenes) sounds like protection/limiting engaging under sustained HDR load rather than standard ABL.
Let’s run through some items to isolate whether this is thermal/driver behavior, tone mapping, or a unit issue.
Key checks and adjustments:
-OSD settings (monitor side)> Ensure HDR Mode is correctly set for your use case. Try toggling between TB400 HDR and the default HDR mode to compare behavior. In OLED Care, confirm any luminance protection features are truly disabled for testing: Logo/Static Protection, Auto Dimming, and Thermal Modulation. Also look for and turn off any “Smart Power”/dynamic brightness features if present. See the
user guide
. Reboot the monitor after changes. Set Peak Brightness to High/On (if available) and HDR Tone Mapping to Standard/Default.
-Connection and signal path> Test with the bundled/high‑quality cable (Lenovo cable is recommended)  DisplayPort first. If you’re running 4K at very high refresh, temporarily test at 120 Hz in HDR to see if the behavior persists. A lower refresh can reduce sustained panel load and help tell whether thermal limiting is involved. If possible, try HDMI 2.1 at 120 Hz HDR as a comparison. Also test on another PC/GPU if available.
-Windows and GPU driver settings> Update GPU driver to the latest release and Windows to the latest build. Then reinstall the Lenovo monitor driver/ICC from the support page.
-NVIDIA Control Panel/AMD Software: set output to RGB Full, 10‑bpc (if available), and disable any driver‑side dynamic contrast/brightness or “auto tone mapping” features. Avoid third‑party overlays while testing.
-Retry running the Windows HDR Calibration after resetting previous calibration data. If the “max full frame luminance” pattern only clears near extreme values (e.g., ~2560 nits in TB400), that suggests the chain (EDID/tone mapping) isn’t aligning, usually driver or OS side. Try the calibration again after the GPU driver reinstall and with G‑SYNC/FreeSync temporarily off.
-Thermal/usage factors (for diagnosis)> Ensure the rear of the monitor has good airflow, not close to walls or heat sources. As a test, set refresh to 120 Hz and cap in game frame rate for 45 to 60 minutes. If dimming does not occur or is delayed, it points to thermal/power protection. If it still occurs on lighter content immediately after a darker scene, capture a video for support.
-Firmware (when applicable) and monitor drivers are posted on our
support site
. If no firmware is posted, the unit is running production firmware .
Test, observe and update us how it goes.
Best regards,
Lorenzo_Lenovo

author: exhale33
text:
Hello everybody. I recently purchased the Legion Pro 27ud-10 monitor and it seems there are some issues with it that i cannot solve (issues that other people have reported, elsewhere over the internet). The most important (and also annoying) one is the aggressive ABL behavior. I have set the monitor to TB400 HDR mode, disabled Dolby Vision and loaded the specific HDR color profile from Lenovo's specific Windows 11 driver (the proper one, from 2025). After a fixed 35 to a maximum of 40 minutes of gaming, ABL kicks in and relegates the monitor's display to very low brightness levels.
Now this behavior happens regardless of me turning off every option in the OLED Care OSD menu (including Thermal Modulation). If a less bright scene or portion of the game comes up, the ABL is still ON. It does not properly adjust the brightness and i believe this is a firmware issue, most likely the ABL detecting the game as a static image (which obviously, it is not). I tried factory resetting the monitor, same issue. I tried calibrating its display using the Windows HDR Calibration Tool, same behavior. What's even worse, when using the HDR Calibration Tool, the second and third screen (max detail and max full frame luminance) will have me dragging the slider up to 2560 Nits in order for the cross to disappear (which, again, should not be the case, especially in TB400 mode with DV off).
My questions are: is there any way to fix this? To prevent the (overly) aggressive ABL behavior? Will this monitor receive any firmware updates, with fixes for these issues? Can the monitor even have its firmware upgraded? I am still within the return window and i would like to know if it's worth holding on to a promise or simply returning it and getting a different model (since from what i have read, so far, everyone who's using this is experiencing the same issues as i am).
Kind regards!

author: Hassen_Lenovo
text:
Hi @guest57461,
Thanks for the detailed info. Since HDMI works, the issue is likely related to DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB‑C (port capability, cable compatibility, or configuration). Please try the following:
1) Verify the correct USB‑C port - On the Legion Pro 5 Gen 8,
not all USB‑C ports may carry video
. Use the USB‑C port that has a
DisplayPort (DP) icon
next to it. If your unit has multiple USB‑C ports, test each one. - You can confirm your exact sub‑model’s port specs in PSREF:
Lenovo Product Specifications Reference (PSREF)
.
2) Cable/adapter checks - Ensure the USB‑C → DP cable explicitly supports
DP Alt Mode (DP 1.2/1.4)
. If possible, test with another known‑good USB‑C → DP cable, or use a
USB‑C → DP adapter + DP cable
to isolate the cable from the adapter function. - Connect directly (no hubs/docks in between). Plug into the monitor’s DP input firmly.
3) Monitor settings - Manually set the monitor input to
DisplayPort
(disable auto input if available). - In the monitor OSD, try setting
DP version to 1.2
(some handshakes fail on 1.4) and
disable Deep Sleep/Power Saving
. Then power‑cycle the monitor. - Start with a conservative mode like
2560×1440 @ 60 Hz
, then increase refresh rate later.
4) Graphics/driver configuration - Run updates in
Lenovo Vantage → System Update
for chipset, graphics, and USB/Thunderbolt drivers:
Lenovo Vantage
. - Update GPU drivers (NVIDIA and Intel, if applicable) from
Lenovo Support
. - If your system uses a MUX/Hybrid mode: - In Lenovo Vantage (or BIOS), set graphics to
Hybrid
and reboot. USB‑C DP is often routed through the iGPU; Discrete‑only mode can affect USB‑C display output on some configs. If already Hybrid, briefly test
Discrete
and reboot to compare. - In Windows, press
Win+P → Extend
, then go to Settings → Display →
Detect
. Also check Advanced display settings for the external screen when connected.
5) Additional steps - Shut down the laptop, connect the USB‑C → DP to the monitor, then power on the monitor first, followed by the laptop. - Test with another DP monitor if available, to rule out monitor‑side DP port issues.
If none of the above helps, there may be a hardware issue with the USB‑C video path. In that case, please contact us so we can assist with deeper diagnostics or service: - Contact Support:
https://support.lenovo.com/contact-us
- Create a Service Request:
https://support.lenovo.com/servicerequest
- Authorized Service Centers:
https://support.lenovo.com/lenovo-service-provider/
Feel free to share which USB‑C port you used (side/rear and any icons), your current graphics mode (Hybrid/Discrete), and the exact cable model—this will help narrow things down.
Best regards, Hassen_Lenovo

author: @michaaustralia2738
text:
Hey guys, I need a final "Pro vs. Con" sanity check on my new dual-OLED setup! ☀️⚖️

I just scored an insane deal and already ordered 2x Gigabyte MO27Q28G (the matte 280Hz WOLED version) for just €489 each brand new. They are arriving this Thursday, but I’m struggling with a major trade-off decision.

My Hardware & Usage:
 * Laptop: Lenovo Legion Pro 7i Gen 10 (Intel Ultra 9 285HX, RTX 5080, 64GB RAM, 2TB Gen5 SSD).
 * Gaming: Fast-paced FPS shooters and WoW (heavy on animations/spell effects).
 * Work: I spend 8+ hours a day reading and working on this setup.
 * Connection: Main monitor via HDMI 2.1 (1440p @ 280Hz), side monitor via USB-C to DP 1.4 to utilize the built-in KVM switch.
The Environment & Future-Proofing:
Right now, my room is dark. However, I want to be prepared for the future. I’m planning a move to a very sunny region (Australia) next year, and I’m worried about reflections from windows or ambient light during long workdays.

The Dilemma:
 * Keep the Matte (Current Order): I got an incredible deal (€489). It’s the "safer" bet for future-proofing against glare in bright/sunny rooms. But will I regret not having that "perfect" glossy clarity for text and colors?
 * Wait for Glossy (MO27Q28GR): I’d have to return these and wait. It will likely cost me €150–250 more for the pair. I'd get the "glossy pop" and potentially better text sharpness, but at the risk of every lamp or window becoming a mirror in a bright room later.

The Question for you guys:
Which trade-off is smarter? Keeping the €489 matte deal for peace of mind in any lighting situation and saving €250? Or is the jump in text quality and visual "crispness" on a glossy WOLED worth the massive extra cash and the potential struggle with reflections in a sunny environment?

Keen to hear your thoughts and suggestions! 

What would you do in my shoes?

Thanks Michael :)

author: @T33K3SS3LCH3N
text:
3:03 yeah people are used to "wildly inaccurate colours" because almost the entire PC ecosystem is about SDR content.

If you have already tuned your settings around SDR, then HDR will look "washed out" by crushing vast differences between mid-range colours into smaller ones, to make more space for distinction within very bright and very dark colours respectively.

HDR only makes sense with actual HDR content, of which there still isn't much on PC.

author: Lorenzo_Lenovo
text:
Hello Miysis56,
Welcome to Lenovo Community
I understand that you are looking for the information about the
Legion Pro 27q-10
OLED Care system and screen protections.
About OLED Care and automatic protections:
Lenovo OLED monitors generally include several protections under the OSD “OLED Care” (names may vary): pixel/Panel Cleaning, Screen Move (pixel shift), Logo Luminance Adjustment, and Screen Saver.
Short “Pixel Cleaning” routines usually run automatically when the monitor enters standby or is powered off after use, while a longer compensation cycle can be started manually from the OSD. Exact trigger conditions (timers/durations) can vary by firmware and model.
You can always run the routine manually from the OSD if you prefer not to wait for the automatic cycle.
As for this model, it seems that it is manually configured via the OSD. See page 2-9 of the
monitor user guide
.
Hope this helps.
Best regards,
Lorenzo_Lenovo

source_title: Lenovo - Legion Pro 27Q-10 Longterm review ("don't do it!"); incredible MOTION RESOLUTION.
author: @whitedragem
text:
No- it is a software rather than hardware setup (cheap); its a Lenovo "budget" product- probably cheapest 3rd gen QD OLED on market.
It doesn't happen often, but it does happen often enough.. (to call it out!)

All inputs lag in response.. vs proper 'costly' monitors that use hardware chips to with embedded controls, and respond instantly, a cheap product can have these sorts of RANDOM issues.

Its the random nature that makes it annoying.
I could have sorted this quicker, but wanted to capture on camera a process of elimination.

Swapping panels puts me at mercy of panel lotteries anyhow, plus time investment...
I'd rather downgrade its importance to me (use less frequently/rely on other products as daily drivers) and keep this colour accurate panel. (delta e of about .5).
The downtime to swap it is a significant cost that could be better invested in a replacement part 
(don't buy Lenovo!)

text:
Venom bhai logo ke liya hai ye , vaise kaise hoo ap


Unboxing and Build Quality (0:42-1:40): The monitor comes with a sturdy metal-reinforced base, a DP cable, and a power cord. It features a polycarbonate build in black, with slim bezels. While the stand offers full adjustments (tilt, swivel, height, pivot), the OSD controls are button-based rather than a joystick, which the reviewer finds less user-friendly (2:07).
Connectivity and Display Specifications (3:12-4:12): It includes two HDMI 2.1 ports and one DisplayPort 1.4, along with an audio out jack. The 27-inch IPS panel offers a 240Hz refresh rate, QHD resolution, 8-bit color, and a 1000:1 contrast ratio. It boasts 100% sRGB coverage and 90% P3, with a typical brightness of around 320 nits.
Key Features and Performance (4:13-6:18):
MPRT Mode (4:13): This mode significantly reduces response time to 0.5ms for competitive gaming but lowers brightness to about 18 nits, making it suitable only for dark rooms.
HDR Performance (4:41): The HDR implementation is subpar, causing washed-out highlights and poor tuning, so it's recommended to use the monitor with HDR off.
AMD FreeSync Premium (5:06): This feature helps prevent screen tearing across various GPUs.
Overdrive (5:18): It offers four levels to reduce ghosting during fast-paced motion, though it might occasionally lead to pixel overshoot.
Display Experience (5:30): The IPS panel delivers excellent viewing angles and good color reproduction, making it suitable for content consumption and color-sensitive tasks. While blacks are decent, they lean towards greyish-blue, unlike the deeper blacks found in VA or OLED panels.
Gaming Experience (6:19): The 240Hz refresh rate provides a competitive edge in e-sports, and the monitor performs well for story-driven games like God of War.
Conclusion (6:28): Despite minor drawbacks like poor HDR performance and OSD button controls, the monitor is considered a strong option for its price, especially given its 1440p resolution and 240Hz refresh rate. It also comes with a 3-year warranty. The reviewer recommends it for users with a budget around ₹20,000 looking for a high-refresh-rate monitor for competitive gaming.

author: @sravankumar3969
text:
if you have dell laptop , do this

Check Dell EcoPower in BIOS

If the screen still dims before Windows even loads, the setting is likely hidden in your Dell BIOS.
1.Restart your laptop and tap the F2 key repeatedly when the Dell logo appears.
2.Navigate to Video or Display.
3.Look for Dell EcoPower or Dynamic Backlight Control.
4.Set this to Disabled.
5.Click Apply and Exit.

author: @dave-bet-tech
text:
I thought I was going to be in the WOLED camp until the vertical dark gray banding issue. I think I'd be really sensitive to this and unsure if I'd get over it.

I am also very sensitive to reflections and glare. It extremely bothers me when there's another light source within 10ft. Even my other monitors displaying mostly white (e.g. word doc) will cause an adjacent screen to be less readable/obfuscated to me.

I think I might want my next monitor to be less matte to avoid this. I'm sensitive to reflections too so maybe this is a no win. Will probably use some monitor hoods in the future to help minimize.

TL/DR: I'm thinking QD OLED might be the better choice.

text:
PG27AQWP-W Tandem WOLED owner here,
Been very impressed with it. The banding issue I was aware of when I ordered it and luckily my panel only came with one individual band that did in fact go away after a week of periodic pixel refreshes. The much more  prevalent dirty screen effect is not really a huge issue to me, but if having greyscale screens having a "texture" is problematic for you, than you will not like the panel.
I came from 1440p 170Hz IPS so obviously the extra hertz is insane for smoothness but if you already have  360hz or more I have to assume it won't blow you away. Glossy screen is goated, and white bezels are not as distracting as you will think.

author: @Longgshot
text:
You forgot the issues Woled have with gamma shift.
I tried a 280hz tandem Woled and if you used it in any setting other than the max refresh rate and without VRR, you will get wildly altered colours.

In the end i ended up returning it and going back to my 144hz IPS monitor with Gsync.
The Woled had too many problems, and without being able to use VRR the woled actually felt laggier when playing games (unless you are ok with the very noticeable VRR flicker and gamma shift as Hz change).
When not interacting with the content, it was good, but losing VRR is a huge hit in many aspects.

5th gen qd oleds look promising because of the more standard pixel layout and at least the model showed by MSI looked like it had a competent anti VRR flicker mode, although with the drawback of having half of the refresh rate in lfrc and a gap without vrr in the middle.
I'll have to test it to see if that is also a problem, but in paper it sounds like it could improve oled + VRR quite a bit.
Stripe Woled is another thing to check how it goes, but having tried a tandem woled i dont have high hopes, unless they completely fix the gamma shift and improve VRR compatibility.
