author: @Gravoxx
text:
Luminance (Luma) overshoot
in Tandem WOLED (White OLED) panels refers to a visual artifact where pixels transitioning out of near-black states momentarily "flash" or exceed their intended brightness level. This is a known issue with WOLED technology that persists in the newer 2025/2026 Tandem panel generations, such as those found in the ASUS ROG Swift PG27UCWM
and LG 27GX700A-B
. 
Key Characteristics of Luma Overshoot

    Near-Black Instability: The effect is most visible in very dark scenes where subtle shadow gradations are present. Instead of a smooth transition from black, pixels may "overshoot" to a brighter gray before settling.
    Visual Appearance: Users often describe it as a "halo" or "aura" around moving objects in dark environments, or a "pixelated/blocked" effect in dark shadows.
    Flicker and Noise: It can manifest as flashing lines or dancing noise in dark grey areas,.

Comparison to QD-OLED: QD-OLED (Quantum Dot OLED) generally does not suffer from luminance overshoot because it uses a different pixel driving method, often making it preferred for "cleaner" near-black performance.

source_title: 1440p WOLED vs QD-OLED in 2026 - Everything You Need to Know
author: @HDJess
text:
There’s a big difference people overlook: blue‑light output and the “quality” of the white light, similar to CRI in LED bulbs.
QD‑OLED uses only blue emitters, converting some to red/green with quantum dots. That means:
- Some pure blue always leaks through
- White is made by mixing RGB + that blue leak
- The resulting “white” has poor spectral quality, which you can see on skin tones and objects in a dark room
- Blue OLEDs wear out fastest, limiting peak brightness
Its only real advantage is slightly richer color volume from the narrow RGB peaks.
WOLED uses a true white subpixel from a blue+yellow stack, giving a broad, smooth spectrum with fewer harsh blue spikes and higher possible brightness since it doesn’t rely on overdriving blue.
That's why WOLED is the superior technology, and I would never consider QD-OLED.
Also glossy > matte.

source_title: 1440p WOLED vs QD-OLED in 2026 - Everything You Need to Know
author: @Asterra2
text:
"Everything" you need to know, except:
1) You can force windows to adhere to an alternative subpixel layout, making the text concern moot for literally years at this point.
2) WOLED's subpixel structure inherently leads to a dealbreaking artifact unique to the tech, called chroma or luma overshoot.  Any darkly-lit scene is likely to exhibit a soft glow trailing behind moving objects.  There is no un-seeing this artifact after you play a dark game and inevitably spot it for the first time.  Because of the white subpixel, this issue can never be fixed.

text: @belec5964  As I earlier intimated, this is tantamount to saying DLP won the projector wars, ignoring the detail that almost all DLP projectors are single-chip and therefore exhibit the dealbreaking phenomenon of rainbow artifacting.  You're trying to make a mountain out of a few hundred nits and a few cents more of electricity, and I'm talking about legitimate problems which cause people to refund their purchase or try their luck again with the lotto.  (Check forums for folks with buyers' remorse over overshoot and patterns they can see in dark scenarios.)  HDTVTest were the first to point out the overshoot issue.  In that video, QD-OLED "won every category" by not exhibiting a gobsmacking dealbreaker.

source_title: 1440p WOLED vs QD-OLED in 2026 - Everything You Need to Know
author: @Asterra2
text: @haewymetal My recommendation is that you don't go looking for it.  I know people who can't see bad frame cadence, DLSS upscaling artifacts, DLP rainbow artifacts, LCD dithering, late frame stuttering, post-digital interlacing, dot crawl, you name it.  So yeah, definitely don't find videos from HDTVTest or The Display Guy.  It's just not possible to un-see it.  I feel kind of bad for LG given they have no good options (other than abandoning white subpixels), but the closest thing to a solution they've come up with is to temporally dither spots that they know in advance will exhibit the overshoot.  And that really sucks, because 1) dithering should have died with LCD, and 2) when you dither the image, you are removing detail, meaning you are no longer getting your full 4K.

author: @hugevibez
text: @WaterspoutsOfTheDeep  Because of heat dissipation, which is the main driver of burn-in on OLEDs (OLEDs have a shorter lifespan in high heat). A large TV is able to spread out the heat a lot more and so you are able to drive the brightness up a lot higher, whereas on a monitor even a 32" one that heat is a lot more concentrated and will much more easily wear out the OLEDs resulting in burn-in.

author: @MarcusTheDorkus
text:
I think part of the experience is going to depend on the monitor's HDR capabilities. With TrueBlack 400 on mine keeping it enabled all the time and letting AutoHDR boost highlights for SDR games works well enough for me. But if I wanted the optimal HDR experience the monitor can provide with Peak 1000, then I would need to toggle depending on what I'm doing because the brightness limiter is extremely obvious on the desktop (I don't even understand why it's so aggressive when the overall brightness of SDR content mapped into HDR should be the same regardless of TB400 or P1000). 

And before someone tells me that 400 nits is not really HDR, that is untrue. You still get more dynamic range than SDR and you get the larger color gamut. The ambient light for my setup also isn't over-bright so I keep my paper white point around 120 nits which means that there's plenty of headroom for the brilliant whites to shine above that.

source_title: 02-19-2026 15:16:32 Lenovo 32UD-10 Oled care byVechtrulinY Gaming Accessories & Curved Gaming Monitors Hi there, based on the limited information available in the user manual of the Lenovo 32UD-10 GamingMonitor, I do not understand the following: 1.In this case, does the monitor do the refresh first
author: Adriel_lenovo
text:
Hi and welcome to the Lenovo Community
Vechtrul
,
I understand your queries about the Screen Protection feature on your Lenovo Legion Pro 32UD-10 monitor. And great job being proactive about OLED care.
Based on how OLED maintenance features are designed on the 32UD-10:
Automatic “Screen Protection”
(every ~4 hours): When you accept the prompt, it runs a short compensation/pixel refresh cycle. This typically completes in about 1–2 minutes and is intended to clear minor image retention from recent use.
Manual “Panel Protect” (OSD): This initiates a full (deep) compensation cycle, which takes longer—around 5 minutes—and performs a more thorough recalibration of the panel. It’s safe to use, but not necessary to run frequently unless you notice persistent image retention.
If you miss the screen-protection prompt: The monitor will
defer the short cycle and typically perform it the next time the monitor is idle/enters
standby or is powered off normally. To ensure it can complete, avoid cutting power at the wall immediately—let the monitor go to sleep or power off via the button/OS so it can run any scheduled maintenance.
What’s recommended: For most users, leave the automatic protection enabled and let the monitor manage the short cycles. Use Panel Protect occasionally (e.g., if you notice retention that doesn’t clear after regular use or after an automatic cycle). Running the deep cycle too often won’t harm the panel, but it’s unnecessary for routine care.
Additional OLED care tips: - Enable features like Pixel Shift and Logo Dimming/Screen Saver in the OSD to reduce static element retention. - Vary on-screen content and avoid long periods of static UI elements at high brightness.
Hope this helps you out. Please let us know if you have any other concerns or queries.
Best regards,
Adriel_Lenovo

source_title: 02-19-2026 15:16:32 Lenovo 32UD-10 Oled care byVechtrulinY Gaming Accessories & Curved Gaming Monitors Hi there, based on the limited information available in the user manual of the Lenovo 32UD-10 GamingMonitor, I do not understand the following: 1.In this case, does the monitor do the refresh first
author: Vechtrul
text:
Hi there, based on the limited information available in the user manual of the Lenovo 32UD-10 Gaming Monitor, I do not understand the following:
1. Automatic screen protection notice every 4 hours, if accepted, does the same thing as the manual "Panel Protect" action in the OSD? Or is the latter the deep refresh that is not recommended;
2. The screen protection notice stays on the screen for 3-4 seconds so I usually miss it. In this case, does the monitor do the refresh first thing after stand by?
3. Ideally, should I just use the manual Panel Protect action or just leave the monitor do everything itself?
I usually missed the screen protection notices and I just ran the manual Panel Protect. However, I have noticed a difference in the time each operation takes (automatic screen protection when chosen yes on the notice - 1-2 minutes, whereas the manual panel protect - 5 minutes).
Thank you in advance. I am just trying to take care of the monitor, given how finnicky OLEDs are.

source_title: 02-19-2026 00:05:05 Legion pro 32UD-10 HDR modes byMetasotkuinY Gaming Accessories & Curved Gaming Monitors Hi What HDR modes give the full 1000 nit brightness?
author: Adriel_lenovo
text:
Hi and welcome to the Lenovo Community
Metasotku
,
I understand your question on if what HDR mode will give 1000 nit full brightness on the Lenovo Legion Pro 32UD-10 monitor.
To address your concern:
• Peak brightness: The advertised 1000‑nit level is reached only during HDR playback with appropriate scene content (small bright highlights) and with local dimming active. The specific HDR preset that consistently drives full peak luminance can vary by content and settings; please refer to the monitor’s PSREF/spec sheet for the official brightness spec and supported HDR formats: Lenovo Product Specifications Reference (PSREF) by clicking
here
.
• Oversaturated colors in HDR Photo/Movie/Gaming: Those presets are tuned for a more vivid look and can oversaturate compared to accurate HDR tone mapping. To reduce oversaturation: - In the monitor OSD, switch from the HDR “Photo/Movie/Gaming” presets to a more neutral/standard HDR mode if available, or select a user/custom mode and set Color Gamut to Auto or sRGB. - Disable any image enhancement features (e.g., dynamic contrast, vivid/color boost) within the OSD when using HDR. - Ensure the GPU output is set to full-range and high bit depth (e.g., RGB Full, 10‑bit where supported) in your graphics control panel. - Re‑enable local dimming for correct HDR contrast. - Calibrate HDR in the OS (Windows HDR settings and calibration) and confirm your content is HDR10.
• Firmware/updates: If the OSD does not provide a neutral HDR preset or you still see over‑saturation after the steps above, check for the latest monitor firmware/driver on the Lenovo Support site via this other
link
.
Hope this helps.
Thanks,
Adriel_Lenovo

author: @silentsnoop1899
text:
​ @drunkhusband6257 HDR certifications just measure the quality of a panel. HDR is software, but like any software, it has hardware specs requirements to work. 

For HDR it's a high threshold of brightness, contrast ratio and color gamut coverage. Regular IPS and VA aren't able to meet them, so they're not good enough for HDR to properly work. You can enable it, because manufacturers keep adding HDR10 signal support to bad panels for devious marketing. But without those specs HDR won't work as intended. That's what "proper" HDR means.

source_title: HDR For Monitors Explained (And How To Configure It!)
author: @drunkhusband6257

source_title: HDR For Monitors Explained (And How To Configure It!)
author: @silentsnoop1899
text:
​ @drunkhusband6257 that's straight up wrong, HDR entirely depends on the hardware. That's why VESA DisplayHDR certifications exist. 

The display needs to control dimming by physically adjusting brightness of individual LEDs for LCD displays or self-emissive pixels on OLED.  

Non MiniLED IPS and VA physically can't do that, so they don't support proper HDR, even though they support the software.

source_title: HDR For Monitors Explained (And How To Configure It!)
author: @xenonisbad
text:
It's kind of marketing thing. Nvidia pumps enormous amount of money into RT marketing since like 2018. They sponsored countless amount of games to make them implement RT. They even maintain their own version of game engine, that is used by games like Wukong, that is focused on RT features. They worked closely with Microsoft to make RT work well on Widows. I don't think anyone is investing to promote HDR, and I'm sure nobody sponsor games to implement proper HDR or maintain AAA game engine, and Windows is mostly bad at HDR.

HDR also suffers from the fact that it can't really be showed to people who don't have it. You can show people recording of RT game and they can play that recording on any device they own, but showcasing HDR on SDR screen generally produces worse results than SDR on SDR screen. Dualsense also have the similar problem, I'm in shock how much it can enrich the experience when implemented well, but it's impossible to record what difference it makes.

author: Tomas_Lenovo
text:
Hi
johnlee9168,
Thank you for sharing your concern regarding the Legion 25-10 monitor's behavior during standby mode. Based on your description, the issue might be related to the monitor's power management settings or compatibility with the DVI connection. Here are some steps you can try to resolve this:
Test with HDMI Connection:
If possible, try connecting the monitor using an HDMI cable instead of DVI to determine if the issue persists. This can help identify if the problem is related to the DVI interface.
Update Graphics Drivers:
Ensure your graphics card drivers are up-to-date. You can use the
Lenovo Vantage App
to check for updates.
Reset Monitor Settings:
Access the monitor's on-screen display (OSD) menu and reset its settings to factory defaults.
Reset power settings
in Windows, use the Command [prompt](open as admin) for a full reset with
powercfg -restoredefaultschemes
, or go to Control Panel > Power Options and click "Restore default settings for this plan"
Best regards,
Tomas_Lenovo

Also a request for Lenovo: could you please update the manual with proper explanations
author: Hassen_Lenovo
text:
Hi Kermonen,
Thank you for your inquiry regarding the Lenovo Legion Pro 32UD-10 OLED Care menu. I appreciate your feedback about the manual and your request for more detailed explanations.
The
Low Power
option in the OLED Care menu is designed to optimize energy consumption and reduce power usage during operation. When enabled, it may adjust certain display settings to achieve lower power consumption, which can contribute to prolonged panel lifespan and reduced energy costs. However, this might slightly impact peak brightness or performance in certain scenarios.
If the feature is enabled by default, it is generally recommended to leave it on unless specific usage requirements necessitate its deactivation.
For further assistance or detailed specifications, you can visit the
Lenovo Product Specifications Reference (PSREF)
or contact
Lenovo Support
.
Best regards, Hassen_Lenovo

I understand you're experiencing an issue wherein your Dell P2414H monitor won't wake up on cold boot while plugged to your Lenovo Legion 5 Pro laptop. Based on the details provided, I recommend the following steps to address the situation:
Update BIOS and Drivers: Ensure your system's BIOS and USB-C/DisplayPort drivers are up-to-date. You can use the

text:
Hey Hassen,
thank you for the response. To address your point/ask follow up questions:
Update BIOS, chipset, and GPU drivers through Lenovo Vantage → System Update.
I did and my system is completely up to date.
In NVIDIA Control Panel, set the external monitor to a stable refresh rate (for example 60Hz or 120Hz) and disable G‑Sync if enabled, as HDMI handshake can fail with variable refresh.

source_title: 12-12-2025 03:21:56 External Monitor Flickers When Connected to Legion Pro 7 16IAX10H via HDMI Cable bydanielmitinGaming Laptops Hello, I recently bought a Legion Pro 7 16IAX10H.The way I use this laptop is by connecting it to my monitor via an HDMI 2.1 cable.The issue I am having is that on boot, a
author: Hassen_Lenovo
text:
Hi danielmit,
Thank you for reaching out to the Lenovo Community regarding your Legion Pro 7 16IAX10H and the external monitor flickering issue. Does the flicker happen only during boot and gaming, or also during normal desktop use?
I’m sorry that you are having this issue, and I know how frustrating it can be when your external monitor keeps flickering despite trying different cables and monitors. Since you’ve already ruled out the cable and monitor, the problem is most likely tied to HDMI handshake or driver/firmware settings on the laptop.
Here are some steps worth trying:
Update BIOS, chipset, and GPU drivers through Lenovo Vantage →
System Update
.
In NVIDIA Control Panel, set the external monitor to a stable refresh rate (for example 60Hz or 120Hz) and disable G‑Sync if enabled, as HDMI handshake can fail with variable refresh.
Test with a certified HDMI 2.1 cable shorter than 2m, as longer cables sometimes cause intermittent signal drops.
If your monitor supports DisplayPort or USB‑C input, try connecting that way to confirm whether the issue is HDMI‑specific.
In Windows Display Settings, disable “Dynamic refresh rate” and set a fixed refresh rate to reduce flicker.
If the flicker only happens during boot but stabilizes afterward, it may be a firmware quirk. If it persists during gaming, it’s more likely a driver/handshake issue.
Best regards, Hassen_Lenovo

source_title: Legion Go 2. Holy freaking OLED
author: @Wobble2007
text:
For this screen, I highly recomend driver level integer-scaling at 2X 600p on global, this base resolution will fully saturate a 1200p screen under 14 inches easily, and lool beautiful, and even though you get zero fidelity loss, you gain twice the FPS, its amazing how good it looks, even more so thanks to the much high 1 percent frames, whivh gives you a much better motion resolution, and better frame-times, resulting in much better gameplay quality, and for many games, even a 400p base resolution at 3X 400p integer-scale is plenty, for 3X FPS, this is my favourite screen setup for 1200p sub 14 inch OLED displays, and will easily manage a locked 144 FPS on the 144Hz OLED display without stutter or jitter in games like DOOM Eternal or Shadow of the Tomb Raider, I even have a 4X 300p integer-scale preset for many simple graphival games or retro style indie games, which gives me 3 to 4 times the battery life in games like Steamworld Dig 1/2 or Shovel Knight. 

You can get reak fancy, and use subpixel-rendering, for for extra pretty image quality that avtually beats stock rendering, specifically RGB-stripe subpixel rendering in ReShade, set to boot by default at startup, this will make even a base res of 200p look good on a 1200p OLED, RGB-Stripe subpixel-rendering 400p at 2400p looks stunng on a 10 inch OLED, especially for games like Psyconauts 2 or Hi-Fi Rush, and emulation looks really pretty too, you get just shy of three tImes the FPS and zero added percievable latency, minimal frames are ateast 280 percent higher too, simple driver level integer-scaling might be prefered by some, using at least 2X 600P by default is a no brainer on a device like this, along with 144Hz RBFI, aka rolling-scan, or at least standard 144hz BFI, my fave is 3X 400p integer-scale with 144Hz HDR-black-frame-insertion, for super smooth frames and superb motion-resolution, FPS games have never been so good on a handheld as they are today, same for SHMUPS, platformers and so on.

author: @sighange
text: Great point. That’s exactly where I’m heading. I currently have a tab s9, a rog ally x and a desktop. Most of the time I’m either on the desktop (hooked to OLED tv) or streaming to the rogx. Only a couple of games played here and there natively. I got a cold realization that I was “wasting” every gaming potential by streaming them this way. The rog x fully bright and max colors is pretty impressive (when playing games with plenty of illumination) but when directly compared with OLED in dark environments/games, it’s a slap in the face. I ordered a razr kishi v3 and plan to sell my rog ally x because I very rarely use it out of the house. I’d have considered the SD OLED but 800p won’t cut it. The legion go 2 would be perfect but again I will likely use it more than 80% of the time as a streaming device

author: @LordMaxed
text:
Why? What’s stopping your budget on a handheld pc from going over 1000$? Performance? The 395 APUs exist with 4060/4070 grade performance. Even the z2e isn’t bad. Spend your money on stuff you like and want, don’t limit yourself because of some stupid internet community or standard that people made up to stop you from enjoying things. The Go2 is a great device and as Chinese handheld and general pc enthusiast myself personally spending over 1000$ is pretty normal. I’m getting the Onexfly apex soon as a main pc and handheld as I’m tired of going budget and then regretting my purchases later down the line needing to upgrade. If you’re mindset is using the steam deck as a price point I wouldn’t, its nearly outdated hardware at this point and most of anyone pushing its value it’s satisfied with it which is perfectly fine by the way or they own a stronger pc already. Unless you own a strong pc already and this is just a hobby or you simply don’t care to game like that I don’t see why 1000$ would be a limit for you?

Keep in mind these are full computers, not game consoles.
Obviously finances depend on the user but my main takeaway is don’t limit yourself on your fun and enjoyment because of people on the internet (not CyberD but other YouTubers and commentators). 
Enjoy what you like and buy what YOU want

text: @deusvlad2.083  So for step 3, yes, set it to the darkest option. (NOT step 1 and 2). Step 3 is your minimum luminance, so controls the blacks and for an OLED, having that at the lowest is 100% what you want to ensure you get those deep true blacks.

source_title: Every PS5 User Gets This WRONG! - HDR Settings Guide
author: @Octorious
text: @deusvlad2.083  If you have HGIG, you SHOULD do it visually. If not though, and you aren't able to disable tone mapping properly as a result to set it up, then the level you set it at, whilst it might look right, wouldn't actually be right. So the numbers give a more accurate result for non-HGIG TVs based on their rated peak brightness and how the number of clicks correlate to that.

author: @Octorious
text: A few reasons, but mainly because setting it according to the 2% window could overdrive the display a bit. Some TVs struggle to maintain consistent brightness across larger areas, especially at huge highs like this, so could cause uneven performance or unnecessary dimming in real-world use. The 10% window is better fit for most HDR content in real-world use too, and the balance between power required & performance is better

source_title: Every PS5 User Gets This WRONG! - HDR Settings Guide
author: @Octorious
text:
This should cover those as it's a general guide for all displays! :) I see you mentioned the QN90C in a different comment, but QN90D here, so I'll just give you the best for both. If you want to know the how for doing this for non HGIG displays, I go through it at about 1:20 onwards, and you want to use that graph based on your peak 10% brightness window of the TV in HDR gaming (found on RTINGS.com).

QN90C: Has a 10% peak of 1996 nits, so from the graphic, that will round up to the 2000 nits option which wants 20 clicks. So for steps 1 and 2, go to the very lowest option, then from there, click up on the d-pad 20 times for each. For step 3, set it to the minimum value.

QN90D: Has a 10% peak of 2109 nits, so from the graphic, this would round up to the 2300 nits option which wants 21 clicks. So for steps 1 and 2, go to the very lowest option, then from there, click up on the d-pad 21 times for each. For step 3, set it to the minimum value. Note that because this isn't muuuch higher than the 20 steps option, you might want to try 20 steps too and just check which is best.

Hope that helps!

source_title: Every PS5 User Gets This WRONG! - HDR Settings Guide
author: @corey_massey
text:
Most of these videos on the best settings for your TV are misleading as most games do not use the system level HDR settings to calculate the HDR10 metadata you see in games. 

At best these settings govern the HDR of the display page of the game and videos that play in the PS store which support HDR. In truth....there are only a handful of games that use the system level HDR10 setting, namely the Insomniac Spiderman games (which is why its the only game shown in this video) and a few others. Every other game uses the in game HDR10 settings for the metadata and are the only settings that need to be properly calibrated for HDR. 

If anything your display settings control things like color saturation, overall screen brightness and the contrast (the difference between the darkest parts of the display and the brightest parts.) Everything else is controled by the in game HDR menus and should be adjusted on a game by game basis. 

In general there are things at a display level you will want to be mindful of....brightness does not make HDR brighter. Most of these videos are some person playing in torch mode (max brightness) which is only good for fighting background light sources. Its also why the max brightness of your TV doesn't matter for games and why colors appear washed out. If you are playing in max brightness in a dark room 9 times out of ten you are why the game looks washed out when using HDR, because the brightness is past the point of fighting reflections of outside light sources and is starting to make colors appear less saturatured than they actually are. You should set the display brightness and color saturation to a point where colors look rich, not dull or overly garish. This is going to be different for every display and for every room as the lighting conditions of your space will have a big impact here. Also with contrast, you should set the contrast to a point where black apears black given your room lighting. You want to find a point where objects in the dark are not completely crushed but not so bright where your blacks are grey. Again this is going to vary based on display and outside lighting conditions. 

Once you have your display values you never need to change them for games as everything else with how the game looks in HDR will vome down to how you vonfigur the in game HDR setting. In game you want to be using the directions that are given to achieve the best image the developer intends. If it says barely visible it means barely visible....clipping past that point will cause black crush. For brightness, you want to make sure that you maintain detail in the brightess parts of the scene...never clip past that point as that is where colors will start to get washed out or you can create white crush which is where you can't see other objects in a bright scene. 

If done right the game should look natural....not like a cartoon and not like a dull black and white photo. For gaming displays matter very little and things like Dynamic tone mapping will make it more difficult to get the few settings the TV does control right. While DTM does make the screen brighter again it is important to note that brightness is not always better since it does more to wash out color than it does to make your screen appear to have more contrast ratio. Its also why you feel you have to turn the color up to cartoon levels to get deep color saturation. 

As for the few games that do use the system level HDR you want to be one click past barely visible on an OLED on the white screens and barely visible on a LED TV. The reason is because OLED lighting comes from the pixel itself vs an LED TV which uses a backlight. LED tv's are generally better for a bright room or for people who game with the lights very bright and OLED is better for darker room.

What display is it? To be honest, when it's that low, it's unlikely HDR is going to benefit you much anyway. I'd advise setting it up as described in the first part (so as if it has HGIG, even if not), and see what it looks like.

That said, I think you'd get a nicer picture here just turning HDR off entirely, then bumping the TV's backlight and contrast a little. This is what I've done on a TV I have that has a similarly low peak, and it does look a lot better than using it with HDR, but obviously it'll vary from display to display.

source_title: HDR For Monitors Explained (And How To Configure It!)
author: @akyhne
text:
To my knowlwdge, there's not a single game out there, that uses anything other than sRGB sprites. Sprites are the images, wrapping around 3D models (UV mapping). So, they are using 8-bit images all the way, which is why most games don't look great in HDR.

There is free software out there, that can show you scopes in most games, and will confirm that despite the game being shown in HDR, no color goes outside the sRGB color space. Some of these software can also stretch the sRGB to a wider color space, but in most cases it just doesn't look great, because you are simply stretching 8-bit colors to a wider color space, so you are simply not getting more colors, but essentially just moving those potential 16 million colors to an area, that can support 1 billion.
And 16 million colors sounds like a lot, but any scene of any given time, usually only shows a fraction of those colors.

text: I used your sites review of my OLED to get the brightness values and set them in the windows tool. The tool was going up to about 2K but your actual measured peak was 700, big difference. I landed on throttling back to 400 for peak and just 200 full frame and 0 for min. It looks amazing! So much better not trying to push it to its limits, better overall brightness and detail not chasing the peaks. I keep my desktop in SDR and only switching over to HDR for gaming with the (alt-win-b) shortcut.

oled monitors in general are looking very rough in comparison to TVs and laptops. you just can't win with HDR no matter which technology you pick, QD-OLED and WOLED each have their own issues

we'd need to wait for True Black 1000 certified monitors, which could be 7-8 years from now at the rate we're currently progressing
my endgame monitor is probably a 45" 5k2k HDR True Black 1000 240z QD-OLED True Black Glossy monitor, at least for casual AAA gaming

motion clarity is going to be an entirely different can of worms for competitive gaming. i hear 1000hz BFI oled is approaching CRT motion clarity, which seems to be the ultimate goal in that regard. theres also projects like shader glass which seem also to be revolutionary concepts going forward
smartest idea is probably to buy a decent last gen oled on sale for now and just ride that out until the truly endgame upgrade options arrive, or just go mini-led. until then, we have a lot of waiting to do

source_title: Is HDR Worse? - HDR vs SDR On Monitors & TVs
author: @getsideways7257
text:
What you really meant is that SDR content looks beyond awful on Windows in the HDR mode — and that's mostly the UI elements anyway. HDR stuff can look majestic on the other hand (not sure if Windows supports DV or HDR10+ though), just as it should be.
Now, if you are dealing with an SDR movie or a game (especially the ones based on Unity and Unreal Engine), there are ways to extrude the output into HDR — sometimes to a great effect. If anything else fails, you can simply adjust the Nvidia Control Panel sliders until you got a palatable picture. Unlike with SDR monitors, one can be pretty liberal with those sliders in the HDR mode, but a huge downside is that there are no profiles management in the Control Panel (outside of the 3D settings, of course). Personally, I prefer it having configured for the best HDR picture unless I have a lot of work to do in SDR... but even then you can temporarily change things for best SDR until you are done and then just Cancel the adjustments (NOT "Restore defaults")

author: @dimaz3
text:
Reasons I don't use HDR - 

1.  It's extremely finicky on a game by game basis . Very few games have good HDR implementation and even worse on PC with windows fucking up things from time to time.

2. Even on a good LG OLED panel , you need to mess around with a lot of settings including power saving mode and what not to get a good picture that doesn't look like shit. 

3. Years of using SDR has honestly made my eyes used to saturated bright colours and HDR just looks dull and bland to me. At the end of the day I will rather enjoy my personal preference over what is technically correct when it's comes to entertainment consumption.

4. Most movies and Shows are still mastered with SDR in mind first. 

I enjoy the deep inky blacks my OLED provides and I can't be bothered to mess around with HDR so much .

source_title: Is HDR Worse? - HDR vs SDR On Monitors & TVs
author: @getsideways7257
text: It can still remain 8 bit in Rec.2020. You'll just have serious banding, since 8 bit was meant as "enough steps between black and full color" in the sRGB space (256 steps, to be precise). In fact, you won't see many panels that can properly display 10 bit color without resorting to FRC — and most likely not a single one handling 12 bits for real (as in Dolby Vision), since that would require every subpixel of a pixel to produce 4096 distinctive steps of brightness without significant errors across the whole pixel.

source_title: Is HDR Worse? - HDR vs SDR On Monitors & TVs
author: @exposeacademy
text: Most content is in the sRGB color space, which is only 8 bits per channel. You will only see the benefit of an HDR monitor if you play games that produce visuals with more than 8 bits per channel or use graphics software that produces HDR color spaces. Watching sRGB content on an HDR monitor is like listening to a mono audio file on stereo speakers.

author: @getsideways7257
text: People who say their HDR looks washed out while showing HDR content (and not just the Win10 UI), make sure you have at least a 10- series Nvidia GPU. Also, try juggling the cables: different input and output ports. If you have an HDR monitor and not a TV, the best bet is to go for Display Port (but who knows, maybe some work better with HDMI). The last but not the least, your monitor (or a TV) needs to be pretty expensive if you are expecting it to wow you. And it can do in three ways: either great colors but not extremely popping out highlights, great highlights with only marginally better than sRGB colors... or both. Or none, if the unit is a scam.

author: @aggressiveaegyo9344
text:
For kids, two years seems like a long time. But if you're around 30, you realize that five years will fly by pretty quickly. Only someone without life experience would buy something temporary, hoping it will last. 
But you've forgotten one small thing: you live in a country with one of the strongest economies in the world! North America or Europe. I doubt there's a single person there who earns less per month than this monitor costs. Now imagine that prices are universal worldwide, and in poor countries in Asia, Eastern Europe, Africa, and South America, people buy these monitors, video cards, or iPhones, saving up for half a year. If you're hesitant and watch videos like this on YouTube, OLED isn't for you. You'll regret it and be nervous every day, even afraid to leave your browser open to make coffee. Only if $1,000 is objectively a small amount for you (even if you're greedy and don't want to spend half your monthly salary) should you confidently buy OLED.

A reminder for my poor friends: you're watching this video on your monitor! All those incredible images with excellent contrast and perfect black levels are shown on your IPS or VA display. The OLED you see in the video is what you'd see on your monitor. Treat this image as if it had the warning "Image has been altered to demonstrate differences and does not correspond to reality."

text:
I've been using the LG C3 for 3,590 hours and am still far from any issues. But... here's my detail
- I use about 8 hours per day, mostly
- I only use this for a PC monitor with zero movies, because I have a separate home theater room
- I use brightness when I'm using the web at 15 and 30 for long sessions of YouTube videos. This is pretty damn bright for my room.
- In gaming, I crank up the brightness to 40-50, but mostly I use it at 45 because it's good enough for my environment.
- I'm using every OLED care feature since day 1
- I'm using ba lack desktop background since day 1
- Still never use pixel cleaning, but I heard LG TV will run soft cleaning or something after the user turns off the TV for a while.

You might say, "Hey, this guy is taking care too much. Your OLED TV is not a child." Yeah, you were right, but trust me, even I crank up the brightness to 100% all the time. Your eyes will be gone before the panel. The point is, OLED might have a better endurance than you think because you might be on full brightness all the time, and this does not include your content.

I bought my C3 for 845 USD a year ago, and I think I won't turn back to LCD anymore.

author: @bennja010
text:
Im genuinely confused. Do people actually think OLED will burn in after months or a year of usage? I never understood the point of those updates over such short periods of time. The average OLED panel wont burn in until several years down the line, hence why most manufacturers offer a 3 year burn in free service. If a panel would burn in in under 3 years something really went wrong during production.
Peoples concern regarding OLED and burn in comes with the shortened life expectancy compared to non oled like mini-led or something. A regular ips/va/tn lcd panel can easily last you a decade whereas an OLED will often do around half of that before showing issues.
If you upgrade your panel ever 3-4 years, go with an OLED but if you want your purchase to last as long as a regular lcd OLED just isnt there yet on a technical level and probably never will be. 
These types of update videos give a lot of people that dont know better a false sense of security.

Would you buy a brand new car from the dealership, and celebrate 6-12 months later that the brakes arent worn out?

source_title: OLED Burn-in : 1 Year Update
author: @dejvidos02
text:
I own an 27GS95UE from LG for a year now - I wanted LG's WOLED specifically cause I thought it could be less harmful to burn in, thanks to the additional white pixel (and it also has better peak brightness than QD-OLEDs I think). My monitor now counted around 1300 hours of usage and my experience was great so far - the brightness and overall picture quality is awesome and I can't see any burn-in whatsoever, despite I used this monitor for static apps a lot when I was studying for a state final exam and I also wrote a bachelor's thesis on it. Worth noting is that I use the monitor at 100 % brightness 90 % of the time (mostly set to low peak brightness so it peaks around 600 nits with no ABL) but I also have all OLED care features turned on. So I let system automatically hide taskbar, OLED screen move is set to level 4 and I also let it do automatic Image cleaning function that runs every 4 hours of use. After those 1300 hours I also spotted that monitor did automatic Pixel cleaning feature twice (every 550 hours I guess) that should specifically resolve burn-in problems if any are found. The only downside I had with this monitor at the beginning was an integrated active cooling feature, so you can heard a small fan spinning at the back of the monitor when you are on desktop (while gaming you can't notice that noise whatsoever). However, after that time, even this annoying sound somehow disappeared and I can't hear that noise even when I'm on desktop and put my ear close to the monitor.

So, if you are planning to go OLED in the future and you are worried about burn-in and you know that you'll use this monitor for gaming only, you shouldn't be scared. After the year I also noticed that the monitor somehow gets less warm after a gaming session, despite the overall brightness of the monitor didn't changed. Also, the monitor I own is only a second generation of WOLED panel of this type and the new dual-layer OLEDs that are being released this year are going to be much better in terms of overall performance and burn-in.

text:
Hi petergottstein,
Thank you for reaching out to the Lenovo Community. I'm sorry to hear about the issues you're experiencing with your DisplayPort connection. Is the monitor detected at all in Windows when connected via DP? (Check under Display Settings > Multiple Displays or Device Manager > Monitors.) Let's try a few troubleshooting steps to resolve this issue:
Check Display Settings
: Ensure that the monitor is set to the correct input source (DisplayPort) and that the display settings on your PC are configured to use the external monitor.
Update Graphics Drivers
: Sometimes, outdated or corrupted graphics drivers can cause connectivity issues. Use the
Lenovo Vantage App
to check for and install any available updates for your system.
Test with Another Device
: If possible, connect your monitor to another device using the DisplayPort cable to determine if the issue is with the monitor or the PC.
Inspect Ports
: Carefully inspect the DisplayPort on both the PC and the monitor for any visible damage or debris that might be obstructing the connection.
Reset Monitor Settings
: Try resetting your monitor to its factory settings. This can sometimes resolve connectivity issues.
I hope this helps! Please let us know if you have any further questions.
Best regards,
Hassen_Lenovo

text:
I agree, that these "solutions" disable G-Sync and reintroduce input lag.  

I have found, with G-Sync, that some drivers flicker more than others when G-Sync is enabled. Try rolling back drivers one by one until you don't get the flicker.  I found that with MAME.  Some drivers had terrible flickering with G-Sync enabled, while an older driver had no flickering, so I stayed with that one until I found a later one, that didn't reintroduce flickering.

author: @Art0r1a
text:
I think it's very risky to call a potentially washed out image on a monitor "more accurate", simply because when I look out my windows what I see is NOT washed out. The SDR image in those cases look much closer to "reality".
From my experience crappy HDR monitors are a blight on the planet.
A while back I bought a 32GP850 and the image looked really washed out. Why? Because while the max brightness was very high, the contrast was bad, so it ended up with an washed out image.
If you want HDR that looks amazing, go OLED. When I tried an LG CX, I was like "now this is looking amazing."
For me personally deep blacks are more important to HDR than max brightness. (Both is best, but one is more important than the other.)

source_title: Is HDR Worse? - HDR vs SDR On Monitors & TVs
author: @paul2609
text:
When people use SDR, they don't put it on sRGB mode. So they got used to really bad, uncalibrated, oversaturated image. Blame manufacturers for this, they don't use sRGB by default because they want to sell more TVs and monitors on a retail showfloor by oversaturating their TVs compared to the competing TV next to it so that they can make a sale. 

The industry is now aware of this and is trying to reverse this with HDR. HDR have strict standards that displays must be calibrated for atleast Rec709 (basically sRGB) or DCI-P3 (only 25% more colours than sRGB) out of the box. So when someone goes from uncalibrated, non-sRGB SDR to HDR Rec709/DCI-P3, they think it looks washed out but that is what colours are suppose to look like. Human skin are not supposed to look like it's red and sunburnt all the time, but that is what people who leave their monitors on non-sRGB mode thinks that looks good for some reason.

author: @cortbelmont
text: If a game has no way to dim or avoid static elements consider lowering the light. I know most people like bright panels but to avoid burn-in the secret is lower the light. 120 nits is enough to watch SDR content and get all the goodness, if you are not in front of a window during daylight that is. OLED burn-in is caused by the energy heating up and degrading the material, less light, less energy, less heat. at 120 nits the ABL won't even trigger on full white screen and your panel will last a lot longer. HDR is another story but to be honest I've seen just four games doing HDR right and faking it by tone mapping, anyway HDR is unhealthy for long gaming sessions

author: @paul2609
text:
When people use SDR, they don't put it on sRGB mode. So they got used to really bad, uncalibrated, oversaturated image. Blame manufacturers for this, they don't use sRGB by default because they want to sell more TVs and monitors on a retail showfloor by oversaturating their TVs compared to the competing TV next to it so that they can make a sale. 

The industry is now aware of this and is trying to reverse this with HDR. HDR have strict standards that displays must be calibrated for atleast Rec709 (basically sRGB) or DCI-P3 (only 25% more colours than sRGB) out of the box. So when someone goes from uncalibrated, non-sRGB SDR to HDR Rec709/DCI-P3, they think it looks washed out but that is what colours are suppose to look like. Human skin are not supposed to look like it's red and sunburnt all the time, but that is what people who leave their monitors on non-sRGB mode thinks that looks good for some reason.

author: @cortbelmont
text:
I think most people refers to the SDR on HDR washed out look, and that is unavoidable... Only solution use SDR content on SDR and only turn on HDR to watch HDR content, that's what I do.

"SDR" has a size on the color and luminance spectrum, the HDR size is just bigger, to put it in simple terms. When you try to fill the HDR with SDR you have to get things out of place and stretch them in order to fill the bigger space. When you map SDR black point cero luminance to the HDR space, what was cero now is positioned at the coordinate 0.1 luminance (just an example) this causes black to look a very dark grayish but not black, consequently all the other tones will be displayed a bit higher than they should to fill the space (we end up with raised gamma), and what happens when you display a tone on a higher luminance level, yes it looks washed out. This is the correct direct translation of SDR to HDR there's no way to do it better without heavily altering the image. You could do something different introducing digital processing to remap every tone to a new position altering heavily the intention of the original SDR image, you'll end up with over saturated colors, an over brightened image and probably not a pleasant image at all, but you get black to be cero again and gamma may be closer to what's expected of SDR

author: @greyroo
text:
I have a late 2023 Lenovo Legion 5i. Using Lenovo Vantage software it is possible to adjust fan speeds. You click on Thermal Mode in the main screen. That takes you to Performance Mode/Balance Mode/Quiet Mode/Custom Mode. Custom Mode allows you to control the fan speeds for the other three modes, unfortunately you cannot lower the fan speeds, only raise them. 
Fn + Q will also toggle between the Modes. 
Personally I found tweaking fan speeds in Balance Mode and ticking the option to Enable Legion AI Engine dropped my temperatures by almost 15C. It will depend on what games you play. I am not a competitive FPS player and generally play isometric turn based games like Baldurs Gate 3 and Jagged Alliance 3, so the variable cpu clock speeds that this setting gives is not noticeable.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @5abivt
text:
Been using my legion 5 pro daily at work for 1.4 years now straight.  I absolutely love this laptop. Could it be better ? Sure. For the price I’m glad I gave it a try after 25 + alienwares over the last 15 or so years.  

What I wanted :
1600p screen. Since the original 19x1200p 17 I’ve despised 1080 and widescreen screens. Alienware at the time had none. 
Power plug at the rear . Heavy thick cable stays out of the way when I use it on my lap or on the table. Ports on the rear but wanted a usb for a wireless mouse on the right side. Thus is from 2009 memories of a unibody MacBook 17 that had it on the left side and the metal of the chassis interfered with the signal 💀. Use the port on the rear for the usb end and works great and looks great out of the way. 
Keyboard. Absolutely great spacing and layout of keys especially f1 keys. This is unique to me and I’m actually frustrated playing level 2600+ arena in wow I’m finding I’m having more misclicks and key issues on my $300 desktop keyboard vs the fantastic keyboard on this legion 5 pro 🥲.
Happy that I can put it into balance and low power modes easily and have more than an hour to tune my m4 and flash the computer multiple times without worrying about the battery life. I definitely couldn’t do this with my 18xr3 with dual 980ms which gave me about 300 seconds 🤣 
I use an m2 skin and used a hair dryer moved the ugly stickers on the palm rest to the bottom and used a dark skin on the palm rest and I used a white skin on the outer lid which looks absolutely amazing with the legion tri star. I think legion dropped the ball on going away from the logo . It looks amazing and I’m happy I got the model with it. As an Alienware fanboi it adds just enough style 👌. 

I do wish the chassis and palm rest area was metal but for the price totally acceptable.  
I wish there was a way to have the screen go to 60hz and an ultra power savings mode to at least extend unplugged life then it would be even better.

author: @randomPoeGuy
text: I’ve been using the Lenovo Legion 5-15IMH05H - Type 81Y6. It was a great machine and I couldn’t ask for more, it served me almost 2 years. One month short of 2 years anniversary, my GPU died. And I mean the GPU, not integrated graphics (that one works fine). As long as you don’t install the drivers for the GPU, computer runs fine (although obviously you are not using that power of GPU at all), but as soon as I would attempt installing a video driver via NVIDIA website, System Update or Lenovo Vantage software for the graphics card - the artefacts would pop up and make the computer completely unresponsive and flashing with different squares and all that. That’s very concerning to be honest. I really like the machine, but the longevity of Lenovo products is very questionable. And that comes from a person that truly likes the product a lot. Just a little heads up for anyone looking into Lenovo products. I also do get these issues where a program of some sort would automatically assign integrated graphics instead of dedicated GPU instead and it’s a real problem. Trying to deal with it can be very messy and Lenovo doesn’t necessarily make it work straight of the box right away, you might need to tweak some things in NVIDIA control panel and all that.

The laptop has an annoying coil whine so I have to shut down every night before going to sleep, it's that annoying.

Besides all this, the performance is amazing ._.
That's not good enough, might as well buy a PC. If I could refund this laptop I'd just buy a PC or a more expensive gaming laptop.

text:
@TabalugaDragon  
I have balance charged and soldered Lithium battery cells, and i will take 60% over 80% anytime. 
Thats Nice If you can select the exact percentage in dells.
2. I think lenovos cooling is superior to most brands, you can play with voltages and fans but you will never get good temperatures If the case is too slim or the fans or pipes etc are bad.
There is so many fucked up designs and component combinations that I am just happy if my gpu/cpu works as the manufacturer intended.
You are right though, voltage control should be an option.  
But I find the display a much bigger issue. The market is flooded with bad display panels and its basically a lottery which exact panel you get in your box. i guess what was laying around in the factory at that time.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @TabalugaDragon
text:
@zsoca31  umm what?
1. 80% is the perfect balance between capacity and longevity. My 11-year old Samsung laptop with the limit of 80% still has like 50-60% of original capacity. It's the last 20% that are the most harmful for the battery. Yes it's optimial to keep the battery charged at 40-50%(not 60), but in case you need to use your laptop suddenly you'd have to spend time to charge it, it's very inconvinient to switch back and forth between 60 and 100% to reach needed capacity. Others offer 60 or 80% choice, heck with Dell you can select the EXACT percentage, ranging from 55 to 100%. 
2. Voltage control is definitely needed in gaming laptops. They often reach 90+ degrees in heavy loads(some heavy games included) and throttle, with undervolting not only you lower temps, you also get more performance back, limited by laptop formfactor. 
3. What does GPU wattage have to do with it? I was talking about CPU undervolting, unlike HP and MSI, Lenovo don't allow it on their Legion 5 and 5 pro. CPU is what gets the hottest. Besides, voltage control on Nvidia GPU-s have been available on all laptops since 1000 series via MSI Afterburner.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @zsoca31
text: Lithium batteries optimum charge for storage is around 60%. Look it up. Other brands use 80 because the users usually forget to fully charge it before disconnecting and then they would be left with a 60% battery. So they will eventually turn off this feature. Voltage control is not necessary in my opinion since its gpu (mine 3070) runs at true 130watt limit, not like in the gigabyte laptop or hp omen.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @TabalugaDragon
text:
it's far from perfect. It has no fan control(a must for a gaming laptop), no voltage control even in BIOS(MSI and HP have it), with battery charge limit for prolonging it's lifespan you can only choose 60%, not the optimal 80% like others offer. 

It's very close to perfection but unfortunately Lenovo screwed it for enthusiasts.

That's not good enough, might as well buy a PC. If I could refund this laptop I'd just buy a PC or a more expensive gaming laptop.

Hey everyone,

 I'm having an issue with my LG - 27GL850-B monitor. When I turn on HDR my monitor frequently does a seemingly random, subtle, but noticable, brightness adjustment. It's really annoying, but I really love how much better the colors look in HDR and don't want to not use it.

source_title: Screen Automatically Changes Brightness (Fix)
author: @BiteSizeRandom
text:
THIS IS WHAT'S AVAILABLE TODAY!
(it seems that Microsoft decided somewhere in 2019 to remove this feature, making a lot of computers almost unusable)

1. In Intel Laptops - open intel graphics command center find the power option > on battery > Turn off adaptive brightness, go to "plugged in" and turn off adaptive brightness there as well.
2. AMD laptops - the issue that causes it is called Vari-Bright turn it off in the Radeon settings.
3. In Dell Laptops  - the setting is moved to the BIOS, restart the computer get into your BIOS > video > Dynamic backlight control > Disable that.

- my unit has a realtek wifi card. So it should pose a problem of lagging when playing games or surfing the web. It may be slow in loading the site but i didnt see any sudden drops in the internet latency.

- My unit uses a slower SK Hynix RAM ( 16GB single rank i think ) but i didnt changed it to a newer RAM as I was short on money.  However , getting a 100fps in every game is still considered a great deal for me as i didnt play much games. 

- this unit comes with 300W brick. I have no issues at the moment as im currently working from home. However it may cause an extra weight if im gonna use it  outstation. 

- mine has 165hz screen. Colour is accurate, brightness is same as your findings. No issue so far for me. 

- for fan speed issue, i didnt hear noises from fan when im using quiet mode . It only goes to fighter jet mode when i turned on performance mode and the jet fan noise can be heard quite loud but not too annoying to me. 

Thank you Jarrod for highlighting these issues. It helps me aware of my unit more. 👍

It has Samsung M471A1G44AB0-CWE RAM which on their site says 1Rx8.  It has the Intel WiFi 6 AX200 adapter.  

A sticker at the top of the left side of the keyboard, "FN + Q" with blue, white and red icons.  It cycles between quiet, auto and performance power modes, if you switch to quiet whilst on battery the fan turns off but back on once you plug it back in.  I guess there is some kind of fan control somewhere. 

I haven't updated it yet to the latest BIOS (firmware).  

I am really happy with it so far after deciding not to wait for a 5 Pro or 7 RTX 3070 model which Lenovo originally told me would arrive on the 26th August before pushing that back to mid November.

I think pretty much every laptop has some issues and yes the power brick is heavy but for my use as a portable gaming machine rather than my every day workhorse, I have a Yoga Slim 7 14 for that, it is not an issue.

author: @93vxhybridhatchback
text:
Saw the title and my first thought was , well guess I’m selling this thing. But after watching I think I’ll keep it....maybe. I have my dual booted,1tb windows nvme and the other 1tb with Ubuntu 20.04. I’m a Linux user and before installing I tested it out with an external ssd. The WiFi was definitely a problem(came with Realtek ) so I bought an ax200ngw card for $20 off Amazon and WiFi worked under Linux. I noticed that the fan modes work OOB with Ubuntu so that great. My only other agreement with this video is the price. When I bought it it was $1500 before tax and shipping. Not terrible when compared to what was included and price comparison to the zephyr but still a bit more than I’d like. Other than that, great laptop. 

Also, if you’re into vfio/gpu pass through this thing is perfect. Under Linux I have the 3060 passed through and can load windows 10 in a vm for gaming. What’s the point you may be asking? Because why not. Plus I’m working towards it being Linux only. I'd love something with a little bit of portability that I could take to bed of an evening when I'm away from my custom rig, but what I've learned is that they're all stupidly loud and there's not a single laptop on the market that can cool a CPU properly. They basically all go over 95c and throttle. Whether that be the quad fans on the Alienwares, the liquid metal on the asus ones or vapour chambers on the new razers and some legions, they all hit 90/95c within minutes and throttle. 

I don't care if that's made to spec. I'm sure it is and it's why I won't dumb load of money one any of them yet. Someone out there build a system that can maintain a temp between 80-90c max without throttling, vapour chambers, silly fans and liquid metal ain't doing it. Someone make me that laptop and I'll snap it up!

author: @iftea7
text:
I own this model, bought it late June 2021 just before tax time yess!
Anyone considering this laptop for gaming - Buy it, it's excellent. 
yep, power brick is Big.
Fan noise is very good from idle to gaming - trust me, Lenovo software does an excellent job of fan speed management and thus noise. 
The thing is - the fans don't have high pitched noise - it's just a whoosh noise. You won't notice it during gaming. 
It's not loud enough to annoy your other half sitting next to you. 
WiFi is great, no online gaming issues. 
RAM - not affected yet.. But as Jarrod points out the gaming performance is strong for any current gen title. 
Lastly, the screen - it's not as colour accurate as my monitor but close. Gsync is excellent - smooth and fast gaming response on this screen.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @tomatdoras
text:
I have my Legion 5 5800h and 3060 for about a week, after watching all your videos on it. The 2 downsides I have is:

Battery - granted, is a lot smaller than the one you have, my battery looks like it left room for a 2.5" SSD, though there's no option to add one
Networking in general - Either over ethernet or Wifi, my network seems to max out at 11.8mb, no matter where I download from, or if it's wifi or ethernet. 

The odd thing is, is that it can do more, but "shows" me that it's only doing this amount. For example, on any speed test site it tells me my upload is 0.3mb, but I can stream to YouTube at 15mbps not a problem, so i'm not sure what the software is doing to give it this. I've disabled all networking options that could cause it in Vantage, but I've just learned to deal with it's quirks, hoping that there may be an update down the line, and as you mention, updating the wifi card will really help.

All in all, I'm happy enough, I got this model with a 120hz screen and 8gb ram (upgraded that, too) for €1099, which was also the cheapest gaming laptop the store had with an RTX card, but was also the best laptop in the store from what I saw on the specsheets.

Thank you for showing me this laptop, I'll always be appreciative of it

I am using Lenovo Legion 5i 2020. As this is desktop replacement laptop I care little for battery life. author: @23vikky
text:
This is an awesome laptop and I am really loving using it over the last 1 month. That said, I have 2 major gripes and that is with the display.

1. Cannot reduce the Refresh rate. While 165 Hz is really awesome to have, users should have been given the option to reduce it to 60 Hz to save battery life when we are doing activities that do not need the high RR. I tried all options and there is absolutely no option to reduce the refresh rate.

2. Not sure if the issue is with my unit or an overall one. The default color configuration of the screen has a prominent yellow tinge - like, it has the night light mode turned ON by default. This is with both Optimus and NVIDIA. I have calibrated the display to make white look white in both of these but I an not 100% happy with the colors as end of the day, I have made a manual adjustment. Also, I feel that the color reproduction is slightly different when I use Optimus vs NVIDIA.

Also, when I switch from Optimus to NVIDIA, the original color configuration comes up. I have to open the "Calibrate Color Display" and move 1step forward and close it to get my custom re-calibrated color. Please let me know if there is any way to correct this issue.

I have had a legion 5 (R5 5600H + RTX 3060) for a couple of months now. Generally speaking, it is a good laptop for the price (about 1250 USD after conversion). Here is my list of problems: 

1. WiFi performance = I do not care about the best speed possible but I have problem with the signal reception. In the same spot where my old Precision 5510 had almost a full signal, I now have almost none. Also the wifi performance is not very consistent. 

2. My touch pad is a little loose on the left side. 

3. Sometimes strange gaming performance = I am in turbo mode, running only dedicated GPU, power mode slider set to best performance, laptop on a cooler pad, no throttling and still not very good performance. It gets better after restarting the computer (and there is no process slowing the computer down in the background).

4. It is not possible to switch to 60 hz mode to save battery. So the battery life is very bad for a 80 wh.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @Demoodite
text:
I'm using that exact device for about 4 months.
Though some might think you are going over really minor things, I have to say you summed the biggest issues pretty good.
My device had 8 gb of slow ram and It was underperforming. I don't know if it is good or not in general, but I added another 8gb stick with faster timing and I got a really great performance uplift. Without removing the old and slow stick and just by adding a faster one alongside it.
For the Linux wi-fi problem I have to say I installed Manjaro Linux from the first day I got the laptop and my wi-fi is working perfectly since that day. I don't have any ideas about ubuntu. Maybe it is related to the Kernel and new only versions have Legion 5's wi-fi driver. Manjaro Linux's kernel is updated as fast as any new release rolling out and Ubuntu gets updated less often. (In a fixed 6 month schedule to be precise)
Other than that, the brick is heavy in itself and also the cable is one hell of a beasty cable! It is not a light package but I guess that is the price of one of the best performing 3060 laptops.
Despite all of this, some Legion 5s like mine have a mediocre 120hz display. I'm not a big color accuracy lover and the display is fine in my opinion. But it could be a real problem for graphic designers and people who are more sensitive to color inaccuracy.
In the end I absolutely love this laptop! I'm currently playing DOOM Eternal on ultra (high textures due to vram limitation but basically it makes no difference) with Ray Tracing and DLSS quality at constant 120fps. This machine is really really good as a powerful midrange gaming oriented laptop.

text: @xt355 I’m not an expert but I will give you some of my personal thoughts on these. The Lenovo legion 7i seems very good to me as the performance is great, decent battery life, nice build quality and well done rgb (if that’s your thing,) it also has a 16:10 aspect ratio screen which is very nice. only downside the Legion is that you get some slower x16 memory. This laptop comes with advanced optimus. The MSI GE76 is a good pick if you want the most elite gaming performance in a laptop. Although this is compromised with meh build quality and battery life. This laptop has a MUX switch. The Asus S17 is a good laptop with a good screen, nice build quality, ok battery life (6ish hours with normal use.) the only thing that’s holding me back from recommending this one is that the performance is a little lacking compared to the others as the 3080 only has a 140w power draw compared the others 165w power draw. I’ve also heard that there is this weird rattling sound when running from other reviewers. The Alienware X17 is also very good with some large overclocking head room, very solid build quality, decent battery life. Although the Asthetics aren’t for everyone. Pretty good gaming performance too. This laptop has advanced optimus. Overall, I would pick the Lenovo legion 7i as it is (in my opinion) the best all rounder. Although if you REALLY need that extra performance then I would go for the GE76

source_title: Screen Automatically Changes Brightness (Fix)
author: @FlareSFM
text:
This is kind of late but Bite-size random, Please pin this so that people can see it! (Read below for help)




Option no.1 : 


Find your way to the control panel, Then press on power options. Then a setting should be selected (Like high performance or balanced or power saver) 
Depending on what setting you have selected, Press on the "Change plan settings button". Then a click on the blue text "Change advanced power settings".
There now should be a list with a bunch of pluses ( + ). Scroll down to display and click on the plus. There should be an "Enable adaptive brightness" Tab.
Click on it and turn that setting off. If there is no adaptive brightness tab. Go down to step 2.

Option no.2

If you don't have the adaptive brightness option, your monitor should have some sort of button that opens a menu or something.
I have the MSI MAG271CR Curved monitor, And it has a red button behind it on the bottom right of it. When I click it it opens up a menu with some tabs and different display options.
If you see an HDCR option, Turn it off or disable it. HDCR stands for 'high dynamic contrast range'. It essentially changes the contrast or brightness on your monitor depending on how bright your screen is. If you turn that off, Your monitor should stay at the desired or set contrast/brightness until enabled again.

author: @kyletsit
text:
i bought the cheapest oled i could find (from lenovo), thinking i cheaped out after i experienced some unexpected flaws like the absence of a peak brightness mode, despite the spect stating 1000 nits at 3%, or the fact you need DSC to run it at full spec 2k 280hz HDR, even tho the marketed HDMI 2.1 port should have been fine without compression.
but seeing how the vastly more expensive OLEDs have these kinds of arctifacts, im actually satisfied in the end.

btw my monitor is a QD-OLED and i browse the internet a lot on it. i easily noticed the text issue, but i got used to it pretty well.
also im on linux and was able to get a QD-OLED verison of the program responsible for subpixel rendering, which i believe made it better

also FYI: standard RGB stripe pixel layouts have theoretically the same problem as qd-oleds with their text rendering (maybe slightly better), but its long been remedied by subpixel rendering TUNED FOR RGB STRIPE LAYOUTS. this rendering is, as far as i understand, baked into most software. So the problem is not only getting the right subpixel rendering into all apps which dont use the system solution, but avoiding the wrong one as well. basically, out of the box qd-oleds theoretically look worse because all software expects rgb stripe. not because qd-oled is way worse at subpixel rendering. i think

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @Moshe_Dayan44
text: Thanks for the overview of issues with the Legion 5. By no means is this a bad laptop: it's actually still arguably the best Ryzen 5800h+3060 combo machine you can buy (if you CAN buy it). But I actually returned mine for reasons related to some of the issues you mentioned here, such as the lack of fan control. Frankly, I'd also like more control over the CPU speed, but that just doesn't seem possible. The combination of these two omissions produced a gaming experience where the fans would speed up whenever the CPU went over 79 degrees, and then slow down again whenever it went below 80 degrees, which happens frequently enough in my favorite game to make it annoying. Really, I wanted to just either slow down the CPU a little bit, or change the fan curve to ignore temps of up to 82 degrees, but I couldn't do either. The other annoyances I had were the cheap-feeling keys. Yes, I know it's a Lenovo, and they're supposed to have some of the best keyboards, and I use T-series Lenovos at work all the time, and they do have great keyboards. But the one in the current Legion 5 just feels delicate and cheap, like the keys will stop working way before the laptop is obsolete. I think they just keep making the plastic thinner and thinner until there's an issue or something. However, in the end, what compelled me to return it before it was too late was the 6GB video memory. Even at 1080p, that's not quite enough for ultra settings in some games, and I'll be damned if I'm going to turn down the texture quality settings on a brand new, not-cheap gaming laptop because it already comes out of the box with insufficient video RAM. Just one last thing: I didn't have a problem with the 300w power brick, as I frequently see power bricks burn out when they're overspecced (paired with a laptop that requires very nearly the full wattage of the PS). I was actually pleased that the 300w brick was shipped with the 3060 model I had because it means the brick runs much cooler and will likely last as long as the laptop.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @MintyLime
text:
I'm still on a 2080ti but I don't even care much to upgrade it at this point because getting an OLED feels like way more of an upgrade than if I spent thousands on the latest GPU. It makes all the older games I play look so much better than any graphical upgrade could ever achieve. I finally went back to Bioshock and it's stupid how good it looks with the Luma mod enabling native HDR. Even just auto HDR is good on the games it supports. I'll take Halo at 250fps HDR any day over the performance riddled mess a modern AAA title provides. But even in those games I don't care as much as I used to about running ultra settings. I just want it to look presentable enough to let the monitor do the work making it pop. There are so many great new games from AA and indie devs that run perfectly and for those an OLED is a huge upgrade compared to a new GPU. Boltgun 2 for example.

Worst case whenever there's a AAA game I'm interested in with the usual PC issues I just hook up the Series X to my monitor and play on that since at least most games will play stable enough on performance mode and the monitor helps make up for any visual downgrade. But generally I've been playing games with stylized graphics over "realism" and they look incredible with a good OLED when compared to forced RT at 30fps with constant boiling artifacts.

Online you'll sometimes see people talk down about HDR and stuff but I guarantee they've never seen it for themselves. But I don't blame people too much for not understanding what it's actually like when it's constantly poorly marketed and their opinions are colored by a LED TV with like 400 nits claiming to have HDR. I thought my mini LED TV with local dimming looked good but HDR didn't seem like that big of a deal. Then I got an OLED and realized that TV could barely even be considered HDR. There's still people who think HDR is just another word for bloom or some color thing.

I'm excited to get back into some classic horror games now that the blacks aren't washed out and flashlights are actually like real blinding flashlights. I intend to play Amnesia: The Bunker and it's gonna be fuckin terrifying how dark the bunker is.

text: Ultrawide OLED (21:9) for Ultimate Immersion, 34" 1440p, or 39" 5K2K if you have the power. Never going back to 16:9 after having Ultrawide for 5 years now, first 2 with LCD 144 Hz, last 3 with OLED 175 Hz. I even had a 4K/UHD 32" OLED at home for a few weeks just to try it, and there is absolutely no way I will be using a 32" 4K over a 34" even if that 34" is 1440p. Only if you play fast paced shooters and nothing else, then stay at 16:9, but don't go bigger than 27" because thats too big here.

text:
I am not sure but with OLED panel uniformity shouldn’t be an issue anymore. Because that is usually from uneven backlighting, but on OLED there is no backlighting. I also know the weird grey but it’s not bad on my OLED, I just wondered why I didn’t read about it in any reviews. Actually I also realized my eyes‘ „contrast“ is worse than the OLED because there are situations where I see slight ghosting around e.g. a white text on black background that ISN’T THERE, it’s just stuff happening in my eyes due to lack of perfect vision. I do not really read anything off my OLED though because I got so conditioned by the 4h refresh that I only use it for watching video or playing video games, otherwise it is turned off and I use my IPS display. Even if burn-in is not an issue yet, HDR got dimmer since I have it. I think Mini-LED might be the future, but it’s still too expensive. OLED has a lot of drawbacks though but I am so happy I don’t have to worry about grey corners that should be black :).
Edit: 
I don’t think I mean Mini-LED, there is another technology similar, without backlight, that is more expensive. 
But mini-LED is what I would have tried if a friend would have recommended against an OLED. 
OH and also, why is text clarity, grey or burn-in not an issue on phones anymore but on big displays? That is the panel technology we need in desktop screens.

author: @boogiexx
text:
Hi, love your reviews — really top-notch, detailed stuff.

I'm a bit baffled by your LatencyMon results across the Legion Pro 7 lineup. In your 2025 tests (275HX, different GPU tiers) I'm seeing very different peak DPC numbers — one config came in around 463 µs, another around 830 µs. Then in your review of the new 2026 version (290HX Plus / RTX 5090), the peak DPC jumped to roughly 1,900 µs and LatencyMon actually flagged it as having trouble with real-time audio — worst result of the bunch, despite being the newest chip the problem is the same with 5070 12 GB GPU version.

A couple of things stood out that made me want to ask:

1. Is each unit tested with a clean Windows install, or the same OS install reused/updated across review units?
2. Are Vantage, RGB control software, and any power-management utilities uninstalled or disabled before the test, or left as shipped?
3. Is Windows Update / background telemetry disabled during the test window?
4. For the 290HX Plus unit specifically — I noticed the hard pagefault count was over 11,000, versus 400–500 on the earlier units. Any idea what drove that? It makes me wonder if something (indexing, updates, low free RAM at test time) was running in the background rather than it being a clean idle measurement.
5. Are all your LatencyMon runs done idle, right after boot, on AC power, same duration?

Not trying to nitpick — I'm genuinely trying to figure out if the 290HX Plus result reflects the platform (new BIOS/power management still maturing) or just test conditions on that particular run, since I'm deciding between these for audio production (Cubase) and DPC stability matters a lot for me. Would really appreciate knowing your test protocol so I can weigh the numbers properly. Thanks for the great content either way!

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @StePloOseNsoN
text:
This is all very interesting, of course, but in the final analysis, if you cut through all the fluff, an OLED only outperforms a good IPS or QLED in a completely dark room, in scenes with a full black level. Otherwise, if you have a good IPS or QLED panel, you won't notice any difference. However, pixel shifting is clearly visible if you're focused on one point (shooter or working with documents), and you constantly need to try to remove all static images as much as possible. The start menu, the browser's top bar, and so on and so forth. And it's a constant hassle. They still burn out, maybe more slowly than before, but still. And what about turning it off every 4-6 hours to clear the pixels? That's just brutal: you're in the middle of a heated battle, and the monitor just keeps turning off. Sure, you can delay it, but then the pixels will burn out. Overall, I'm not discouraging you from buying one. You might use it for the first couple of days in some scenarios where OLED looks great, but then you'll get tired of it. Even in daylight, even in a 1:1 comparison, there's no difference.

By the way, it's worth noting that OLEDs often have issues with grayscale, with gradients and uneven fills. Personally, this really irritates me. I haven't encountered this with other types of panels.

Anyway, thanks for the video.
