source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @ppevader-u2t
text:
I remember when I got my 5090 at launch for 2500 after tax. People called me stupid. I agree, buying a gpu at that price was a bit much for gaming, but I have always settled for the xx80 tier ir x80 tier back in that day. I wanted to get a halo gpu. Man am I glad I didn't listen. 

As for the topic, OLED ruined me as well. I love oled, but hate that I ever tried it. Now I have a G5, S90D, and just got the c6 48 inch for my pc (wanted 1500 nits and it was also confirmed to be 1st gen tandem like the g5). I just got a TCL qm8l for my folks which is absolutely overkill for them and in all honesty I noticed right off the bat the dip in quality. Everyone told me it was OLED like and I just don't see it. Don't get me wrong, for the price it is great. However at the end of the lifespan of mid tier oleds you can get some amazing deals. I just hate I can notice the difference so much. 4 years ago I was using cheap Insignia brand tvs or bottom tier Samsung LCD tvs and was completely happy. Then I got a great deal on a S95B at the end of 2022 and it absolutely made me an OLED snob. 

Hell I just sold my OneXplayer Apex for the X2 mini pro so I could get a stupid OLED panel. Granted it only cost me $150 of new money after the sale, but still. I hate I love OLED so much. I'm not one of those people who shit on LED though. There are still some benefits to that tech, especially in certain watch scenarios. I wouldn't get an OLED if I watched a lot of news or sports with the logo up all the time, even with the advancement of burn in tech. I also wouldn't get OLED if you aren't a movie buff or serious gamer. Even if you are those things and like massive screens it may be better to go LED for the price at larger sizes. I would have never got my g5 at 77 inches for 3k plus. I got it for like 2500 off greentoe.

I guess to sum it up. Don't try OLED if you haven't lmao. Sure most phones have it now, but I always chuckle when people say they don't think oled is that great if all they have tried is their phones. Don't let people fomo you into oled if modern miniled is enough for you. Like I said, miniled is solid especially for the price to size ratio. If you have tried a newer oled tv or monitor and it doesn't make that much of a difference to you stay with the cheaper option. If you want OLED I would never get them when they first come out. They are super overpriced. If it is your first OLED tv I would always wait until black friday or look at the previous year tvs. I would also stick with mid tier s90 for samsung or c series for LG. IMO the bottom tier B series and s85 series are a bit too dim for someone use to a decent miniled. Finally if you are looking at miniled and oled and they are around the same price or hell if the miniled is more expensive like a Sony.....get the OLED every time. Especially if you are gaming.

author: @Octorious
text:
Nope, this is incorrect. The instructions are misleading. Having it barely visible tells your TV that your display caps out at a peak brightness level 1 to 2 clicks lower (which can be a couple hundred nits!), than it actually does.

I wasn't aware of this myself either until a couple of months ago as it was highlighted by TV & display calibration experts like Vincent from the HDTVTest channel, and a few others. These menus really need updating to better explain what should be done here. Doing it as they suggest gives okay results, but it's not what it should be. author: @sheep7255
text: was confused why headphone show was reviewing monitors lol. You have different issues with OLED's than I have. I don't find any issues with text fringing with my 27" 1440p QD-OLED, so you're incredibly sensitive to it, I'd say. The problems I have is that I don't make use of the contrast ratio a lot, considering that the content I consume simply doesn't have much (CS2, valorant, tf2, and some racing sims driving daytime all the time).Another problem I have is that the motion clarity on my 500hz OLED is shit compared to my crappy crt. And, due to sample and hold, lower fps only makes it worse, whilst CRT's dgaf about that. I didn't go G-Sync pulsar because nvidia exclusive and the 500hz oled was cheaper. I've tried using the testufo shaderglass CRT emulator, and it has problems I can't tune out, and ends up not being a nice experience, and it doesn't even properly fix the motion clarity at lower fps'. In general, I've been constantly sad when using my OLED, because the ways it is so good are things I don't use or they suck at. Zowie has DyAc 3 on the way, so if that is a gpu agnostic pulsar system. I'm quite keen on it, but it will probably be limited to 24" 1080p and cost double my current OLED. Also, HDR sucks, but I'm currently trying just having it on all of the time, so let's see how I feel about it after some time. The colors also kinda suck, because you get so much color space, but the computer doesn't know that you do, so everything becomes horridly oversaturated. HDR kinda fixes it, because the pc knows what colors it can do, and ACM can also fix it, but I find the best results just using the inbuilt sRGB mode. Brightness isn't great, considering that Mini LED can do sustained 1000 nits 100% coverage, mine can do about 300, so in those bright scenes, it's just not particularly bright, but I haven't compared against a good mini led, so maybe I'll eat my words

What you'll also forget is some important things when it comes to windows hdr: Microsoft forces scRGB over the SDR content in short which is wrong and that's why HDR is looking washed out when displaying SDR content inside HDR or when HDR is activated. This is also applicable to the HDR Calibration App which will only effect HDR content mastered in SRGB which most content including sdr content such as the desktop are not. 

Basically the HDR Calibration app is only then useful if you exactly know that the content you display is origianally mastered SRGB or scRGB.

Most content is in gamma 2.2 which makes the calibration app not really reliable because it messes with content which is in HDR10 PQ for example or sdr content with gamma 2.2.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @dkindig
text:
I have a 3rd gen QD-OLED panel, 32" 240 Hz.  I have over 3400 hours on it so far, have all the anti-burn-in stuff turned on (unnoticeable, btw), and while I try to keep up with pixel refreshes every 4 hours I have only done about 70% of those because of long gaming sessions.  I check my monitor periodically with varying shades of gray backgrounds and have yet to find ANY evidence of burn-in.  QD-OLED has the best color saturation, the extra backlight in WOLED tends to wash out colors in HDR mode.  The response time of OLED monitors is both a blessing and a curse.  If you're going to run frame rates of 140 and up, you're golden.  Once you drop down below 80-90 fps the motion clarity really shows the low frame rates.

OLED really shows off one of the most dramatic visual improvements: proper luminance from black to full white.  I'm a home theater enthusiast and calibrate my own stuff, I have a colorimeter and a spectrophotometer.  These days most televisions and monitors are very good with color calibration right out of the box.  Where calibration has the most impact is getting light output, or luminance, set correctly across the intensity range from 0% to 100%.  This gives you the best contrast levels and the best upgrade to the performance.  A note on HDR:  most peak 1000 modes on QD-OLED's will end up dimming overall light levels at lower percentages in order to make 1000 nits.  If you see a scene darkening overall when you switch from True HDR mode to Peak 1000, you're seeing the effect in action.  I like more accurate lighting levels so I run my monitor at True HDR 400.  If you're looking for the best HDR in a game that doesn't have real HDR, RenoDX is a great option.

The thing about fringing is that your brain gets used to it, it's almost hard to believe.
When i first got my AW3423DW (1st gen QDOLED) i immediately noticed the fringing on the Aleinware logo when it first turned on. it was TERRIBLE. I could not stop looking for it.
But after a almost a week my brain tuned it out completely.

Here's an experiment you should try. Get a monitor that you think has no fringing, then turn it 180 degrees upside down (if you have a monitor arm or if the stand supports it) and change orientation to landscape (flipped). You will notice fringing instantly because now the arangement of the subpixels is different and your brain isn't used to it.

TLDR it's a problem but there is significant brain burn in.
OFC now with the new RGB Stripe QD‑OLED panels should be way better.

source_title: QD OLED Is Better Than WOLED
author: @paulcox2447
text:
@Andrey_Kor The difference in spectral power distribution changes how the same colors look to your eyes even though a meter will say it's the same.  QD OLED colors are more intense subjectively speaking all things equal.  It's either a love it or hate it kind of thing.  For me it's almost too intense like playing a game on acid. It's great on bright colorful tech demo's though and content where it's appreciated. The spectral power distribution is very different than real life even if it's technically reproducing it accurately so more plain "real life" scenes seem to intense.  Conversely when I boost the colors on an oled it never has quite the same effect due to the color brightness and spectral power distribution differences.

The best calibrators can tweak by eye to account for this and keep the overall look of the different techs in line with each other.  The meter gets you close, but it doesn't tell the whole story.  As far as I know most content is graded on dual layer LCD's or WOLED panels.  So QD OLED becomes the one that is critical to tweak if you want it to look natural.

source_title: QD OLED Is Better Than WOLED
author: @rweasp
text: @Andrey_Kor Not fantasy at all, there are small differences in the electronics and panel design that change the way light/colours are transmitted even in SDR. Side by side, there are differences between them, they are small but noticeable, but not something you would even notice if using one on its own and for 99% of people they won't even care/notice. And certainly not enough to warrant the toxic shitflinging between QD or WOLED owners who try and gaslight people into the differences make any tangible difference after making the shift from IPS > OLED. I do colour critical work for a living so I am susceptible to tiny differences, but I am an edge case here.

source_title: QD OLED Is Better Than WOLED
author: @rweasp
text: In a dark/very dimly lit room (which is what you SHOULD be using OLEDs for, regardless of panel type) my Penta QD beats the Tandem WOLED. Perfect uniformity, zero banding, greater colour volume, better presentation overall. Not saying Tandems can't have these of course (panel lottery), but I've had multiple premium-level screens of both types, and it is the same result every time for me. My current king is the PG32UCDM3, it is absolutely glorious in my light controlled room (VERY dim warm lamp off to the right, perfect blacks with no raising tested against my WOLED).I also use my screens in SDR 99% of the time fully calibrated at 90 nits, and again the Penta QD outshines the Tandems here. I also just want to say the level of rhetoric of QD vs WOLED at the moment is absolutely cancer and toxic, people really just need to chill out and enjoy their screens. If you are using them in their intended ideal environment, both are fantastic (panel lottery nonsense excluded).

text: @poke-you-tube  SDR calibration is done to 100 nits, HDR sets paper-white to 203 nits.  The only items in HDR that get set to maximum are any highlights in the image.  It looks bright, but it's not set to maximum.  ZeNeo.X is correct on this.  What you're seeing and confusing with maximum brightness is either a monitor mode setting error OR terrible Auto HDR.  If you go into HDR mode and everything looks overly bright and washed out you either have your monitor set incorrectly or you are trying to wring HDR out of something like an IPS monitor.

source_title: Lenovo Legion Pro 7i (2026) Review - Still one of the Best?
author: @ExHunt
text:
I'm using last year's black Lenovo Legion Pro 7 16IAX10H

For a machine that costs around €4,000, it simply doesn't feel premium at all. I have no complaints about the performance - the CPU and GPU are excellent - but the overall build quality, materials, and user experience are disappointing.

Here are my main issues:

• It attracts fingerprints everywhere, even on the keyboard keys, and some of them are surprisingly difficult to clean off.
• It constantly drains the battery even while plugged into the wall using the massive and mostly pointless 400W power brick.
• Lenovo's software is extremely buggy. You can't properly configure the RGB lighting, and despite contacting support, the issues were never fixed. It also frequently charges the battery above the 80% limit even when the charging threshold is enabled.
• The worst part is the audio. These are some of the worst laptop speakers I've ever heard. The sound quality is absolutely terrible. Even my phone sounds better than this expensive laptop.
• The OLED display is also a mixed bag. Lenovo's heavily advertised burn-in protection features will most likely stay disabled because they're incredibly annoying in daily use. For example, the screen keeps dimming while watching videos. In practice, the only protection you'll probably end up using is the Windows screen timeout. As I mentioned earlier, Lenovo's software is simply not reliable enough.
• The lack of both an SD card reader and a fingerprint scanner is frankly ridiculous

Before this, I owned an older Asus Zephyrus G16, and honestly it felt better in almost every way. It was a laptop that you actually wanted to pick up and use, and the speakers were fantastic. Unfortunately, I no longer trust Asus either because that laptop started developing hardware issues and gave me several technical problems.

That said, I wouldn't buy Lenovo again either. Paying a premium price just for a powerful CPU and GPU isn't enough for me. At this price point, the entire experience should feel premium, and the Legion 7 Pro simply doesn't.

source_title: Every PS5 User Gets This WRONG! - HDR Settings Guide
author: @apoorvacharya3158
text:
Turn HGIG on (mandatory) and use below calibration guidelines for OLED, Mini-LED,QLED or similar tvs.

For Sony’s first party games (like Spiderman 2 , GOW Ragnarok etc.) that uses PS5 HDR calibration menu:
Screen 1 & 2 => Make sun barely visible (Doing this will still allow first party games to display tv’s max peak brightness without clipping in highlights).
3rd Screen => One click up from the lowest value to make the sun barely barely visible - Doing this won't raise black level in first party games. Instead It will give nice shadow details in dark/scenes areas while still displaying inky/deep blacks.

Third Party Games(Like Hogwarts legacy, Jedi Survivor, etc) that uses PS5 HDR calibration Menu:
Sreen 1 & 2 => Make sun completely invisible (One step higher from barely visible or else third party games won’t output your tv’s max peak brightness).
3rd Screen => All the way down to zero clicks (anything other than zero clicks will turn deep blacks to greyish blacks on third party games).

Note: To make most out of PS5 HDR gaming, Ensure that your tv supports HDMI 2.1  and is an OLED screen OR LCD/LED that has local dimming algorithm. Anything other than this will result in washed out HDR experience

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @joem80000D
text:
Here’s my advice:

The latest QD-OLED panels are 5th-gen and feature a full RGB-stripe subpixel layout. However, they’re not available in 4K yet, so you’re stuck with lower pixel density (PPI). Personally, I’d wait a few months for a 32-inch 4K 5th-gen QD-OLED rather than buy one of the recently released 4th-gen WOLED monitors, which also feature the new RGB-stripe layout.

QD-OLED is generally considered the better choice for gaming visuals, especially when it comes to HDR colors and overall image quality.

When buying a gaming monitor, I’d focus on three things: panel technology, panel generation, and what your PC can comfortably run.

For demanding games at 4K or 5K, I’d personally recommend an RTX 5090. An RTX 5080 is still powerful, but you’ll have to lower or disable certain graphics settings in some games to maintain high frame rates. Obviously, that matters less in lightweight games like Valorant, which are much easier to run.

Beyond the panel itself, pay attention to the monitor’s physical controls, OSD (on-screen display), and overall usability. Personally, I’d avoid Samsung monitors.

One thing worth understanding is that brands like MSI and ASUS often use the same underlying OLED panels from the same manufacturers. So if both brands offer a monitor using the same generation and model of QD-OLED panel, the differences generally come down to things like the power supply, cooling, firmware, OSD, physical controls, build quality, and warranty.

In other words, don’t choose a monitor based on the brand name alone. Choose the panel first, then compare how each manufacturer implements it.

source_title: Is HDR Worse? - HDR vs SDR On Monitors & TVs
author: @desmondbrown5508
text: Nah, yeah it is 100% not the end user's fault that the industry at large makes this such an issue.  People rightfully expect that plugging in and using HDR SHOULD be as easy as plugging it in and enabling it and then it looks great, maybe with some subtle tweaks at best.  The issue right now is that there are too many standards and no one is agreeing on the one to stick to for now and so on some monitors/TVs it looks bad, hell then there's Window's dog** implementation of it, which works in some instances but doesn't in others.  And finally there are games not using it properly (possibly b/c the APIs are convoluted nonsense, who knows).  On controlled platforms like consoles, HDR tends too look fine, better even in all cases.  But the industry really needs to codify a 10 year standard and then every 10 years upgrade to the newer better one (once all existing tech is ready for it).  There needs to be an actual plan here, instead of everyone adhering to whatever the hell they want, leading to all kinds of crappy incompatibility issues and worse overall results that are inconsistent between each user.  There are tools to "fix" this but right now it's a big f***ing mess, because realistically people shouldn't need to use tools.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @electronichq974
text: It looks like a lot of people had this problem when upgrading. I'm not gonna say "it's common sense" because that sound disrespectful, but when it comes to any PC upgrade it's essential to see how that upgrade gels with whatever hardware you already own. You wouldn't buy a Ferrari sports engine and throw it into a Peugeot 205 because the rest of the Peugeot won't be able to keep up with it unless other Peugeot parts are replaced too. I too bought a 4K MSI QD-OLED, but that's only because I did research and saw my new rig would be able to utilize it to its full potential, and with additional headroom. I chose 165hz over a 244hz because I wanted that additional headroom for when games become even more demanding. Another example is I had to choose a powerful CPU so as to not bottleneck my GPU too much. I wouldn't have known this had I not thoughly researched before handing over large sums of money. My point is there's a lot to consider, and doing your research before handing over large amounts of money for anything should be par the course. Anything less is negligence.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @SmoothSportsGaming
text:
I have a 3060 t.i/ i7 10700 and with demanding/newer games on a LG C3 1440p-1600 look nearly indistinguishable. Ive tested it I'd rather run higher/ray tracing settings in this scenario because it looks better.

Granted, I've optimized the heck out of my TV settings and PC. My hardware punches way above it's weight class because of it. The C3's interpolation also replaces the need for 120hz 120fps. The motion looks incredible, which gives you more headroom for higher settings.

It also allows my TV to use the full extent of features. When you use gsync, 120hz a lot of features get grayed out. The TV's input delay is so phenomenal that there's no percievable difference. Coupled with having the GPU do the scaling. I've switched between Gsync/stripped vs Vsync/Full features and the only big difference is how much worse the picture looks with stripped down TV features. Especially if you have to turn down settings. 

Deep optimization is not only needed for the look, but also functionality. Most of my games work great and my setup is beating PC's with better hardware. I constantly hear people having stutters,  frame drops etc....using 3080's and up using the same settings as me at 1440p-1600p.

It almost makes me feel i wasted my time playing game on monitors I've had before, and before that I've had ips with good and accurate color coverage. I will certainly upgrade to oled when time comes.

My miniled was the best thing i upgraded about my pc setup period, and now i tell everyone, that any upgrade is worthless before you get a good screen. Hell i rather stay on my arc b580 with miniled or oled than switch to 5090 but being forced to use regular ips.

This monitor is titan army p275ms+, it's 27", 1440p, fast ips, miniled, 10 bit hdr, it's something like 1100 nits, it's brighter than my s25u when shining light onto it. But it's probably hard to get depending on region you in, i ordered it from china and got it for $250.

author: @givemeanameman1
text:
ambient temps matter...
Temperature at OLED layer
~20–30°C Ideal operating range; slow degradation
~30–40°C Normal for many monitors; some acceleration
~40–50°C Noticeably faster aging, especially at high brightness
~50–60°C+ Significantly increased degradation risk
Gaming/high brightness puts the Oled at 10-20c over ambient.
So if you live in a climate thats 30-40c part of the year, and gaming the OLED is going to burn in far faster then a 18c aircon controlled 24h room.

author: @67L48
text:
Thanks for the update.  My use model is less about portability and more about convenience.  When I was in the corporate world, I was traveling 60,000 miles per year and a lightweight, minimalist laptop was key.  100% Microsoft Office use and similar loads -- minor, easy, no gaming.  I wanted light, portable, and minimalist.  As a home user, I am not looking for actual portability ... I'm not taking my laptop on cross-continental journeys.  I just want to be able to work and play on my couch, as opposed to a desk in an office ... and I want a hefty GPU that can handle gaming demands.

So, with that said, I appreciate huge 400W power bricks and design choices (e.g., heavier heat sinks and fans) that prioritize performance over portability.  Similarly, I don't care tons about battery life and performance caps when the power cord is disconnected.  Again, I'm just sitting on a couch with the PC still plugged in.

The one thing that keeps ringing true with Lenovo is that it does not throttle the laptop.  It allows massive amounts of power to both be supplied and used by the hardware.  While I understand that this becomes inconvenient when traveling from Denver to Tokyo, I am most interested in maximizing performance when I'm moving about my own home.

I'm currently living with an HP with a hardware defect, along with various hardware limitations.  I'm waiting (in summer 2026) for the Lenovo Pro 7i to become affordable to me, which basically means waiting a few months until Black Friday deals hit again. (i.e., that 7i 5080 is around $2,500 - $2,600 for the past few months in June 2026; the lowest price was in the 2025 holiday shopping months for around $2,000 - $2,1000.  I'm waiting for the 7i 5080 to again hit that ~$2000 price point. Wish me luck)

I appreciate your quick-hitting, data-driven approach to these videos.  No long narratives, I don't have to hear stories about what you had for breakfast, and so on.  Just awesome feedback on actual usage, objective performance data, and conclusions derived from the former with the unspoken invitation for the audience to then make ultimate purchase decisions on how those data intersect with their personal use needs and preferences.  Cheers!

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @rfrakctured
text:
Got my Legion 5 in March 2021. I've been extremely satisfied with it as my daily work and play machine. However, after 2 years of active use and transportation, it has developed some quirks. The first thing to fail was my stock hard drive. After that, keyboard's function row began to die. The Esc key, F4 - F6, and left Alt key have stopped working. My E doesn't always work, either. (Important for gaming!) Since these control the most useful functions, like brightness, and Alt-Tabbing, it's disappointing to have to manually adjust these settings. Also, the LCD screen has suffered some burn-in. The bottom of the screen has permanent vertical streaks staining my view of the taskbar at all times, which itself leaves a slightly permanent shadow of its outline on the display.

I still recommend it, as it has survived more than its fair share of travel (and moisture) over the last 3 years. I think if I can replace the bad keys, I would be happy to keep this machine for another 5 years. For other long term users, I recommend keeping your brightness down a notch, setting your taskbar to Auto-Hide, and picking a short delay for your screen saver! And always make regular backups of your data, no matter what you buy, because you never know! :)

Good luck!

source_title: Is HDR Worse? - HDR vs SDR On Monitors & TVs
author: @dnd6379
text: HDR doesn't actually have much wider color gamut support over SDR in the real world, no skin tone is outside the SDR range, nothing in nature is outside SDR range. Brightness is relative and your eyes will compensate for a dark or bright picture. Every display manufacturer will have their own way of calibrating an HDR image (which is not how the artist intended), properly converted SDR will look identical to HDR 99.99% of the time. Even the highest end thousands of dollars studio monitors cannot display all of bt2020 or 2100. If HDR looks more vibrant it's because it's over saturated if SDR looks dull it's because it was improperly converted from HDR. No animal needs HDR to authentically represent it's colors, SDR can do all of that, the YouTube "tests" only show how badly HDR content is converted to SDR or how over saturated HDR is and that's why you see a difference, you shouldn't actually be seeing any difference between HDR and SDR in almost any case.

author: @ysesh463
text: RGB stripe also significantly improves the banding issues on W-OLED. Typical W-OLED displays have an RGWB stripe subpixel layout, where there's a dedicated white subpixel. Similar to how the triangular subpixel layout screws with the way computers expect text to be rendered, having that extra white subpixel screws with how large fields of solid color are rendered, and banding is a common side effect. W-OLED panels with just RGB stripe and no extra white subpixel are starting to come out (the new AW3926QW is one of the first ones, and initial reviews have shown it to be much improved in this respect).

author: @techsamurai11
text:
Questions: 

Why aren't there any comparisons of SDR and HDR anywhere?  

Why did TV manufacturers fake the initial comparisons by turning down the brightness to nearly 0 for SDR TVs?  If HDR was better, why fake it?

I've asked everyone on the planet to make a HDR vs SDR comparison and they avoid it like the plague. Why can't all the reviewers do a comparison and show us how HDR is better or worse?

Why do manufacturers not allow us to toggle SDR and HDR easily like we stitch scenes from Standard to Cinema?  

I'm one of the few people that has had an A/B version of SDR and HDR with an OLED laptop that hits nearly 1000 nits full window.  I've done more testing than just about anyone here and I'm not convinced about HDR.  I feel it's a mode with metadata.  It's not bad, it's not great always, and it's not better than SDR on a real SDR display.

It's just different and it can have massive issues.  Imagine watching the movie Coco in calibrated mode.  It's going to look horrible.  Same with HDR - it can be worse in a lot of content and it is. In some scenes, it can occasionally be better but overall I personally prefer a medium between SDR and HDR, maybe 75% SDR and 25% HDR.  Just highlight SDR a bit more - push it to HDR in some areas but keep that vibrant image of SDR the way it is - it's gorgeous.

source_title: HDR For Monitors Explained (And How To Configure It!)
author: @mmad1que
text:
I went through a lot of trial and error with HDR, so here are some additional recommendations to save you the trouble: that weren’t covered in the video:
1. Windows HDR Calibration app limitations
The Windows HDR Calibration app can be misleading. For example, on a Samsung Odyssey Neo G7 (with a measured peak brightness of ~1200–1300 nits for a 10% window, per Monitors Unboxed), following the square test often results in a value around ~850 nits. This is inaccurate.
Additionally, the app may suggest similar values for both peak brightness (small window) and full-frame brightness, which is not technically correct—these values should differ due to panel behavior (ABL, etc.).
Recommendation: Do not strictly rely on the square test. Instead, refer to trusted measurements (e.g., RTINGS, Monitors Unboxed) and input those values manually for more accurate calibration. UPD: This was covered in the video:)

2. Check panel-reported luminance (dxdiag)
You can export a dxdiag report and review the luminance-related values. Some OLED and Mini-LED displays already come reasonably well-calibrated at the firmware level, which can provide a more reliable baseline than the Windows tool.

3. Game-level HDR calibration matters more
Many modern AAA games (e.g., Cyberpunk, The Last of Us, Resident Evil) use their own HDR pipelines and bypass Windows HDR calibration settings.
Recommendation: Always perform HDR calibration within each game’s settings menu, as those values will take precedence over the system-level configuration. UPD: This was also covered in the video:)

4. By default, NVIDIA may use an 8-bit color depth and limited dynamic range, which is not suitable for proper HDR.
Before configuring HDR, go to the NVIDIA Control Panel (or NVIDIA App) and set:
Output color depth: 10-bit (or higher, if available)
Output dynamic range: Full
Proper HDR requires at least a 10-bit signal path, so ensuring these settings are correct is essential for accurate HDR output.

source_title: Is HDR Worse? - HDR vs SDR On Monitors & TVs
author: @paul2609
text:
When people use SDR, they don't put it on sRGB mode, which is the creator intent of game developers and filmmakers. So they got used to really bad, uncalibrated, oversaturated image without sRGB mode. Blame manufacturers for this, they don't use sRGB by default because they want to sell more TVs and monitors on a retail showfloor by oversaturating their TVs compared to the competing TV next to it so that they can make a sale. 

The industry is now aware of this and is trying to reverse this with HDR. HDR have strict standards that displays must be calibrated for atleast Rec709 (basically sRGB) or DCI-P3 (only 25% more colours than sRGB) out of the box. So when someone goes from uncalibrated, non-sRGB SDR to HDR Rec709/DCI-P3, they think it looks washed out but that is what colours are suppose to look like. Human skin are not supposed to look like it's red and sunburnt all the time, but that is what people who leave their monitors on non-sRGB mode thinks that looks good for some reason.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @rinsenpai135
text:
Hi! Last week I just got a used Legion 5 2021 (Ryzen 5 5600H + 3060 115-130W, 8GB RAM, 512GB SSD) for 840 euros and still 1 year warranty remaining (it was initially bought by someone else in early-mid 2022 and sold to a big online retailer in my country, with very little traces of use).
I could have gotten a brand new Ideapad Gaming 3 with 5800H + 90W 3060 directly from Lenovo, or an Acer Nitro 5 also with 5800H + 95W 3060 for the same price, but then I searched for some feedback online and apparently the Ideapad Gaming 3 feels cheap and runs quite hot, and the MUX switch is a deal-breaker for me as I don't want to deal with the iGPU (my previous experience with an AMD iGPU was quite disastrous in the last few months). AMD Laptop GPUs are almost non-existent in my country (7600S was 1500-1900€ which was at the same price point as some 4070 laptops earlier this month, 5500M and 6500M also fell right in the price range of most 3060 laptops) and they weren't compatible with a few things I currently wanted to do until earlier this month. And if you wonder why I didn't get a desktop PC: Simulated on PC Part Picker, a build similar to my laptop in benchmarks would have costed me 50-150 euros more, so slightly outside of my initial budget.

I bought the Legion 5 as my old laptop was starting to be very limiting in modded Minecraft, modded Cities: Skylines (Cities: Skylines 2 is right around the corner too!) and Anno 1800. I'm coming from a now 4 years-old HP Pavilion Gaming Laptop 15-ec0xxx (Ryzen 5 3550H + GTX 1650 50W) which served me quite well all this time.

I was waiting for the 4000 Laptop GPU series benchmarks to decide which laptop to choose, and just saw in another one of your videos the 4050 Laptop GPU was just barely the same as a Max-P 3060 because of its voltage limit and most laptops with a 4050 came with DDR5.
I had already bought a kit of 2x16GB DDR4-3200 CL22 Dual Rank x8 RAM several months ago and got a 1TB Samsung 970 EVO Plus earlier this month as it was getting very cheap.

So far I didn't have any problem with the Legion 5 and I'm very happy about its raw performance! (maybe because my previous laptop was ultimate-bottom tier)
It's surprisingly quiet most of the time, and even pushing the 3060 at 95-100W barely puts it above 70c. The 2 SSDs in the Legion 5 are running so cool they rarely go above 50-55c (even the 970 EVO Plus which is known for running hot).
Battery life is actually surprising: 3 hours, charged at 80%, browsing/watching YT videos and Discord without the iGPU, only using the 3060. I also didn't find the 230W power adapter to not be enough so far.

Overall, I consider it as a pretty good deal, as performance stagnation didn't make the prices drop as fast as expected... Waiting to see how it'll perform in the future! Thank you for your videos!

LG Display brands Tandem WOLED as their fourth generation of technology. However there have actually only been three generations of 1440p panel, and even fewer generations of the other panels.

It also gets even more confusing when using the brand names because both 1440p Tandem WOLED and the upcoming 27-inch 4K WOLED are "4th gen" even though the 4K model uses a completely different subpixel structure with different brightness spec

Samsung Display don't refer to generations any more for this reason

source_title: 1440p WOLED vs QD-OLED in 2026 - Everything You Need to Know
author: @amariel3310
text:
On the QD-OLED side it's also important to note that while not specifically marketed by Samsung until just recently (possibly today at the time of this post), all 4th generation and 5th generation QD-OLEDs are Primary True RGB Penta Tandem OLEDs, which means they are true RGB as in no other subpixels, and are penta stacked tandem or 5-layer tandem OLED. 5th Generation QD-OLED is also penta-tandem true RGB-stripe OLED, meaning it has higher text clarity compared to older generations.

The reason why QD-OLED has a tinting when touched by light is because the Quantum Dot layer on it gets activated by the presence of light interacting with it directly.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @MagnumForce51
text:
Recently upgraded to an OLED myself. The one I got is a LG 27GX704A-B. A 27 inch Tandom OLED with glossy finish. So lights reflect off it more. But since My PC/Monitor setup is under a loft bed there's not much light to reflect off. OLEDs with no anti-glare on them tend to be brighter and better blacks/contrast so that's what I got. My unit runs at 1440p at 240hz so not a full 4k display but my GTX 1060 would struggle to run games at that resolution anyways so 1440p is better for my more budget oriented machine. Heck even Fall Guys can't reach the full 240FPS the monitor can handle so I still plan to upgrade that eventually to something that should handle that. A full 4k capable video card is still way out of my price range though. :P

Before this I was mainly using a CRT monitor because yeah...LCDs just don't cut it for me. CRTs still have OLEDs beat in terms of response times and motion clarity. They also handle lower resolutions better since they are analog and don't have a native resolution. So when I did decide to upgrade it would be OLED or nothing. CRTs main disadvantage is brightness and resolution. Only really high end hard to find CRT monitors can come close to the resolutions modern OLEDs get. They also can't get to as high refresh rates...but then again CRTs were so good with motion clarity that you could easily get away with anything past like 67hz. (You start to notice flicker if you are at 60hz or less with CRTs but thankfully most of them you can run a bit faster then that to avoid it). Definite trade offs. I'd say these days CRT monitors would be great for retro setups but for the main PC in your room, OLED is the only acceptable monitors to be using in the modern age. :P

Here’s my experience with my first OLED, as I have not had these issues. I want to recommend my monitor and tell you my experience. 

Despite the recent controversy about the adware problem, I’ve been a happy LG user for years and have grown fond of the menu UI.

I recently went from an LG 165hz 27” IPS, to a 27” LG WOLED with a GLOSSY panel and 240hz (both were 1440p) 

I was looking up best settings and practices with my new monitor. I had clicked on a google ai response to one of my searches , it opened up the Google Ai site in dark mode. Vertical banding was extremely noticeable. I couldn’t believe it. I got really nervous and began to research it. 

Apparently this is common with these monitors when they are brand new , but I read it will goes away. So, I did pixel cleaning cycle, did some video editing in Davinci resolve for an hour, played a game for an hour, then BOOM. It disappeared completely, no vertical banding.

I did grey scale testing and have used the monitor a lot for a couple of weeks now. There is no vertical banding at all and hasn’t been since I spent a couple hours with it.

This monitor was on sale recently for $380 on Amazon. I think regular pricing is closer to $499? 

At 90% brightness and peak brightness set to medium even, the monitor is EXTREMELY bright. 

The color calibration is immaculate, and I see no difference in text.

I’ve played games, read articles, edited full videos, did Lightroom photo editing, and did a lot of music production work in ableton. All were fantastic experiences.

I hope this is helpful! The monitor model is 27GX704a-b … I also want to ask how long did you have the first monitor that had the banding issue?? Maybe I missed that detail, but I wonder if perhaps it had may have improved with usage as well

author: @zhizoviyMe_HDR
text: I should've waited till RGB subpixel QD-OLED if i had that subpixel issues with current QD-OLEDs, because any WOLED also has subpixel issues with clarity but not text fringing. white subpixel was supposed to help image to be better, but ruins it in every single way except the brightness. I had experience with 55" 4K LG TV which was pretty cool experience since that was specifically my first 4K experience with PC, but with time I started to notice that it was not so clear as my previous 22" monitor (or any different display*) was, and that wasn't even a PPI issue, because it was generally worse in displaying proper and clear image unlike with basic RGB screen. RGBW layout worsening picture worse than you could think, with this layout picture looks like it's being drawn diagonally instead of normally. basic pixel size divided 1/3 horizontally, so they're look like squares or circle dots on distance, but with RGBW\RWGB layout it's still being drawn to basic 1/3 horizontally layout, but there's another subpixel left, which being combined with next 2 subpixels and they don't even disturb each other*, but it's vertical alignment isn't normal, it's diagonal, for which reason horizontal white *or any color lines, will look normal, but vertical ones will be thicker twice, and it will be noticeable that two line diagonal stepped lines, which ruining not only text clarity, but the whole picture clarity even on distance, unlike with QD-OLEDs which have their own subpixel layout, but it's proportions still fits in normal 1x1 pixel size, and in games or in movies it will be better in terms of clarity and even colors because also the W-subpixel of WOLED or any RGBW* panel, changes color reproduction. so the calibration, precision, deepness and vibrance of colors are allways better on QD-OLEDs (but theres also technical dependencies and production methods that really impact on that factors*) and still QD-OLED is better overall, while to avoid text fringing on QD-OLEDs I'd recommend to use 150% scaling (which equal to 1440p 27" in case with 2160p 27"), and use it at distance over 40centimeters or 15,748inches .

author: @haewymetal
text:
What the video doesnt tell you because HUB doesnt go indepth anymore and arent as honest as they used to be: 
WOLED: vertical banding against dark gray
QDOLED: grid pattern + vibrating vertical scanlines (short ones) against very dark colors and gray (especially in motion, even more so in slower panning)
Also the picture shown at 21:30 is what 3rd gen and 3.5gen qdoleds look like, you see those thin horizontal lines + vertical lines? WOLED only have vertical ones, that photo shows thousands of horizontal lines aswell. What you'll see on a QDOLEDs grid like pattern in dark colors and dary gray such as <5% gray.
Very visible in Dead Island 2 in the HAUS DLC location in the interior Forest with all the gray fog around. Visible on: 271QRX, XG27ACDNG, XG27AQDP, 32M2C8900, 34M2C6500, not visible on: XG27AQWMG, XG27AQDMG or LG C4/C5. If youre curious as to what Im speaking of google: qdoled vibrating vertical lines and you'll see a few results from reddit with video and image examples of said vibrating lines and im not talking about moire effect.

source_title: My 7 Problems With Lenovo’s Legion 5 Gaming Laptop
author: @mistarbeanz
text:
Jarrod - I have a question in regards to this laptop.  So I bought this laptop (Legion 5, Ryzen 5800H, RTX 3060, 144hz 17" screen) and the problem I have with it is that the spec sheet says the laptop panel itself supports Freesync which means that it support variable refresh rate.  However, as far as I can tell, this is absolutely not true and a complete misrepresentation of the product by Lenovo.  I simply cannot get the laptop panel to enable Freesync at all.  It doesn't matter if I'm in hybrid mode and using the AMD drivers, or in non-hybrid mode and using the NVidia drivers.  Both drivers simply act as though the 17" laptop panel does not have Freesync capabilities.  What I believe is reality is that the laptop display supports EITHER 60Hz or 144Hz, but no in between.

For example, if I play Rocket League on the laptop dispaly and I limit the refresh rate in the in game settings to 120fps, I should still have a very smooth experience if the laptop display support VRR and sync's the Hz to FPS.  However, it is noticeably choppy even though the game is easily locked at 120fps.  If I connect the laptop to my external g-sync monitor and perform the same test, this same 120fps is silky smooth.

I think this is a massive issue with the laptop and should be called out on Lenovo's part as they are straight up lying about their product.  Otherwise, the laptop is fantastic and I love it, but I'm sorely disappointed that they led me to believe the laptop panel supports Freesync when it clearly does not.

The downside to this situation is that unless you can keep your game locked to 144fps then you will have a very choppy and poor experience.  You are almost better off setting the laptop display to 60hz and playing it that way.

So long story short, here's my question.  Does your Legion 5 laptop display support Freesync?  Are you able to enable it in either the AMD drivers or NVidia drivers?  As far as I can tell, this is impossible.

author: @BlindEmperor25
text:
Just one thing. It is very important when using SDR (rec 709 color space) to clamp these panels into that color space acordingly in order to prevent oversaturation of colors. Since sRGB modes on these OLED monitors are usually broken (essential options are locked out or gamma is not set correctly) you have novideo.srgb for NVIDIA cards and color clamp for AMD in their control panel.

As far as BURN-IN goes, OLED panels use organic, flurescent light emitters so degradation is inevitable, however, people think that burn-in is directly related to degradation, when in reality it is simply a result of UNEVEN panel wear which makes it apparent in real life usage. So think of it like this. Degradataion is inevitable and expected, and all these panel protections do is work around it to make it as even across the screen as possible. So as long as you dont play competitive games for thousands of hours and/or use static elements on your screen (like desktop icons, taskbar, browser title bar etc) you should not expect to have uneven/localized pixel wear (burn-in). But yo udo have to take precautions like hiding taskbar, if not hiding, then at least shifting desktop icons form time to time and when browsing either using ful lscreen mode or using windowed mode and moving it yourself from time to time. DArk/black theme is not really as important as even pixel wear. Bu using a black theme everywhere you will maybe save couple of wats of electricity, but if you have bright static elements you will cause uneven ware one way or another.

source_title: How OLED Ruined Me
author: @Acroanidd
text:
I got an OLED monitor last year and was blown away by the response time. I was well prepared for image quality, that wasn't the shocker. But every single frame being picture perfect and running super smooth was what surprised me the most. Shooters without any ghosting at all was strange. Even crazier was the racing games where the chain link fence on the side would typically be a blurry mess no matter how good your LCD was, on OLED it was crystal clear like i was there. It's hard to put into words. I have since upgraded my home theater to have an OLED TV as well.

Edit: I just noticed the LOTR poster in the background... respect!
